For completeness, its conjugacy class sizes are \(1,3,2\); the quotient of its three-point permutation representation by the constants has character \(\tau=(2,0,-1)\). Its squared norm is \((4+2)/6=1\), proving irreducibility, and the squares of the three dimensions sum to six, proving completeness by finite-group orthogonality. Put \(F=(1-2\epsilon+2\tau)/3\). Orthogonality gives \(F(1)=1\), \(\|F\|^2=(1+4+4)/9=1\), but its coefficients are not integers. This illustrates why the coefficient and representation conclusions require more than the real Gram identities above.

Example 6.238 — an inseparable quartic fibre and a rank-four height limit. Let \(F=\mathbb F_2((t))\), let \(D\) have degree four, and write its cyclic model as \(\Pi a=a^2\Pi\) on \(\mathbb F_{16}\), \(\Pi^4=t\). Put \(E=\mathbb F_2((\Pi))\), \(s=\Pi I_4\), \(p(T)=T^4-t\), and \(P=p^4\). The valuation \(v_F(\Pi)=1/4\) proves that \(p\) is irreducible. Then \(E/F\) is purely inseparable of degree four, \(\Delta=E\), \(Q=2,m=4,a_E=4\). The four nonclosed partitions and their proper block sizes are \[ \begin{array}{c|c} (4)&(1,1,1,1)\\ (3,1)&(2,1,1)\\ (2,2)&(2,2)\\ (2,1,1)&(3,1). \end{array} \qquad \eta_s=-\frac{21}{16},\quad g_{P,(1^4)}(\gamma)=-\frac{16}{21e(F[\gamma]/F)}. \tag{6.523} \] All four have zero compact discrete-test and Euler orbitals. The elliptic character formula is \(\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})=-16O_s(f^\circ_{\pi,m_0,P})/21\). The Steinberg elliptic character is \(-1\), by (6.280) and (6.309) on regular orbits. Consequently its compact discrete test has closed orbital \(21/16\). This calculation uses the compact germ formula, without asserting an ordinary orbital value for its noncompact matrix coefficient at \(s\).

Here the extreme-height estimate of Theorem 6.223 cannot be extended to rank four. Write \(\mathbb F_{16}=\mathbb F_2[z]/(z^4+z+1)\), set \(\xi=z^3\), and \(v=(\xi,\xi^2,\xi^4,\xi^8)^t\). The four entries are \(z^3,z^3+z^2,z^3+z^2+z+1,z^3+z\); their differences recover \(z^3,z^2,z,1\), so they are \(\mathbb F_2\)-independent. The polynomial is irreducible: it has no \(\mathbb F_2\)-root and has remainder one modulo the only irreducible quadratic \(T^2+T+1\).

Let \(\sigma(x)=x^2\), and take the columns of \(K\) to be \(\sigma^2v,\sigma^3v,\sigma v,v\). The Moore argument of Theorem 6.192 makes \(K\) invertible. Entrywise Frobenius permutes them by the cycle \((1\ 2\ 4\ 3)\), so \(K^{-1}\sigma(K)=P\) for that permutation matrix. For every \(n\ge1\), \[ \begin{gathered} g_n=K\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^{3n},\Pi^{2n},\Pi^n,1),\qquad \Sigma g_nL_0=L_0,\\ \text{relative Cartan list}=(2n,n,-n,-2n),\qquad \rho_G=7n,\quad \sigma_G=4n. \end{gathered} \tag{6.524} \] Normalization follows from the independent residue coordinates of its last column. The relative matrix is exactly \(\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^{-\lambda_i})P\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^{\lambda_i})\), \(\lambda=(3n,2n,n,0)\). Its monomial entry valuations are \(n,2n,-2n,-n\), giving (6.524) by permutation and unit elimination. Thus \(\max(a,c)=2n\), while the greatest quotient length is \(3n\); no fixed additive constant repairs the rank-three extreme-height inequality for this family. The compact germ and finite character conclusions above do not depend on that inequality.

Figure 19. Example 6.238 gives the exact monomial matrix, its four entry valuations and its sorted Cartan list. The arrows record the column permutation, with labels \(\lambda_j-\lambda_i\); their Euclidean lengths have no metric meaning. Lemma 6.229 and Theorem 6.230 use the proper primary blocks instead of the false rank-four extreme-height extension.

Figure 20. Theorem 6.234 bounds the elliptic Gram approximation and realizes it by compact regular-support traces. Corollary 6.236 identifies the complementary trace limit exactly. The small table is the additive measure example (6.522), whose all-index formula proves the distinction between fixed-index convergence and the uniform condition (6.518).

These arguments concern ordinary orbitals, compact germs, elliptic character functions and the stated trace limits. They do not supply a general locally integrable character density across singular elements. For the positive-characteristic scope and slice-comparison difficulties, see Aizenbud–Gourevitch–Kazhdan–Sayag's free preprint, §1.1 and Appendix B. For the limitation of fixed-space dimension estimates, see Meyer–Solleveld's free author paper, §8. All estimates and implications used in this section are proved above or in the exact preceding results cited in their proofs.

6.40 Euler profiles, smooth transfer and elliptic trace duality

Let \(F\) be a nonarchimedean local field of either characteristic, let \(D/F\) have degree \(d\), and put \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), \(N=rd\). Let \(\mathcal D/F\) be the division algebra of invariant \(1/N\). Fix a smooth unitary central character \(\omega\). Write \(\mathcal H_\omega(G)\) for the smooth functions compact modulo \(Z=F^\times\) satisfying \(f(zg)=\omega(z)^{-1}f(g)\), with convolution on \(G/Z\). Its algebraic cocenter is \[ \overline{\mathcal H}_\omega(G) =\mathcal H_\omega(G)/[\mathcal H_\omega(G),\mathcal H_\omega(G)], \tag{6.525} \] where the denominator is the linear span of finite convolution commutators. The involution is \(f^*(g)=\overline{f(g^{-1})}\). All assertions about this quotient concern finite sums; no closure of the commutator space is taken.

Give the standard maximal compact subgroups of the two groups volume one and \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) volume one. Thus \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal D^\times/Z)=N\). On an elliptic regular centralizer, the superscript \(\mathrm{unit}\) means that its quotient by \(Z\) has volume one. At a closed primary element, the superscript \(\mathrm{mc}\) means the centralizer maximal-compact normalization of Theorem 6.157. These conventions are different even on some regular elements.

Lemma 6.239 — separation by all ordinary orbitals. In every division rank, a function \(f\in\mathcal H_\omega(G)\) represents zero in (6.525) if and only if \(O_x(f)=0\) for every \(x\in G\). Consequently every admissible representation trace vanishes on such an \(f\).

Proof. First work with compactly supported functions. On the closed polynomial fibre \(X_P=\chi^{-1}(P)\), Theorem 6.141 proves that the finitely many ordinary orbital measures are a basis of all invariant linear functionals on \(C_c^\infty(X_P)\). If all orbital values of \(f\) vanish, its restriction to each fibre is zero in the fibre coinvariants. Indeed any nonzero vector in a vector-space quotient is detected by a linear functional on that quotient.

Lemma 6.91 gives a compact open coefficient neighborhood \(W_P\) on which \(f\) is a finite sum of conjugation differences. The compact set \(\chi(\operatorname{supp}f)\) has a finite such cover. Refine this cover to a finite disjoint compact open partition of a neighborhood of that set. Multiplying a local identity by its coefficient-piece characteristic function commutes with conjugation and preserves compact support. The sum of these finitely many identities expresses \(f\) globally as a finite sum \(\sum_j(\operatorname{Ad}(g_j)v_j-v_j)\).

Each conjugation difference is a convolution commutator. Choose a compact open \(J\) for which \(v\) is bi-\(J\)-invariant, and write \(e_J=1_J/\operatorname{vol}(J)\). In the convolution multiplier notation, \[ a=\delta_g*e_J,\qquad b=v*\delta_{g^{-1}},\qquad a*b-b*a=\operatorname{Ad}(g)v-v. \tag{6.526} \] Both \(a,b\) are actual compact smooth functions; the delta symbols only describe their translates. Conversely Theorem 6.140 says that every ordinary orbital functional annihilates every commutator.

For a function compact modulo \(Z\), put \(f^\circ=1_{\{0\le v_F(\operatorname{Nrd}g)<N\}}f\). This is compact. Since the cutoff is invariant under conjugation, all its orbital values vanish. Apply the compact assertion and then the central pushforward \[ P_\omega a(g)=\int_Z\omega(z)a(zg)\,dz. \tag{6.527} \] There is exactly one central valuation taking \(g\) into this annulus, and the central units have volume one, so \(P_\omega f^\circ=f\). The pushforward preserves finite conjugation differences. Formula (6.526) holds in the fixed-central-character algebra as well, with the central pushforward of the small-subgroup identity. This proves the required cocenter assertion. Admissibility makes the operators attached to these functions finite rank, so their traces are cyclic. \(\square\)

The lemma uses ordinary orbitals at every element. It asserts no density theorem involving only regular orbitals.

Lemma 6.240 — the division orbital profile. For \(f\in\mathcal H_\omega(\mathcal D^\times)\), define the unnormalized average \[ A_f(b)=\int_{\mathcal D^\times/Z}f(x^{-1}bx)\,d\bar x. \tag{6.528} \] It is a smooth conjugation-invariant function with central rule \(\omega^{-1}\). On a regular element, \(A_f(b)=O_b^{\mathrm{unit}}(f)\). If \(E=F[b]\), \(e=[E:F]\), and \(a_E=e(E/F)\), then \[ O_b^{\mathrm{mc}}(f)=\eta_b^{\mathcal D}A_f(b), \qquad \eta_b^{\mathcal D}=\frac1{a_E(N/e)}. \tag{6.529} \] The function \(A_f\) descends to a locally constant function of the reduced polynomial on the set of primary degree-\(N\) polynomials.

Proof. Conjugation preserves quotient Haar measure and central translation gives the stated rule. A sufficiently deep normal principal subgroup \(U\subset\mathcal D^\times\) fixes \(f\) on both sides. Its normality implies \(A_f(bu)=A_f(b)\) for \(u\in U\), so the average is smooth. Such a \(U\) exists by compactness modulo the centre and the division valuation model.

The centralizer of \(b\) is a division algebra over \(E\) of degree \(\delta'=N/e\). Give its unit group volume one. Its quotient by \(Z\) has volume \(a_E\delta'\): the division valuation takes \(F^\times\) onto \(a_E\delta'\mathbb Z\), and the unit quotient has volume one. Disintegrating (6.528) along that quotient proves (6.529). At a regular element, replacing this centralizer measure by the measure of quotient volume one gives \(O_b^{\mathrm{unit}}(f)=A_f(b)\).

Let \(C=\bigcup_{j=0}^{N-1}\Pi_{\mathcal D}^j\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}^\times\). This is compact and conjugation invariant. Its polynomial image \(X\) is compact, and each fibre is a single conjugacy class, by Lemma 6.137 with division rank one. A continuous surjection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a quotient map: images of closed subsets are compact and hence closed. Thus \(A_f|_C\) descends continuously to \(X\). It has finite image; the descended function is therefore locally constant.

Every reduced polynomial in this division group is \(p^{N/e}\), where \(p\) is the irreducible minimal polynomial and \(e=\deg p\mid N\). Conversely Theorem 6.165 embeds the field \(F[T]/p\) into \(\mathcal D\), including when it is inseparable. Its image generator has this reduced polynomial. Consequently \(X\) is exactly the primary-polynomial set in the annulus \(0\le v_F(c_N)<N\). Central scaling gives the assertion everywhere. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.241 — extending a polynomial profile. Let \(Y\) be the space of monic degree-\(N\) polynomials with nonzero constant term. There exists a locally constant function \(\Phi_f:Y\to\mathbb C\) which agrees with \(A_f\) on all primary polynomials and satisfies \[ \Phi_f(z\cdot P)=\omega(z)^{-1}\Phi_f(P),\qquad z\cdot P=T^N+zc_1T^{N-1}+\cdots+z^Nc_N. \tag{6.530} \] On any prescribed finite-dimensional space of division tests the extensions can be chosen linearly.

Proof. On the annulus \(Y_0=\{0\le v_F(c_N)<N\}\), extend the finite-valued locally constant profile on the compact closed subset \(X\) to a compactly supported locally constant function \(\Phi_0\). Explicitly, partition \(X\) into its finitely many compact open value sets, choose pairwise disjoint compact open neighborhoods of those sets in \(Y_0\), and extend by the respective values, taking zero elsewhere. The neighborhood construction is precisely the compact-open extension argument of Lemma 6.91.

Average over central units: \[ \Phi_1(P)=\int_{\mathcal O_F^\times}\omega(u)\Phi_0(u\cdot P)\,du. \tag{6.531} \] The set \(X\) is stable under these units. There the integrand is the constant \(A_f(P)\), so \(\Phi_1=A_f\). Changing variables proves unit covariance. Compactness of the unit group makes this average compactly supported and locally constant: on each compact integration set a finite cover supplies a common constancy neighborhood.

For \(\ell=v_F(c_N)\), set \(k=\lfloor\ell/N\rfloor\), \(P_0=\varpi_F^{-k}\cdot P\), and define \(\Phi_f(P)=\omega(\varpi_F)^{-k}\Phi_1(P_0)\). The valuation annuli are open and closed, so this is locally constant. Writing any scalar as a unit times a uniformizer power proves (6.530). For finitely many basis tests take one common finite partition of \(X\), extend its characteristic functions, and perform these linear operations. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.242 — smooth transfer from a division group in every degree. In every division rank and both field characteristics, every \(f\in\mathcal H_\omega(\mathcal D^\times)\) has a matching test on \(G\). One such test is \[ T f(g)=\Phi_f(\chi_g)\mathfrak e_G(g). \tag{6.532} \] It satisfies \[ O_\gamma^{\mathrm{unit}}(Tf)=O_b^{\mathrm{unit}}(f) \quad(\gamma\leftrightarrow b\text{ elliptic regular}), \qquad O_\gamma(Tf)=0 \quad(\gamma\text{ nonelliptic regular}). \tag{6.533} \] For every closed primary pair \(s\leftrightarrow b\) with the same reduced polynomial, \[ \frac{O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}(Tf)}{\eta_s^G} =A_f(b) =\frac{O_b^{\mathrm{mc}}(f)}{\eta_b^{\mathcal D}}, \qquad \eta_s^G=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(q_\Delta^j-1)} {a_E m\delta}\ne0. \tag{6.534} \] Here the closed centralizer is \(\mathrm{GL}_m(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}})\) over \(E=F[s]\), and \(\deg_E\Delta=\delta\). The support of every test (6.532), modulo \(Z\), lies in the fixed compact support of \(\mathfrak e_G\).

There is also ordinary compact-test transfer: for every \(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathcal D^\times)\), a compactly supported locally constant coefficient extension in (6.532) gives \(Tf\in C_c^\infty(G)\) satisfying (6.533)–(6.534).

Proof. Lemma 6.241 and the Euler test show that (6.532) is smooth, compact modulo \(Z\), and has the required central rule. The polynomial factor is constant on each orbit. Theorem 6.122 and Lemma 6.240 give (6.533). Every division regular class has a match by Theorem 6.2; all unmatched regular classes of \(G\) are nonelliptic. At a closed primary element the same factorization, Theorem 6.157 and (6.529) give (6.534). The embedding criterion in Theorem 6.165 guarantees a division element with this polynomial. All orbital integrations here are of compact-mod-centre tests and converge by Theorem 6.139.

For the ordinary compact assertion, (6.528) is defined without any central covariance condition. Its support is compact: conjugation factors through the compact space \(\mathcal D^\times/Z\), so the union of conjugates of \(\operatorname{supp}f\) is the continuous image of a compact product. The division polynomial map is proper. Indeed a compact coefficient set has its nonzero constant-term valuations in a finite set; its inverse image is closed inside a finite union of compact sets \(\Pi_{\mathcal D}^j\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}^\times\). A proper continuous map of these spaces is closed: near a coefficient point choose a compact neighborhood, and use compactness of its inverse image to see that the image of a closed subset is closed there. Its primary-polynomial image is therefore closed in \(Y\), and it is a quotient map onto that image. As in Lemma 6.240, the compactly supported smooth conjugacy average descends to a compactly supported locally constant profile on this image. Extend it to \(C_c^\infty(Y)\) by Lemma 6.91.

The product in (6.532) now has ordinary compact support. Choose compact representatives for the Euler support modulo \(Z\). On their central translates, requiring the polynomial to lie in a fixed compact subset of \(Y\) restricts the central valuation to finitely many integers, since the constant term scales by \(z^N\). Central units are compact. Thus the support is closed in a finite union of compact sets. The same orbit factorization proves (6.533)–(6.534). \(\square\)

Define the subspace \[ \mathcal V_\omega(G)=\{f\in\mathcal H_\omega(G): O_x(f)=0\text{ on every orbit outside the closed primary orbits}\}. \tag{6.535} \] This condition concerns singular as well as regular elements. All commutators belong to this subspace by Theorem 6.140.

Proposition 6.243 — a canonical cocenter map in division ranks at most four. Suppose \(r\le4\). Formula (6.532) defines a linear map \[ \overline T:\overline{\mathcal H}_\omega(\mathcal D^\times) \longrightarrow \mathcal V_\omega(G)/[\mathcal H_\omega(G),\mathcal H_\omega(G)], \tag{6.536} \] independent of the extension in Lemma 6.241, and commuting with the involution.

Proof. For \(r\le3\), Corollary 6.226 gives all the proper-orbit Euler zeros. For \(r=4\), Lemma 6.229 gives them. Therefore \(Tf\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\). If two extensions agree on the primary-polynomial set, their difference times \(\mathfrak e_G\) has zero value on every primary orbit. On every other orbit its ordinary orbital is zero by these Euler zeros. Lemma 6.239 identifies their cocenter classes. The same argument with \(A_f=0\) shows dependence only on the division cocenter class. Applying it to a sum of extensions proves linearity.

The Euler test is self-adjoint: each stabilizer is inverse invariant and its real permutation sign has the same value at an element and its inverse. Let \(P^\iota\) be the reduced polynomial of \(g^{-1}\) when \(P=\chi_g\); its coefficients are rational expressions in those of \(P\), with nonzero denominator \(c_N\). Then \(\overline{\Phi_f(P^\iota)}\) is an allowed extension of \(A_{f^*}\). This proves the assertion about involution. In particular a self-adjoint division test has a self-adjoint representative of its image, by replacing \(Tf\) with \((Tf+(Tf)^*)/2\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.244 — the inverse profile and cocenter isomorphism. For \(r\le4\) and \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), the regular profile \[ B_f(b)=O_{\gamma_b}^{\mathrm{unit}}(f) \quad(b\text{ regular in }\mathcal D^\times) \tag{6.537} \] extends uniquely to a smooth class function on all of \(\mathcal D^\times\), with central rule \(\omega^{-1}\). At a primary polynomial \(P=\chi_b=\chi_s\), its value is \[ B_f(b)=\frac{O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}(f)}{\eta_s^G}. \qquad S f=\frac1N B_f. \tag{6.538} \] The maps induced by \(S,T\) are mutually inverse linear isomorphisms between the two spaces in (6.536).

Proof. Cut \(f\) to the compact reduced-norm annulus containing \(P\). In (6.326), every coefficient outside the closed primary orbit is zero by the definition of \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\). For \(r\le3\), the closed germ is Theorem 6.166 and the consequences of Corollary 6.226; for \(r=4\), it is Theorem 6.230. The volume-one torus conversion gives, on nearby elliptic regular elements, exactly the constant \(O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}(f)/\eta_s^G\). Apply this at every division element \(b\). The constants agree on overlaps because the regular division set is dense, by the nonzero discriminant polynomial. They therefore define the unique smooth extension in (6.538). Conjugation invariance and central covariance follow by the same density argument. Compactness of the division group modulo \(Z\) makes \(Sf\) a test function.

Since \(B_f\) is a class function and the quotient volume is \(N\), (6.528) gives \(A_{Sf}=B_f\). Formula (6.534) shows that \(T(Sf)\) and \(f\) have the same ordinary orbital at every closed primary element. Both vanish at every other orbit, so Lemma 6.239 gives \([T(Sf)]=[f]\).

In the other direction, the continuous extension of (6.533) gives \(S(Ta)=A_a/N\). Choose a normal principal subgroup \(U\) fixing \(a\). The conjugation action factors through the finite set \(\mathcal D^\times/ZU\); thus \(A_a/N\) is a finite probability average of conjugates of \(a\). Its difference from \(a\) is a finite sum of conjugation differences, hence is zero in the division cocenter. This proves \([S(Ta)]=[a]\), and the asserted inverse maps follow. The isomorphism is linear; no multiplicative property is asserted. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.245 — elliptic linear independence. For \(r\le4\), the restrictions of the discrete-series characters of central character \(\omega\) to the elliptic regular set of \(G\) are linearly independent. In particular a discrete-series representation with a prescribed elliptic transfer character, if it exists, is unique.

Proof. Suppose \(\sum_{\pi\in\Pi}c_\pi\Theta_\pi(\gamma)=0\) on the elliptic regular set, with \(\Pi\) finite. Let \(f_\pi\) be the compact discrete tests of (6.267). They belong to \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), by Corollary 6.226 and Lemma 6.229. Theorem 6.120 gives \(O_\gamma^{\mathrm{unit}}(\sum c_\pi f_\pi)=\sum c_\pi\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})=0\). Thus the inverse profile is zero, and Theorem 6.244 makes this sum a finite commutator sum. Its actual trace on any \(\sigma\in\Pi\) is zero by Lemma 6.239 and is \(c_\sigma\) by (6.267). All coefficients vanish. Applying this to a difference proves uniqueness. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.246 — exact finite trace duality. Suppose \(r\le4\), and let \(\Pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k)\) be a nonempty finite list of distinct discrete series with central character \(\omega\). Set \(\epsilon_r=(-1)^{r-1}\). By Theorem 6.231 there is a finite set \(K\) of division irreducibles containing all their expansion supports, and a real matrix \(A=(a_{i\rho})\), such that \[ F_i(b)=\epsilon_r\Theta_{\pi_i}(\gamma_b) =\sum_{\rho\in K}a_{i\rho}\chi_\rho(b). \tag{6.539} \] Let \(p_\rho=N^{-1}\overline{\chi_\rho}\), and choose a self-adjoint transfer representative \(t_\rho\) as in Proposition 6.243. Define \[ B_{i\rho}=\epsilon_r\operatorname{Tr}\pi_i(t_\rho). \quad B\in M_{k,|K|}(\mathbb R),\qquad BA^{\mathsf t}=I_k. \tag{6.540} \] The elliptic Gram matrix \(H=AA^{\mathsf t}\) is positive definite and satisfies \[ \lambda_{\min}(H)\ge \|B\|_{\mathrm F}^{-2}>0. \tag{6.541} \]

Proof. Lemma 6.240 gives \(A_{p_\rho}=\overline{\chi_\rho}\). Unitary inversion and the reality of the coefficients in (6.539) imply \[ S f_{\pi_j}=\epsilon_r\sum_{\rho\in K}a_{j\rho}p_\rho, \qquad [f_{\pi_j}]=\epsilon_r\sum_{\rho\in K}a_{j\rho}[t_\rho]. \tag{6.542} \] The first identity is an equality of actual division functions, first on the dense regular set and then everywhere. The second follows from Theorem 6.244. Taking the actual trace on \(\pi_i\) and using (6.267) proves (6.540). Self-adjointness and unitarity make these traces real. Each is the trace of a finite-dimensional operator on the fixed vectors of a sufficiently small common compact open subgroup.

For any \(c\in\mathbb R^k\), (6.540) gives \(\|c\|=\|BA^{\mathsf t}c\|\le\|B\|_{\mathrm F}\|A^{\mathsf t}c\|\). The matrix \(B\) is nonzero because \(k>0\). Squaring proves (6.541) and positive definiteness. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.247 — exact separation by regular-support tests. With the preceding hypotheses, for all sufficiently large \(n\), the actual trace matrix \(H_n\) of Theorem 6.234 is invertible. The tests \[ g_{i,n}=\sum_{j=1}^k(H_n^{-1})_{ji}\,\zeta_n f_{\pi_j} \quad\text{satisfy}\quad \operatorname{Tr}\pi_\ell(g_{i,n})=\delta_{\ell i}. \tag{6.543} \] They are compact modulo \(Z\), supported in the regular set, have zero ordinary orbital on every nonelliptic regular class, and can be taken at levels \(m_n\le dn+C\).

Proof. Put \(M_i=\|F_i\|_\infty\). For \(N>1\), Theorem 6.234 bounds each entry error by \(B_NM_iM_jq_F^{-n/[N(N-1)]}\). Cauchy–Schwarz therefore bounds the operator norm of \(H-H_n\) by \(B_N(\sum_iM_i^2)q_F^{-n/[N(N-1)]}\). Choose \(n\) so that this is less than half the lower bound in (6.541). For a unit vector \(c\), the quadratic form of \(H_n\) is then at least \(\tfrac{1}{2}\|B\|_{\mathrm F}^{-2}\). Thus \(H_n\) is invertible. Formula (6.543) is matrix multiplication of actual traces, not an integral across a singular fibre. All the support, orbital and level assertions hold for its summands by Theorem 6.234 and hence for their finite linear combinations. For \(N=1\), \(\zeta_n=1\) and \(H_n=H\), so the conclusion is immediate. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.248 — the complementary trace of a transfer test. For the same finite sets, let \(a_{i\rho}(n)=\int_{\mathrm{ell}}\zeta_n F_i\overline{\chi_\rho}\,d\nu\). Then \[ \epsilon_r\operatorname{Tr}\pi_i(\zeta_n t_\rho)=a_{i\rho}(n), \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty}\epsilon_r\operatorname{Tr}\pi_i((1-\zeta_n)t_\rho) =B_{i\rho}-a_{i\rho}, \qquad I_k-H=(B-A)A^{\mathsf t}. \tag{6.544} \] For \(N>1\), the error in the trace limit is at most \(B_NM_i\dim\rho\,q_F^{-n/[N(N-1)]}\).

Proof. The test \(\zeta_n t_\rho\) is supported away from the singular set. The regular trace formula of Theorem 6.70 and the Weyl formula apply, after the compact norm-annulus cut and central pushforward used in Theorem 6.234. Its elliptic ordinary orbital is \(\zeta_n\overline{\chi_\rho}\), and its nonelliptic ordinary orbital is zero by (6.533). This proves the first identity. Theorem 6.233 and \(|\chi_\rho|\le\dim\rho\) give the stated error relative to \(a_{i\rho}\). Subtract from the actual trace defining \(B\). Finally subtract \(AA^{\mathsf t}\) from \(BA^{\mathsf t}=I_k\). For \(N=1\) the complementary test is zero. \(\square\)

Example 6.249 — two different closed-orbit factors. In Example 6.238 take \(G=\mathrm{GL}_4(D)\) with \(\deg D=4\), and let \(\mathcal D\) have degree \(N=16\). The quartic purely inseparable field \(E/F\) has \(a_E=4\). At \(s=\Pi I_4\), the \(G\)-centralizer has \(m=4,\delta=1,q_\Delta=2\). The corresponding division centralizer has degree \(16/4=4\) over \(E\). Consequently \[ \eta_s^G=-\frac{21}{16},\qquad \eta_b^{\mathcal D}=\frac1{16}. \tag{6.545} \] For trivial central character let \(f=1/16\) on \(\mathcal D^\times\). Its trace in the trivial representation is one. Since the quotient volume is 16, \(A_f=1\). We may take \(\Phi_f=1\), so \(Tf=\mathfrak e_G\). Both volume-one regular elliptic orbitals equal one. The two closed orbitals in (6.545) differ, while both Euler-normalized values in (6.534) equal one. This is a test-function identity.

Example 6.250 — duality does not imply orthogonality. The real matrices \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\[1pt]\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&2\end{pmatrix} \tag{6.546} \] satisfy \(BA^{\mathsf t}=I_2\), whereas \(AA^{\mathsf t}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\ne I_2\). Its smaller eigenvalue is \((3-\sqrt5)/4>1/6=\|B\|_{\mathrm F}^{-2}\). Both rows of \(A\) have sum one, as a central dimension constraint with dimension vector \((1,1)\) would require. This is an example of finite real matrices; no assertion that they arise from discrete-series representations is made.

Theorem 6.242 proves smooth test transfer from the degree-\(N\) division group to every degree-\(N\) inner form. Theorems 6.244–6.247 prove the stated cocenter isomorphism, elliptic independence and finite regular-support trace separation for \(r\le4\). Full discrete-series character transfer also requires existence and the irreducible character identity. In particular the vanishing of the complementary traces in (6.544), elliptic orthogonality and individual coefficient integrality are not consequences of the dual-matrix identity alone. The higher-rank closed Schwartz estimates and the general number-field and function-field representation transfers have their own additional hypotheses and arguments.

6.41 Finite Jacquet traces and cancellation along the central flat

Fix a proper standard parabolic \(P=MN\) of \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), with \(M=\prod_{i=1}^s\mathrm{GL}_{r_i}(D)\), \(s\ge2\). Retain the scalar centre \(Z=F^\times\) of \(G\) when considering representations of \(M\). In particular \(\mathcal H_\omega(M)\) below means compact support modulo this \(Z\), with the prescribed inverse central rule; it does not impose a character on the whole centre of \(M\). Use probability measure on \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\), on \(K_M=K\cap M\), and on the integral subgroup of \(N\). Define the normalized constant term \[ R_P f(m)=\delta_P(m)^{1/2} \int_K\int_N f(k^{-1}mnk)\,dn\,dk. \tag{6.547} \] It is a compact-mod-\(Z\) smooth function by Corollary 6.140. The normalized Jacquet module is \(r_PV=\delta_P^{-1/2}\otimes V_N\).

Lemma 6.251 — a finite model for a principal Jacquet module. Let \(J=1+\mathfrak p_D^lM_r(\mathcal O_D)\), with \(l\ge1\) sufficiently large that \(\omega\) is trivial on \(J\cap Z\). Put \(J_M=J\cap M\), \(J_N=J\cap N\), and choose \(k_1,\ldots,k_t\in K\) for \[ (P\cap K)\backslash K/J,\qquad t\,\operatorname{vol}(ZJ/Z) =\operatorname{vol}(ZJ_M/Z)\operatorname{vol}(J_N). \tag{6.548} \] The normalized Jacquet module of the principal projective is \[ r_P\bigl(\mathcal H_\omega(G)e_J\bigr) \simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^t\mathcal H_\omega(M)e_{J_M}. \tag{6.549} \] Its coordinates are the actual integrals \[ q_i f(m)=\delta_P(m)^{1/2} \int_N f(mnk_i)\,dn. \tag{6.550} \] Here \(e_J,e_{J_M}\) are the central pushforwards of the probability subgroup identities. The functor \(r_P\) is exact and sends finitely generated projectives to finitely generated projectives.

Proof: cosets and volumes. The Iwasawa factorization gives \(G=PK\): intersect a flag with the standard integral lattice and adapt an integral basis successively to these saturated submodules, using the valuation elimination of Lemma 6.4. This proves \(G=KP\), and inversion gives \(G=PK\). The Gaussian factorization of \(J\) is the one in Section 6.6, (6.41)–(6.42). Since \(J\) is normal in \(K\), the sets \((P\cap K)k_iJ\) are the equal-mass cosets of the open subgroup \((P\cap K)J\) in \(K\). Reduction modulo \(J\) gives \[ |(P\cap K)/(P\cap J)| =|K_M/J_M|\ |(N\cap K)/J_N|. \] Taking reciprocal indices proves the volume identity in (6.548) before central quotient. Dividing both the \(J\) and \(J_M\) volumes by \(\operatorname{vol}(J\cap Z)\) proves it after that quotient.

Each integral (6.550) is compact modulo \(Z\) and right \(J_M\)-invariant. To see the support assertion, intersect the compact-mod-\(Z\) support of \(f\) with the closed set \(Pk_i\), and use the continuous factorization \(P=M N\). This gives compact sets of \(M/Z\) and \(N\) containing every contributing coordinate. Conjugating \(J_M\) through \(k_i\) stays inside \(J\), proving the right invariance. Left \(N\)-translation leaves (6.550) unchanged; normalized left \(M\)-translation becomes ordinary left translation on its value. Thus it defines a map from the stated Jacquet module.

Put \[ v_i(g)=t^{-1}e_J(gk_i^{-1}). \tag{6.551} \] Distinct pieces \(Pk_iJ\) are disjoint. Formula (6.548) therefore gives \(q_jv_i=\delta_{ij}e_{J_M}\). The \(M\)-translates of \(e_{J_M}\) span its principal module, so the coordinate map is surjective.

Proof: the kernel and exactness. The unipotent group \(N\) is an increasing union of compact open subgroups \(N_a\): conjugate its integral subgroup by successive inverse powers of a strictly contracting block-scalar element. Every bounded subset of \(N\) lies in one \(N_a\). For a smooth vector, compact averaging is a finite sum of translates, and its difference from that vector is a finite sum of \(N\)-translation differences. Consequently \[ v=0\text{ in }V_N \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e_{N_a}v=0 \text{ for some }a. \tag{6.552} \] The forward implication follows by putting the finitely many translation relations and their vectors into one larger \(N_a\); the reverse implication follows from the averaging observation. The same averaging lifts a vector through any surjection and preserves injections. Taking the directed union proves exactness of coinvariants, hence of \(r_P\).

If all \(q_if\) are zero, write the values on each piece using left-\(N\) coordinates \(nk_i\) preceded, when necessary, by an \(M\)-coordinate. The compact support observation above, and conjugation by the resulting compact set of \(M/Z\), bound all these \(N\)-coordinates in one \(N_a\). At a point where \(e_{N_a}f\) can be nonzero, its left-\(N\) coordinate is then in \(N_a\). Its average equals, up to the fixed nonzero Haar factor, the full \(N\)-fibre integral in (6.550), which is zero. Right \(J\)-invariance covers every point of \(G= \bigcup_iPk_iJ\). Thus \(e_{N_a}f=0\). Formula (6.552) proves that the coordinate map is injective on coinvariants, establishing (6.549).

A finitely generated projective is a direct summand of a finite sum of principal modules at one sufficiently small \(J\): take a common subgroup fixing finite generators and split the resulting surjection. Formula (6.549) carries that splitting to a finite sum of principal Levi modules. These are projective by compact averaging, as in Theorem 6.57. This proves the final assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.252 — the constant term is the Jacquet projective trace. The map \(R_P\) induces a linear map of algebraic cocenters. If \(Q\) is a finitely generated projective \(G\)-module, then \[ [R_P\operatorname{rk}_G Q] =\operatorname{rk}_M(r_PQ). \tag{6.553} \] The rank is the finite idempotent-matrix trace of Lemma 6.118. All these are algebraic identities involving finite commutator sums.

Proof. First let \(a=e_J*a*e_J\). Apply right convolution by \(a\) to the principal module of Lemma 6.251. In the coordinates (6.549) it is a finite matrix of Levi-module endomorphisms. The \(i\)-th diagonal entry is right convolution by \[ b_i(m)=\frac{\delta_P(m)^{1/2}}t \int_N a(k_i^{-1}mnk_i)\,dn. \tag{6.554} \] Indeed \(v_i*a(g)=t^{-1}a(k_i^{-1}g)\), because \(J\) is normal in \(K\) and \(a\) is bi-\(J\)-invariant. Applying \(q_i\) gives (6.554). Each \(b_i\) is bi-\(J_M\)-invariant, so the finite matrix trace in the Levi cocenter is \(\sum_i[b_i]\).

Decompose the \(K\)-integral in (6.547) into its \(t\) equal-mass pieces. The right \(J\)-factor drops by bi-invariance of \(a\). Write the remaining factor of \(P\cap K\) as \(m_0n_0\), with \(m_0\in K_M\). Translations in \(N\) remove \(n_0\), and conjugation by \(m_0\) preserves its measure because \(\delta_P(m_0)=1\). Therefore \[ R_Pa(m)=\sum_{i=1}^t \int_{K_M}b_i(m_0^{-1}mm_0)\,dm_0. \tag{6.555} \] The conjugation average of a compact smooth function over \(K_M\) is a finite average: one sufficiently small normal subgroup of \(K_M\) fixes it. Each conjugation difference is a finite convolution commutator by (6.526). This proves \([R_Pa]=\sum_i[b_i]\).

The calculation applies entry by entry to finite matrices. If \(a\) is an idempotent matrix presenting \(Q\), its Jacquet matrix presents \(r_PQ\), giving (6.553). If \(a=u*v-v*u\), choose one \(J\) fixing both factors. The corresponding finite Levi matrices are a commutator, whose diagonal sum is zero in the cocenter. Hence \(R_P\) sends commutator spans into commutator spans. No theorem asserting separation by representation characters is used. \(\square\)

A projective class here is a formal additive class, with \([Q\oplus Q']=[Q]+[Q']\). Thus cancellation of identical finite projectives proves a class identity before any function trace is taken.

Theorem 6.253 — cancellation along an extra central flat. Let \(M\) be the proper Levi above, and let \(W\) be a finitely generated smooth admissible \(M\)-module with central character \(\omega\) on the common scalar \(Z\). It has a finite projective resolution, in that central-character category, with zero alternating projective class. In particular its alternating projective trace is zero.

Proof: the space and its stabilizers. Put \(a=s-1>0\), let \(\mathcal B_M=\prod_i\mathcal B_i\) be the product of the division-lattice buildings, and set \[ A_M=\mathbb R^s/\mathbb R(1,\ldots,1),\qquad \nu(m)=\left(\frac{v_F\operatorname{Nrd}(m_i)}{r_id}\right)_i \bmod\mathbb R(1,\ldots,1). \tag{6.556} \] The image \(L=\nu(M)\) is a full lattice: all coordinates belong to one fixed rational lattice, and the individual reduced-norm valuations are surjective onto \(\mathbb Z\). Let \(M^0=\ker\nu\). Choose a basis of \(L\), tile \(A_M\) by its unit cubes, and let \(M\) act on \[ X_M=\mathcal B_M\times A_M \tag{6.557} \] by its building action and translation by \(\nu(m)\).

For a product facet \(\sigma\), its stabilizer \(C_\sigma^M\) is compact modulo \(Z_M=(F^\times)^s\). Its image under \(\nu\) contains the full sublattice \(\nu(Z_M)\). There are finitely many \(M\)-orbits of product facets, and \[ M^0\backslash M/C_\sigma^M \simeq L/\nu(C_\sigma^M) \tag{6.558} \] is finite. Thus there are finitely many \(M^0\)-orbits of product facets.

The group \(H_\sigma=M^0\cap C_\sigma^M\) is open and compact modulo the common scalar \(Z\). Here is a direct compactness check. Choose compact representatives modulo \(Z_M\) in \(C_\sigma^M\); their \(\nu\)-values form a finite set. In an element of \(H_\sigma\), the central component cancels one of these finitely many values. Fix one such central component for each value that occurs. The remaining central factor lies in \(Z_M\cap M^0\). Its block valuations are equal, so modulo the common scalar all its coordinates are units, a compact group. This puts \(H_\sigma/Z\), a closed subgroup, inside a finite union of compact sets.

Proof: the coefficient complex and exactness. Choose product congruence depth sufficiently large to fix finite generators of \(W\). On \(\mathcal B_M\) use the coefficient spaces \(W^{U_\sigma}\), with the boundary inclusions of (6.127), one building factor at a time. The resulting product-building complex resolves \(W\). Indeed the generated-subrepresentation functor \(\Phi_i\) for each factor is exact by Theorem 6.56 and has \(\Phi_iW=W\). Compact averages for the other factors commute with it: average any finite expression for a vector in \(\Phi_iW\). Thus the same equality and exactness hold in every row obtained by fixing the other factors. Successively taking rows proves exactness of the bounded total complex. Equivalently a total cycle can be filled row by row, eliminating its largest remaining degree at each step.

Tensor this coefficient complex with the augmented scalar cubical complex of \(A_M\). The latter is exact with finite-chain fillings. In one coordinate, fill \(v_n-v_0\) by the finite edge path from \(0\) to \(n\); its boundary is precisely that difference. Tensoring these coordinate-line contractions proves the assertion for every cube dimension. Row-by-row elimination again proves that the augmented coefficient complex on \(X_M\) resolves \(W\). The action and augmentation are \(M\)-equivariant; a contraction need not be equivariant to prove exactness.

Proof: projectivity and the exact cancellation. A flat face has a subset \(S\) of its \(a\) coordinate directions and a basepoint in \(L\). Translate the basepoint to zero. Its product-cell orbits are now exactly the \(M^0\)-orbits of \(\sigma\); its stabilizer is \(H_\sigma\), independent of \(S\). Flat translations preserve orientation. Thus for every \(\sigma\) of dimension \(p\), the degree \(p+q\) chain module contains exactly \(\binom aq\) copies of the same projective module \[ Q_\sigma=\operatorname{c\!-Ind}_{H_\sigma}^M \bigl(\epsilon_\sigma\otimes W^{U_\sigma}\bigr). \tag{6.559} \] The coefficient is finite-dimensional by admissibility. Projectivity is compact averaging modulo \(Z\), followed by compact induction. There are only finitely many \(\sigma\)-orbits and flat-face types, so all modules are finitely generated projective and the length is \(\sum_i(r_i-1)+a=r-1\). For each \(\sigma\) its alternating contribution is \[ (-1)^p[Q_\sigma]\sum_{q=0}^a(-1)^q\binom aq=0. \tag{6.560} \] This is cancellation of identical finite projectives. It proves the assertion before taking their cocenter traces. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.254 — every proper ordinary orbital of a compact Euler–Poincaré test is zero. Let \(V\) be finitely generated smooth admissible with central character \(\omega\), and let \(f_{V,m}\) be its compact Euler–Poincaré test (6.136) at a generating level. For every proper parabolic, \[ [R_Pf_{V,m}]=0\quad\text{in }\overline{\mathcal H}_\omega(M). \tag{6.561} \] In every division rank and both characteristics, \[ O_x(f_{V,m})=0 \quad\text{if the orbit of }x \text{ is not closed primary}. \tag{6.562} \] In particular (6.562) holds for the Euler test and for all the compact discrete tests.

Proof. The finite projective building resolution in Theorem 6.57 has alternating projective trace \(f_{V,m}\), by the compact-induction trace calculation (6.136) and Lemma 6.118. Apply Lemma 6.251. The result is a finite projective resolution of \(r_PV\). This module is admissible by Lemma 6.22 and finitely generated by Lemma 6.40. Theorem 6.253 gives a second finite projective resolution with zero Euler class.

The alternating projective traces of these two resolutions agree. Explicitly, lift their augmentations successively onto cycles using projectivity; the two comparison composites are homotopic to the identities by the same lifting. Their bounded projective mapping cones are contractible. Splitting their cycles cancels identical summands in consecutive degrees, so their alternating finite matrix traces agree by Lemma 6.118. Theorem 6.252 now gives (6.561).

For a nonclosed primary orbit, use its proper intrinsic kernel flag and (6.323)–(6.324). For an orbit with several primary factors, use its proper primary-factor Levi and Corollary 6.140. In both cases its ordinary orbital is a fixed positive multiple of a Levi ordinary orbital of \(f_P^0\). The function \(R_Pf=\delta_P^{1/2}f_P^0\) has zero cocenter class, so every such Levi orbital is zero by Theorem 6.140. The modulus is constant on a Levi orbit, hence the same zero holds for \(f_P^0\). This proves (6.562). All integrations are of compact-mod-centre tests; their convergence is Theorem 6.139. No ordinary orbital of a noncompact coefficient is used. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.255 — closed primary compact germs in every rank. Let \(P_0\) be any primary polynomial with closed representative \(s\in G\). Write \(E=F[s]\), \(a_E=e(E/F)\), and \(G_s=\mathrm{GL}_m(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}})\), with \(\deg_E\Delta=\delta\). Choose the closed coefficient in (6.326) to be \(O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}\), and put \[ \eta_s=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(q_\Delta^j-1)} {a_E m\delta}\ne0. \tag{6.563} \] Then the closed germ is \[ g_{P_0,\mathrm{cl}}(\gamma)= \begin{cases} [e(F[\gamma]/F)\eta_s]^{-1},&\gamma\text{ elliptic regular},\\ 0,&\gamma\text{ nonelliptic regular}. \end{cases} \tag{6.564} \] For every discrete series \(\pi\), on a sufficiently small coefficient neighborhood of \(P_0\), its actual elliptic character satisfies \[ \Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1}) =\frac{O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}(f_{\pi,m})}{\eta_s}. \tag{6.565} \] One neighborhood works for a prescribed finite packet. All field extensions here may be inseparable.

Proof. Cut the Euler and compact discrete tests to the compact reduced-norm annulus containing \(P_0\). Theorem 6.254 makes every nonclosed coefficient zero in their compact germ expansions (6.326). The Euler closed coefficient is the nonzero value (6.563), by Theorem 6.157. Its regular orbital is \(1/e(F[\gamma]/F)\) on elliptic classes in maximal-compact torus measure, and zero on nonelliptic ones, by Theorem 6.122. Division gives (6.564). The compact discrete test has volume-one elliptic orbital \(\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})\) by Theorem 6.120; converting that measure gives (6.565). Intersect the finitely many germ neighborhoods for a packet. These are compact germ identities, with no closed-orbit Schwartz assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.256 — finite real elliptic character expansions in every degree. For every \(r,d\), every discrete series \(\pi\) of \(G\) with central character \(\omega\) has a unique smooth extension to the division group of the function \[ F_\pi(b)=(-1)^{r-1}\Theta_\pi(\gamma_b) \quad(b\text{ regular in }\mathcal D^\times). \] It is a finite real character expansion \[ F_\pi=\sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}\chi_\rho,\qquad a_{\pi\rho}\in\mathbb R,\qquad \sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}\dim\rho =\frac{d_\pi}{d_{\mathrm{St}}}\in\mathbb Z_{>0}. \tag{6.566} \] Its squared elliptic norm is \(\sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}^2\).

Proof. Every division element has primary polynomial \(p^{N/e}\). Theorem 6.165 gives the corresponding closed primary representative in \(G\). Apply (6.565) to the contragredient to make the matching character constant near that polynomial. The regular division set is dense, by the nonzero discriminant polynomial, so these constants agree on overlaps and extend uniquely. Central covariance and conjugation invariance follow by density. Compact representatives modulo \(Z\) give boundedness and a common normal principal constancy subgroup.

The finite division-character decomposition is therefore exactly the finite quotient argument of Theorem 6.10: remove the unramified central uniformizer phase, take the resulting finite quotient, and decompose its class function. This proves finiteness and uniqueness. Unitary inversion gives \(F_\pi(b^{-1})=\overline{F_\pi(b)}\); division characters have the same identity. Inversion preserves quotient Haar measure, so the character inner products defining all coefficients are real, as in the proof of Theorem 6.231. The central value is Corollary 6.136 and the degree quantum of Corollary 6.117. Character orthonormality and Corollary 6.124 give the norm identity. Individual coefficient integrality and norm one are not asserted. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.257 — the inverse cocenter map and elliptic independence in every rank. The smooth transfer of Theorem 6.242 induces, for every \(r,d\), a linear involution-compatible isomorphism \[ \overline{\mathcal H}_\omega(\mathcal D^\times) \ \simeq\ \mathcal V_\omega(G)/[\mathcal H_\omega(G),\mathcal H_\omega(G)]. \tag{6.567} \] Its inverse is the division test \(Sf=B_f/N\), where \(B_f\) is the smooth extension of \(O_{\gamma_b}^{\mathrm{unit}}(f)\). The elliptic restrictions of the discrete-series characters of fixed central character are linearly independent. Any discrete-series representation with a prescribed elliptic transfer character is consequently unique, if it exists.

Proof. Theorem 6.254 puts the Euler transfer \(Tf\) in \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\) in every rank. Extensions that agree on primary polynomials differ pointwise by zero on those fibres and orbitally by zero everywhere else. Lemma 6.239 makes their difference a finite commutator sum. The same argument gives linearity, independence of the division cocenter representative, and the involution assertion, exactly by reciprocal polynomials as in Proposition 6.243.

For \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), (6.564) makes its regular division profile constant near every primary polynomial, with value \(O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}(f)/\eta_s\). Density glues it to \(B_f\). Thus \(Sf=B_f/N\) is an actual division test. The identities \(A_{Sf}=B_f\) and \(S(Ta)=A_a/N\) prove the two inverse identities: the first gives equality of every ordinary orbital of \(TSf\) and \(f\), and the second is the finite probability average of conjugates of \(a\). Apply Lemma 6.239 and the finite averaging argument of Theorem 6.244.

Every compact discrete test belongs to \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\) by Theorem 6.254. A finite elliptic character relation therefore gives a zero inverse profile for their same linear combination. The isomorphism makes that combination a finite commutator sum. Its actual discrete-series traces are its individual coefficients by (6.267), so all coefficients vanish. This proves independence and the stated uniqueness. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.258 — finite trace duality and regular-support separation in every rank. For any nonempty finite discrete-series packet in \(G\), form the real finite character matrix \(A\) in (6.566), take self-adjoint transfers \(t_\rho\) of \(p_\rho=N^{-1}\overline{\chi_\rho}\), and set \(B_{i\rho}=(-1)^{r-1}\operatorname{Tr}\pi_i(t_\rho)\). Then \[ BA^{\mathsf t}=I,\qquad H=AA^{\mathsf t}>0,\qquad \lambda_{\min}(H)\ge\|B\|_{\mathrm F}^{-2}. \tag{6.568} \] For all sufficiently large \(n\), the regular-cut trace matrix \(H_n\) is invertible. Its inverse columns give the exact regular-support separating tests (6.543), at levels \(m_n\le dn+C\). The signed complementary transfer-test traces converge to \(B-A\), with the error in Proposition 6.248, and \[ I-H=(B-A)A^{\mathsf t}. \tag{6.569} \]

Proof. Theorem 6.256 supplies the finite real matrix, and Theorem 6.257 supplies the cocenter identities \([f_{\pi_j}]=(-1)^{r-1}\sum_\rho a_{j\rho}[t_\rho]\). Taking actual traces proves the first identity of (6.568). The inequality \(\|c\|\le\|B\|_{\mathrm F}\|A^{\mathsf t}c\|\) proves the others. The proofs of Theorem 6.234 and Corollary 6.247 use only a bounded finite elliptic expansion, so apply with (6.566) in every rank. Explicitly the operator error is at most \(B_N(\sum_i\|F_i\|_\infty^2)q_F^{-n/[N(N-1)]}\), and less than half the lower bound in (6.568) for large \(n\). Matrix inversion then gives the actual trace deltas. The regular trace formula for \(\zeta_n t_\rho\), followed by the division discriminant tail estimate, gives the complementary limit exactly as in Proposition 6.248. Subtraction gives (6.569). For \(N=1\) the cutoff is identically one. \(\square\)

Example 6.259 — an inseparable primary germ in division rank six. Let \(F=\mathbb F_2((t))\), and take the degree-six cyclic division algebra with \(\Pi^6=t\). The field \(E=F(\Pi)=\mathbb F_2((\Pi))\) has degree and ramification index six. The polynomial \(p=T^6-t\) is irreducible: its roots have valuation \(1/6\), so a proper monic factor over \(F\) could not have integral constant-term valuation. Its derivative is zero. The field \(F(\Pi^2)\) is separable of degree three, and \(E/F(\Pi^2)\) is purely inseparable of degree two.

For \(G=\mathrm{GL}_6(D)\), take \(s=\Pi I_6\); its reduced polynomial is \(p^6\). Here \(N=36,m=6,\delta=1,a_E=6,q_\Delta=2\), giving \[ \eta_s=-\frac{(2-1)(2^2-1)(2^3-1)(2^4-1)(2^5-1)}{36} =-\frac{1085}{4},\qquad \eta_b^{\mathcal D}=\frac1{36}. \tag{6.570} \] Thus \(g_{P_0,\mathrm{cl}}=-4/[1085\,e(F[\gamma]/F)]\) on nearby elliptic classes. The Steinberg elliptic character is \(-1\), by (6.309) and Theorem 6.122 on regular orbitals. Its compact discrete test consequently satisfies \(O_s^{\mathrm{mc}}(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=1085/4\) by (6.565). This value concerns the compact test; no noncompact Steinberg coefficient orbital at \(s\) is inferred. For the degree-36 division test \(1/36\), the transfer is \(\mathfrak e_G\), and both Euler-normalized closed orbitals equal one.

The finite constant-term calculation and central-flat cancellation prove compact Euler–Poincaré orbital zeros in every rank. They yield (6.566)–(6.569) without arbitrary-test character integration. Theorem 6.271 and Corollary 6.272 supply the zero in (6.569) through the very cuspidal trace pairing. Example 6.250 explains why the left inverse alone does not give it. Individual coefficient integrality, representation-transfer existence and the general global correspondences remain additional mathematical obligations. General closed Schwartz convergence is also distinct from the compact germs proved here.

6.42 Euler representatives with vanishing parabolic integrals

Call \(f\in\mathcal H_\omega(G)\) very cuspidal if for every proper \(F\)-parabolic \(Q=LU\), \[ \int_U f(lu)\,du=0\qquad(l\in L). \tag{6.571} \] All conjugates of a standard parabolic are included. The integral is absolute: its reduced norm is fixed, so the compact-mod-centre support can be cut to one actual compact annulus. The following construction gives this property by finite flag calculations.

Lemma 6.260 — a circular flag identity. Let \(W_n=S_n\). For an ordered composition \(\boldsymbol a=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) of \(n\), let \(X_{\boldsymbol a}\) be its ordered set-partition space, with permutation character \(\xi_{\boldsymbol a}\). The rational class function \[ E_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}k \sum_{\substack{a_1+\cdots+a_k=n\\a_i>0}} \xi_{\boldsymbol a} \tag{6.572} \] is the indicator of the \(n\)-cycles. It restricts to zero on every proper Young subgroup. Equivalently, if nonempty \(T\subset\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\) is taken modulo circular rotation, its circular gaps form \(\boldsymbol a(T)\), and \(s_T\) is its rotation stabilizer order, then \[ E_n=\sum_{[T]} \frac{(-1)^{|T|-1}}{s_T}\xi_{\boldsymbol a(T)}. \tag{6.573} \]

Proof. If \(w\) has \(c\) cycles, a fixed ordered partition assigns each whole cycle to a block. Summing over all compositions of length \(k\) counts all surjections of its \(c\) cycles onto \(k\) labelled blocks, namely \(k!S(c,k)\). Thus (6.572) has value \(\sum_k(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!S(c,k)\). It is one for \(c=1\). The recurrence \(S(c+1,k)=kS(c,k)+S(c,k-1)\) makes the value at \(c+1\), for \(c\ge1\), a sum of two opposite copies of \(\sum_k(-1)^{k-1}k!S(c,k)\). Hence all values with \(c>1\) are zero. A proper Young subgroup contains no \(n\)-cycle.

Marking one cut in a circular subset with \(k\) cuts gives an ordered composition. There are \(k\) markings per subset and \(n\) possible starting indices per composition. Its orbit has \(n/s_T\) subsets, all with the same Young permutation character, because cyclically reordering the blocks conjugates their Young subgroups. These counts transform (6.572) into (6.573). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.261 — finite flags, Frobenius and unipotent averages. Let \(H_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(k)\), with \(k\) finite. Replace \(\xi_{\boldsymbol a}\) by the permutation representation \(V_{\boldsymbol a}\) on \(k\)-flags of quotient dimensions \(\boldsymbol a\). Every field Frobenius \(\tau\) has its canonical permutation action on these flags. Form the rational combination \(U_n\) with the coefficients in (6.572). On the component \(H_n\tau\), its average over the radical of every proper \(\tau\)-stable parabolic is zero. The same holds after conjugating that flag.

More generally, on \(H_g^b\vartheta\), where \(\vartheta\) cycles \(b\) factors and returns with a field Frobenius, use \(V_{\boldsymbol a}^{\otimes b}\) and the coefficients of \(E_g\). Its average over every proper compatible product radical is zero.

Proof: the finite Gram identity. A pair of flags has relative position determined by the dimensions of their successive intersections. Choose bases in these intersections and their successive quotients. This gives a permutation-matrix representative and a nonnegative integer matrix with the prescribed row and column sums. The same matrices parametrize the Young double cosets in \(S_n\). Consequently the invariant homomorphisms between two flag permutation modules have an orbit-indicator basis indexed by those double cosets. Frobenius fixes each basis element: it preserves the intersection dimensions and the representatives have entries zero and one.

Finite-group averaging on the homomorphism space therefore gives \[ \frac1{|H_n|}\sum_{h\in H_n} \operatorname{Tr}(h\tau|V_{\boldsymbol a}) \overline{\operatorname{Tr}(h\tau|V_{\boldsymbol b})} =\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{S_n} (\mathbb C X_{\boldsymbol b},\mathbb C X_{\boldsymbol a}). \tag{6.574} \] For clarity, the left side is the trace of the Frobenius conjugation operator on the invariant homomorphisms: average first over \(H_n\), then apply Frobenius. Its orbit-indicator basis is fixed, proving the equality. Thus a zero relation among Young permutation characters gives a zero function on \(H_n\tau\), since the squared norm of the corresponding function is zero.

Proof: restriction and cyclic factors. Let a proper parabolic have Levi block sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_s\). Its radical-orbits on the flag space form a disjoint union of Levi flag spaces. Indeed factor the parabolic as Levi times radical and use the same relative-position matrices; the stabilizer in each Levi block is the parabolic preserving its row flag. The canonical permutation-matrix representatives are Frobenius fixed. This is precisely the Young restriction formula for the permutation modules. The restriction of \(E_n\) is zero by Lemma 6.260. Apply (6.574), now in the product Levi group, to conclude that its finite radical average vanishes on the Frobenius component.

For \(b\) factors, expand a trace in a tensor-product flag basis. The cyclic permutation identifies its successive indices; the trace becomes the trace on one \(V_{\boldsymbol a}\) of the product of the \(b\) operators, with the return Frobenius. Averaging over a compatible product radical is the same calculation on \((V_{\boldsymbol a}^{U_0})^{\otimes b}\): radical invariants have their radical-orbit permutation basis. The preceding single-factor zero proves the assertion. Conjugating the flags conjugates these averages, so does not change zero. \(\square\)

Use the standard alcove with vertices indexed by \(\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z\). Choose the rotation \(\Omega\) with superdiagonal entries one and lower-left entry \(\Pi_D\); thus \[ \Omega^r=\Pi_D I_r,\qquad \Omega^{rd}=\varpi_F I_r. \tag{6.575} \] Here conjugation by \(\Pi_D\) induces the field automorphism \(\sigma_D\) of \(k_D\). The cyclic division model of Lemma 6.1 permits this uniformizer convention.

Lemma 6.262 — facets on a fixed norm component. Represent each \(G\)-orbit of alcove faces by a nonempty vertex subset \(S\) containing zero. Let \(P_S\) fix its actual standard lattice chain, let \(C_S\) stabilize its homothety classes, and put \(s_S=|\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathbb Z/r}S|\). Then \[ \operatorname{vol}(C_S/Z) =d\,s_S\operatorname{vol}(P_S). \tag{6.576} \] For \(0\le j<N=rd\), put \(g=\gcd(r,j)\), with \(g=r\) if \(j=0\), and \(b=r/g\). A face contributes on norm valuation \(j\) precisely when \(S+j=S\). It then contains \(F_g=\{0,g,\ldots,(b-1)g\}\), and corresponds to a nonempty \(T\subset\mathbb Z/g\mathbb Z\). One has \[ s_S=b\,s_T,\qquad (-1)^{\dim S}\epsilon_S(\Omega^j)=(-1)^{|T|-1}. \tag{6.577} \] The parahoric \(P_{F_g}\) has reductive quotient \(\mathrm{GL}_g(k_D)^b\). The rotation \(\Omega^j\) cycles these factors, with return Frobenius \(\sigma_D^{j/g}\).

Proof. A lattice chain has an adapted integral basis, so every face has a standard-alcove representative; changing its initial vertex is a circular rotation. The valuation of the reduced norm gives the type shift modulo \(r\). Its zero kernel in \(C_S\) fixes each vertex and its actual lattice: a nonzero homothety shift changes lattice covolume. Thus the kernel is \(P_S\). The allowable type shifts have period \(r/s_S\), realized by \(\Omega\), while central valuations have period \(rd\). This proves (6.576).

The \(j\)-orbits on the vertex indices have length \(b\), so stability and inclusion of zero force \(F_g\subset S\). Reduction modulo \(g\) identifies these orbits with \(T\). The kernel of the rotation map to \(\mathbb Z/g\) has order \(b\), proving the first equality of (6.577). There are \(|T|\) permutation cycles of length \(b\) on the \(b|T|\) vertices. Multiplying their sign by \((-1)^{b|T|-1}\) gives its second equality. The successive quotients of the \(F_g\)-chain have dimension \(g\), proving the reductive quotient statement. Following the rotation \(b\) times gives \(\Omega^{jb}=\Pi_D^{j/g}I_r\), which induces the stated return automorphism. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.263 — a finite formula for the averaged component. Form the Euler test (6.279) with these face representatives, and cut it to norm valuation \(j\). Average that compact function by conjugation under \(P_{F_g}\), using probability measure; call the result \(u_j\). It is supported in \(\Omega^jP_{F_g}\). If \(\chi_{\boldsymbol a}^{(b,\tau)}\) denotes the canonical cyclic-tensor flag character of Lemma 6.261, then \[ u_j(\Omega^j h)=\frac1{d\,b\,\operatorname{vol}(P_{F_g})} \sum_{[T]\subset\mathbb Z/g} \frac{(-1)^{|T|-1}}{s_T} \chi_{\boldsymbol a(T)}^{(b,\tau)}(\Omega^j\bar h). \tag{6.578} \] The bar is reduction to \(\mathrm{GL}_g(k_D)^b\), and \(\tau=\sigma_D^{j/g}\) is its return Frobenius.

Proof. A contributing component is \(\Omega^jP_S\). Since \(F_g\subset S\), its parahoric is contained in \(P_{F_g}\), and its reduction is the product of the corresponding \(g\)-dimensional flag parabolics. It contains the pro-unipotent radical of \(P_{F_g}\). Conjugation averaging the indicator of \(\Omega^jP_S\) counts fixed cosets in \(P_{F_g}/P_S\). Its quotient by \(\operatorname{vol}(P_S)\) is consequently the twisted flag permutation character divided by \(\operatorname{vol}(P_{F_g})\). Substitute (6.576)–(6.577). The rotation-orbits of the \(S\)'s are the rotation-orbits of the \(T\)'s, giving (6.578). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.264 — a very cuspidal Euler representative. The functions \(u_j\), extended centrally and summed, give a smooth compact-mod-centre test \(\mathfrak e_G^c\) with trivial central character such that \[ [\mathfrak e_G^c]=[\mathfrak e_G],\qquad \int_U\mathfrak e_G^c(lu)\,du=0 \quad(Q=LU\text{ proper},\ l\in L). \tag{6.579} \] Its ordinary orbital integrals, including all singular ones, are those of \(\mathfrak e_G\).

Proof: parabolic intersections. Fix an arbitrary proper \(D\)-flag defining \(Q\). Suppose \(y\in Q\cap\Omega^jP_{F_g}\). Intersect this flag with the \(F_g\)-lattice chain. Its induced flags in the \(b\) graded pieces are permuted cyclically by \(y\). Their dimensions are therefore equal. For a subspace of \(D\)-dimension \(a\), their sum is \(a\): one period of the chain is multiplication by \(\Pi_D\). Thus each dimension is \(a/b\). If no such integer exists, there is no intersection. Otherwise a proper nonzero subspace gives a proper flag in every \(g\)-dimensional piece.

Choose a basis adapted both to the lattice chain and to the \(D\)-flag. Here is the integral justification. The intersection with its first lattice is saturated and free. Reduce the chain and these saturated submodules modulo \(\Pi_D\), choose a basis adapted to the two resulting flags by their intersection dimensions, and lift each vector in the requisite saturated submodule. The lifted vectors form an integral basis and preserve all the chain lattices. In this basis \(U\cap P_{F_g}\) maps onto the radical of the resulting proper finite product parabolic: each of its elementary strict flag-block entries lifts to an integral elementary entry. After a change of graded bases this is a compatible parabolic for the cyclic action in Lemma 6.261.

The function (6.578) is invariant under \(P_{F_g}\)-conjugacy. If \(lu_0\) meets its support, every contributing \(u\) lies in the coset \(u_0(U\cap P_{F_g})\). This group is compact, and reduction makes its integral a fixed volume times the finite unipotent average of Lemma 6.261. That average is zero. Hence each \(u_j\) has (6.571) for every proper \(Q\).

Proof: central extension and the cocenter. For an element of norm valuation \(j+Nk\), define the extension to have value \(u_j(\varpi_F^{-k}g)\). Only one \(j\) and one \(k\) occurs on any \(lU\), so the preceding zero survives the extension. There are finitely many components modulo \(Z\), proving smoothness and compact support modulo \(Z\).

Choosing a different representative of a face orbit conjugates the corresponding Euler summand and preserves its volume. Its difference is a finite conjugation difference. On a fixed component, the parahoric average is finite, since the pro-unipotent radical fixes the function. Its difference from that component is again a finite sum of conjugation differences. Central pushforward preserves these identities. Formula (6.526) proves the cocenter identity in (6.579); Theorem 6.140 gives equality of every ordinary orbital. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.265 — very cuspidal transfer and cocenter representatives. Every division test of Theorem 6.242 has a very cuspidal transfer \[ T^c a(g)=\Phi_a(\chi_g)\mathfrak e_G^c(g). \tag{6.580} \] Every class in \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\) has a very cuspidal representative, with a finite compact commutator difference. Self-adjoint classes have self-adjoint such representatives.

Proof. For a block triangular \(lu\), its reduced polynomial is the product of its diagonal-block polynomials, so \(\chi_{lu}=\chi_l\). Thus the factor in (6.580) is constant in every parabolic integral, proving (6.571). Multiplication by this conjugation-invariant factor preserves every finite conjugation-difference identity in (6.579), in the correct central-character algebra. Hence \(T^c a\) has the same cocenter class and all ordinary orbital values as \(Ta\).

For \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), take \(a=Sf\) in Theorem 6.257. Its inverse identity gives the required compact commutator difference. Inversion and complex conjugation preserve (6.571), by inversion in \(U\) and conjugation by \(l\), with its fixed nonzero modulus factor. Therefore taking \((f+f^*)/2\) preserves the property and realizes a self-adjoint class. \(\square\)

6.43 Conjugation kernels and the elliptic trace pairing

Write \(Q=G/Z\), retain the length \(\sigma\), Cartan weight \(D_C\) and positive spherical function \(\Xi\) of Section 6.16, and use the normalized discriminant \(\Delta\) of (6.512). For two inverse-central-\(\omega\) tests put \[ K_{f,h}(x)=\int_Q f(g)\overline{h(x^{-1}gx)}\,d\bar g. \tag{6.581} \] The integrand is central invariant. Cutting \(f\) to \(0\le v_F\operatorname{Nrd}g<N\) realizes this integral on one actual compact set, since the central units have volume one.

Lemma 6.266 — compact support of the cuspidal conjugation kernel. Suppose \(f\) is compact modulo \(Z\) and very cuspidal, and \(h\) is compact modulo \(Z\). Then \(K_{f,h}\) is compact modulo \(Z\). More precisely, let their actual support annuli and inverses have entry valuations bounded below by \(-B_f,-B_h\), and let their principal constancy levels be \(\ell_f,\ell_h\). For a constant depending only on \(G\), \[ K_{f,h}(x)=0\quad\text{if}\quad \sigma(x)>A_G(1+B_f+B_h+\ell_f+\ell_h). \tag{6.582} \] In particular a fixed-level \(h\) supported in \(\sigma\le R\) has kernel support in \(\sigma(x)\le A(1+R)\), with \(A\) independent of its values.

Proof. Use the support-annulus cuts in (6.581). They retain (6.571), since the reduced norm is constant on each \(lU\). Write \(x=k_1ak_2\), with \(a=\operatorname{diag}(\Pi_D^{\lambda_i})\), \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_r\). Conjugate the two functions by \(k_1,k_2\). Principal levels are normal in \(K\), the support bounds are uniform, and (6.571) holds for all conjugate parabolics. It suffices to treat \(a\).

Split the coordinates at every gap \(\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge L\), where \(L\) will be chosen below. If there is no gap, the length is less than \((r-1)L\). Otherwise let \(P=MN^+\) be the resulting proper block parabolic, with opposite radical \(N^-\). For \(g\) and \(a^{-1}ga\) in the two support annuli, each upper cross-block entry of \(g\) has valuation at least its Cartan gap minus \(B_h\). Each lower cross-block entry of \(a^{-1}ga\) has valuation at least its gap minus \(B_f\).

For sufficiently large \(L\), the lower-block-triangular projection of \(g\) differs from \(g\) by a matrix whose product with \(g^{-1}\) has norm less than one. The convergent geometric-series inverse therefore bounds that projection's inverse. Its diagonal blocks, and their inverses, are bounded. Successive block elimination now gives \[ g=n^+mn^-,\qquad a^{-1}ga=(a^{-1}n^+a)(a^{-1}ma)(a^{-1}n^-a). \tag{6.583} \] The factors \(m,m^{-1},n^-\) and \(a^{-1}n^+a\) are bounded in terms of the two support bounds. Applying the same argument to the upper-block-triangular projection of \(a^{-1}ga\) proves the latter assertion and bounds its diagonal factors. Uniqueness of block elimination identifies the factors in the two decompositions. The entries of \(n^+\) and \(a^{-1}n^-a\) have valuation at least \(L-C_G(B_f+B_h+1)\).

Choose \(L\ge C'_G(1+B_f+B_h+\ell_f+\ell_h)\). These small factors belong to the constancy groups, so \[ f(g)=f(mn^-),\qquad h(a^{-1}ga)=h(a^{-1}n^+ma). \tag{6.584} \] The Haar Jacobian in block Gaussian coordinates depends only on \(m\): compute it by the successive strict block entries and the diagonal entries, or by the matrix Haar density used in Theorem 6.139. In particular it is independent of \(n^-\).

One may integrate the last variable over all of \(N^-\). Indeed the other factors have fixed bounded ranges whenever the original product is nonzero. With \(m\) in that range, every \(n^-\) for which \(f(mn^-)\ne0\) is bounded too; its conjugate by \(a^{-1}\) remains in the small constancy group of \(h\). Thus extending this last range leaves precisely the product in (6.584). Its integral is zero by (6.571) for \(MN^-\). This proves vanishing when a gap exceeds the stated linear threshold. Only finitely many Gaussian products and inverses, of sizes bounded by \(r\), were used; their valuation bounds are constant multiples of the support bounds. This gives (6.582). For a length-\(R\) support annulus, Lemma 6.33 bounds all entries and inverse entries by a constant multiple of \(R+1\), proving the final assertion. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.267 — a compact angular average. For every compact \(C\subset G\) there is \(A_C\) such that \[ \int_C\Xi(x^{-1}gx)\,dg\le A_C\Xi(x)^2 \qquad(x\in G). \tag{6.585} \]

Proof. In the unitary compact model of \(I_B^G(1)\), every smooth vector is a bounded function on \(K\). The positive inducing weight gives directly \[ |\langle I(x)u,v\rangle| \le\|u\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty\Xi(x). \tag{6.586} \] This uses the defining compact integral for \(\Xi\), not irreducibility of the principal series. Cover \(C\) by finitely many right cosets \(g_iU\) of a compact open \(U\). Its averaging projection \(P_U\) has finite-dimensional image by Lemma 6.74. With an orthonormal smooth basis \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\) of that image, the integral on one coset is \[ \operatorname{vol}(U)\sum_{j=1}^t \langle I(x)e,v_j\rangle \langle I(g_i)v_j,I(x)e\rangle . \] Each of its two factors is bounded by a constant times \(\Xi(x)\), using (6.586); \(I(g_i)v_j\) is again a bounded smooth compact-model vector. The integrand \(\Xi\) is nonnegative. Summing the finitely many bounds proves (6.585). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.268 — a continuous Schwartz trace from a very cuspidal test. For compact very cuspidal \(f\) and \(h\in\mathcal S_\omega\), the outer integral \[ \mathcal I_f(h)=\int_Q K_{f,h}(x)\,d\bar x \tag{6.587} \] is absolute. It is conjugate linear and continuous at every Schwartz level, and \[ \mathcal I_f(a*b)=\mathcal I_f(b*a)\qquad(a,b\in\mathcal S_\omega). \tag{6.588} \] For every smooth discrete-series unit matrix \(E^\pi_{u,u}\), \(\|u\|=1\), \[ \mathcal I_f(E^\pi_{u,u})=\operatorname{Tr}\pi(f). \tag{6.589} \]

Proof: convergence and continuity. Fix the level \(J\) of \(h\). Its Cartan cutoff \(h_R\) is at the same level. Lemma 6.266 makes \(K_{f,h_R}(x)=0\) when \(\sigma(x)>A_J(1+R)\). Choose \(R\) a sufficiently small positive multiple of \(\sigma(x)\), minus a fixed constant. In (6.581) one may then replace \(h\) by its tail \(h-h_R\). On that tail \(1+\sigma(x^{-1}gx)\) is bounded below by a constant times \(1+\sigma(x)\). Lemma 6.267 gives, with the seminorms (6.182), \[ |K_{f,h}(x)|\le C_{f,J,s}\,p_s(h)\,(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}\Xi(x)^2. \tag{6.590} \] On the remaining bounded set the same bound follows directly from (6.585), after changing the constant. For \(s>2b+r-1\), (6.181) proves absolute outer integrability and the required continuity.

For compact \(h\), conjugating its argument by \(y\) sends \(K_{f,h}(x)\) to \(K_{f,h}(xy)\). The integral (6.587) is therefore invariant under this conjugation. It kills finite conjugation differences, hence compact convolution commutators by Lemma 6.239. Approximate \(a,b\) by their compact Cartan cutoffs. The Schwartz convolution continuity in Theorem 6.81 and (6.590) pass this zero to their commutator, proving (6.588).

Proof: a matrix unit. By (6.85), \(\overline{E^\pi_{u,u}(g)}=d_\pi\langle\pi(g)u,u\rangle\). The inner integral in (6.587) is consequently \[ d_\pi\langle\pi(f)\pi(x)u,\pi(x)u\rangle. \] The actual operator \(\pi(f)\) is finite rank on one fixed space. Expand its finite matrix in an orthonormal basis. Each resulting product of two coefficients is absolutely integrable in \(x\), by Cauchy–Schwarz and the discrete-series squared-coefficient formula. Schur orthogonality gives \(1/d_\pi\) times its diagonal trace; the factor \(d_\pi\) cancels. This proves (6.589). \(\square\)

The integral in (6.587) is an iterated integral with the displayed order. The next estimate justifies the discriminant limit needed to identify it geometrically.

Theorem 6.269 — a discriminant bound on conjugation overlaps. Let \(N>1\), put \(\mathfrak d=N(N-1)\), and fix compact \(C,C'\subset G\). There is \(A\) such that for every \(x\in G\) and \(n\ge0\), \[ \operatorname{vol}\{g\in C:x^{-1}gx\in C',\ \Delta(g)<q_F^{-n}\} \le A D_C(x)q_F^{-n/\mathfrak d}. \tag{6.591} \]

Proof. Enlarge the compacts by their \(K\)-conjugates and reduce \(x\) to a sorted Cartan diagonal \(a\). In a bounded Cartan region, \(D_C(a)\) is bounded below. The nonzero reduced-discriminant polynomial and Lemma 6.232 give (6.591) there, since the norm denominator in \(\Delta\) is bounded above and away from zero on \(C\).

Outside that region, split at gaps at least a fixed \(L\), depending only on \(C,C'\). The simultaneous Gaussian argument (6.583) applies. Its variables \(m,m^{-1},n^-\), and \(v=a^{-1}n^+a\) lie in fixed compact boxes. In \(n^+=ava^{-1}\), the upper-radical Haar factor is \[ \delta_P(a)=q_D^{-\sum_{i<j\text{ in different blocks}}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)} \le A_LD_C(a). \tag{6.592} \] The inequality holds because within-block consecutive gaps are less than \(L\), so their total root sum is bounded. The Gaussian Haar density in the remaining variables is bounded on these boxes.

Choose a block-diagonal \(u\) with nonzero reduced discriminant. Such a choice exists: take separable regular elements in each block and translate them by distinct field scalars to avoid common roots. The discriminant of \(n^+mn^-\) is a homogeneous degree-\(\mathfrak d\) polynomial in the \(F\)-coordinates of \(m\). Its coefficient of degree \(\mathfrak d\) in the direction \(tu\) is the discriminant of \(n^+un^-\). When \(n^+=0\), block triangularity makes this the fixed nonzero discriminant of \(u\), independently of \(n^-\). For sufficiently large fixed \(L\), its absolute value is unchanged throughout the compact \(n^-\)-box and the small \(n^+\)-box.

Use a linear coordinate system in the Levi matrix space containing this direction. The one-variable root-factor proof of Lemma 6.232 now has one common leading-coefficient bound for all the other coordinates and both radicals. It gives \(Aq_F^{-n/\mathfrak d}\) for the \(m\)-sublevel measure. The norm denominator only changes \(A\). The Haar density of \(M\) is bounded relative to additive measure on the compact set of \(m,m^{-1}\). Integrate the other compact variables and retain (6.592), proving the bound. There are finitely many block partitions, so one constant works. This proof includes repeated roots of the one-variable polynomials and positive characteristic. For \(r=1\), \(Q\) is compact and the bounded-region argument suffices. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.270 — geometric identification of the cuspidal kernel pairing. Let \(f,h\) be compact very cuspidal tests, and put \(f_n=\zeta_nf\). For \(N>1\), \[ \|K_{f_n,h}-K_{f,h}\|_{L^1(Q)} \le A(1+n)^{r-1}q_F^{-n/\mathfrak d}. \tag{6.593} \] The kernel pairing is \[ \mathcal I_f(h)= \int_{\mathrm{ell}}O_\gamma^{\mathrm{unit}}(f) \overline{O_\gamma^{\mathrm{unit}}(h)}\,d\nu(\gamma). \tag{6.594} \]

Proof: the cutoff estimate. The normalized discriminant of \(lu\) equals that of \(l\), because their reduced polynomials agree. Thus \(f_n\) remains very cuspidal. It has the same compact support bound as \(f\), and principal constancy level at most \(dn+C_f\). Indeed on its compact support the coefficient polynomials are Lipschitz in \(F\)-coordinates, division precision \(\ell\) gives field precision at least \(\lfloor\ell/d\rfloor\), and precision \(n+C\) decides the valuation inequality defining \(\zeta_n\). This is the polynomial-cutoff argument of Theorem 6.234.

Lemma 6.266 consequently supports both kernels, and their difference, in \(\sigma(x)\le C(1+n)\). At every point their difference is bounded by \(\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty\) times the overlap measure in (6.591), using actual compact support annuli. Cartan double-coset volume is at most a constant times \(D_C(x)^{-1}\), by (6.55)–(6.56). The normalized tuples in this ball number at most \(C'(1+n)^{r-1}\). Integrating the bound proves (6.593).

Proof: a regular elliptic representative. Very cuspidality and ordinary descent put both tests in \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\). The inverse profile of \(f_n\) is \(\zeta_n\) times that of \(f\), and vanishes near every nonregular primary polynomial. Its compact support on a central coefficient annulus is therefore away from discriminant zero.

Separable irreducible polynomials form an open subset of coefficient space. To verify this, lift each root of a sufficiently close polynomial in a fixed splitting field by the simple-root contraction. Their disjoint root neighborhoods are permuted transitively by the Galois group of an irreducible polynomial, so the lifted roots remain transitive. Thus the close polynomial is irreducible. Define the cut profile on this open subset and extend it by zero elsewhere. It is smooth: its support on the annulus is compact and disjoint from its boundary. Central scaling preserves this construction.

Formula (6.580) gives a very cuspidal representative \(v_n\), supported pointwise in the elliptic regular set, with the same cocenter class as \(f_n\). Its ordinary elliptic profile is \(\zeta_n O_\gamma(f)\); equality of all ordinary orbitals and Lemma 6.239 identify its class.

Changing variables gives \(\mathcal I_f(h)=\overline{\mathcal I_h(f)}\) for compact very cuspidal functions. The second argument is a compact cocenter trace by Theorem 6.268. Hence \(\mathcal I_{f_n}(h)=\mathcal I_{v_n}(h)\). For \(v_n\) the two integrals may be interchanged absolutely: its support is compact elliptic regular modulo \(Z\), and the uniform elliptic conjugator properness of Lemma 6.18 puts every contributing \(x/Z\) in a compact set. Weyl integration then gives the right side of (6.594), with the additional factor \(\zeta_n\).

The inverse division profiles of \(f,h\) are bounded by Theorem 6.257, and \(\nu\) is a probability measure. Dominated convergence, or the tail bound (6.513), removes this factor. Estimate (6.593) identifies the limit with \(\mathcal I_f(h)\), proving (6.594). If \(N=1\), the cutoff is identically one and the quotient is compact, so the assertion follows directly. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.271 — the cuspidal trace identity and elliptic orthogonality. For every discrete series \(\pi\) and every \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), \[ \operatorname{Tr}\pi(f)= \int_{\mathrm{ell}}\Theta_\pi(\gamma) O_\gamma^{\mathrm{unit}}(f)\,d\nu(\gamma). \tag{6.595} \] In particular, for all discrete series of central character \(\omega\), \[ \int_{\mathrm{ell}}\Theta_\pi(\gamma) \overline{\Theta_\sigma(\gamma)}\,d\nu(\gamma) =\delta_{\pi,\sigma},\qquad AA^{\mathsf t}=I. \tag{6.596} \] These statements hold in every division rank and both field characteristics.

Proof. Choose a compact very cuspidal representative \(g\) of \(f\), using Corollary 6.265. Choose such a representative \(F_\pi\) of its compact discrete test \(f_{\pi,m}\). Lemma 6.118, equation (6.271), and the compact cocenter identities give a finite Schwartz commutator expression for \(F_\pi-E^\pi_{u,u}\).
