Theorem 6.268 therefore gives \[ \mathcal I_g(F_\pi)=\mathcal I_g(E^\pi_{u,u}) =\operatorname{Tr}\pi(g). \] On the other hand (6.594) makes the left side \(\int_{\mathrm{ell}}O_\gamma(g)\overline{\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})}\,d\nu\). Unitary inversion changes its second factor to \(\Theta_\pi(\gamma)\). Compact commutators are killed both by actual traces and by ordinary orbitals, so \(g\) can be replaced by \(f\). This proves (6.595).

Take \(f=f_{\sigma,m}\). Its actual trace is \(\delta_{\pi,\sigma}\) by (6.267), and its ordinary elliptic orbital is \(\Theta_\sigma(\gamma^{-1})\) by Theorem 6.120. This proves (6.596). The finite real character expansions of Theorem 6.256 identify the resulting Gram matrix with \(AA^{\mathsf t}\). \(\square\)

Corollary 6.272 — transfer traces and vanishing complementary traces. For every division irreducible \(\rho\), let \(t_\rho\) be the compact transfer of \(p_\rho=N^{-1}\overline{\chi_\rho}\). Then \[ \operatorname{Tr}\pi(t_\rho) =(-1)^{r-1}a_{\pi\rho}, \qquad B=A. \tag{6.597} \] More generally, put \(M_f=\sup_{\mathrm{ell}}|O_\gamma(f)|\) and \(M_\pi=\sup_{\mathrm{ell}}|\Theta_\pi(\gamma)|\). For \(N>1\) and \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), \[ |\operatorname{Tr}\pi((1-\zeta_n)f)| \le B_N M_\pi M_f q_F^{-n/\mathfrak d}. \tag{6.598} \]

Proof. Substitute \(O_\gamma(t_\rho)=\overline{\chi_\rho(b_\gamma)}\) into (6.595), and use the coefficient formula (6.566), including its sign. This gives (6.597) for any of the compact cocenter representatives.

Multiplication by the conjugation-invariant cutoff preserves \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), since its value factors out of every ordinary orbital. Apply (6.595) to the complementary test. Its elliptic integral is over \(\Delta<q_F^{-n}\). The bounded profiles and (6.513) give (6.598). For \(N=1\) the complementary test is zero. \(\square\)

Example 6.273 — the two norm components for \(\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\). Let \(I\) be the edge parahoric, \(\operatorname{vol}(I)=1/(q_F+1)\), and \(\Omega=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\\varpi_F&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). On norm valuation zero the very cuspidal Euler representative is the inflated finite flag function \[ e_0=1-\tfrac12\chi_{\mathbb P^1(k_F)} \quad\text{on }K,\qquad 0\text{ elsewhere}. \tag{6.599} \] On valuation one it is \(e_1=(q_F+1)1_{\Omega I}/2\). Extend both centrally. The finite Gram identity (6.574), or the two permutation characters of \(S_2\), gives \(\|e_0\|_2^2=1/2\). At every positive Cartan height the lower-radical integration of Lemma 6.266 is already zero: the upper entry of \(g\) is in \(\varpi_F\mathcal O_F\), its diagonal entries are units, and the two finite radical averages separate. Thus \(K_{e_0,e_0}\) is \(1/2\) on \(K/Z\) and zero elsewhere.

Every element of \(\Omega I\) reverses the base edge. Its fixed set in the lattice tree is its midpoint: a second fixed midpoint would force a fixed vertex, impossible for odd type shift. Consequently a conjugate in \(\Omega I\) can occur only when the conjugator stabilizes that edge. Its stabilizer has quotient volume \(2/(q_F+1)\), and on it \[ K_{e_1,e_1}=\frac{q_F+1}{4},\qquad \mathcal I_{e_0}(e_0)=\mathcal I_{e_1}(e_1)=\frac12. \tag{6.600} \] Different norm components have zero cross-kernel. Therefore the full Euler representative has pairing one. These volume and sign calculations apply also in characteristic two.

The trace identity (6.595) is for the stated compact cuspidal orbital subspace and discrete-series traces. It proves elliptic orthogonality and the complementary-trace zeros without asserting arbitrary-test character integrability. Individual coefficient integrality, representation-transfer existence and bijectivity, general noncompact closed Schwartz estimates, and the global correspondences require additional arguments.

6.44 Global Whittaker coefficients and compact cuspidal functions

Let \(k\) be a global field, \(\mathbb A=\mathbb A_k\), and \(H=\mathrm{GL}_n\). A smooth function \(\phi\) on \(H(k)\backslash H(\mathbb A)\) is cuspidal here if its integral along \(R(k)\backslash R(\mathbb A)\) vanishes for the radical \(R\) of every proper \(k\)-parabolic. Smooth means smooth at the archimedean places and locally constant at the finite places. The arguments below apply to such functions without a spectral-finiteness assumption.

Lemma 6.274 — compact additive Fourier uniqueness. There is an additive character \(\psi\) of \(\mathbb A\), nontrivial at every place, for which \[ k^\perp=k,\qquad k\backslash\mathbb A\text{ is compact},\qquad \widehat{k\backslash\mathbb A}=\{x\mapsto\psi(ax):a\in k\}. \tag{6.601} \] On every finite power of this quotient, a continuous function with all Fourier coefficients zero is zero.

Proof for number fields: the rational field. On \(\mathbb R\) use \(e^{-2\pi ix}\), and on \(\mathbb Q_p\) use \(e^{2\pi i\{x\}_p}\), where the fractional part is the finite sum of its negative-power digits. Their product \(\psi_{\mathbb Q}\) is one on \(\mathbb Q\): subtracting the finitely many fractional parts of a rational number leaves an integer. Subtracting those parts from an adèle makes every finite component integral, and subtracting an integer puts its real component in \([0,1)\). Thus \([0,1]\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\) maps onto the quotient, proving compactness. The neighborhood \((-1/2,1/2)\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\) meets the diagonal only in zero, proving discreteness; a discrete subgroup of a Hausdorff topological group is closed, since two distinct subgroup points cannot lie in a sufficiently small translate of that neighborhood.

Every character of \(\mathbb Q_p\) is \(x\mapsto\psi_p(a_px)\). Indeed its open kernel contains \(p^h\mathbb Z_p\); its values on the cyclic groups \(p^{-m}\mathbb Z_p/p^h\mathbb Z_p\) give compatible residues of a unique \(a_p\in p^{-h}\mathbb Z_p\). These groups exhaust \(\mathbb Q_p/p^h\mathbb Z_p\), proving the assertion. On \(\mathbb R\), lifting the character to an angle near zero gives a continuous additive function, hence a linear one; subdivision extends this formula to all real arguments. Continuity on the restricted product forces a character to be trivial on \(\prod_{p\notin S}\mathbb Z_p\) for some finite \(S\): that subgroup can be put inside the inverse image of a circle arc containing no nontrivial subgroup. Consequently every adelic character is parametrized by a unique parameter adèle.

If a parameter annihilates \(\mathbb Q\), subtract a rational parameter to put it in \([0,1)\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\). Testing against one makes its real component zero. Testing against \(p^{-m}\) makes its \(p\)-component divisible by \(p^m\), for every \(m\), so all components are zero. This proves self-annihilation. Characters of the quotient, pulled back to the adèles, are therefore exactly the rational parameters.

For Fourier uniqueness, average a continuous quotient function over successively smaller finite-place compact open subgroups \(J\). Uniform continuity makes these averages converge uniformly. Finite-place additive approximation, obtained by the integer Chinese remainder theorem after clearing denominators, gives \(\mathbb A_f=\mathbb Q+J\). Hence an average descends to \(\mathbb R/(\mathbb Q\cap J)\), a circle, and its characters are among the rational parameters above. On a circle the Fejér kernels have mass one, are nonnegative and concentrate at zero. These properties follow from \(m^{-1}|1+e^{it}+\cdots+e^{i(m-1)t}|^2\): its constant coefficient is one, and outside any fixed neighborhood of zero it is bounded by a constant times \(m^{-1}\). Convolution therefore converges uniformly to a continuous function. Zero Fourier coefficients make these convolutions zero. Apply this to each finite-place average and then take its uniform limit. Products give Fourier uniqueness on every finite power of the rational quotient.

Proof for function fields: the rational field. First put \(K=\mathbb F_q(t)\), \(s=t^{-1}\), and fix a nontrivial additive character \(\psi_q\) of \(\mathbb F_q\). At each place use the character \(x\mapsto\psi_q(\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa(v)/\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{res}_v(x\,dt))\). It is nontrivial: in a local parameter, multiplication by the nonzero differential \(dt\) only shifts a Laurent coefficient and multiplies it by a unit. The finite-field trace pairing is nondegenerate. Indeed finite fields are separable, so their trace form is nondegenerate, as follows by writing the distinct conjugates in a Vandermonde matrix.

Partial fractions show that the sum of these traced residues of a rational differential is zero: a simple finite pole contributes the negative of its contribution to the coefficient at infinity, and higher-pole terms contribute zero. Thus the product character \(\psi_K\) is trivial on \(K\). Removing the finitely many finite principal parts of an adèle by a rational function, and then removing its polynomial part at infinity, gives \[ \mathbb A_K=K+C_K,\qquad C_K=\prod_{v\ne\infty}\mathcal O_v\times s\mathbb F_q[[s]], \qquad K\cap C_K=0. \tag{6.602} \] The principal parts can be prescribed by the polynomial Chinese remainder theorem. A rational function integral at every finite place is a polynomial; membership in \(s\mathbb F_q[[s]]\) then makes it zero. This proves the intersection assertion. In particular the additive quotient is compact and has a compact open additive group of representatives.

Suppose an adèle annihilates \(K\). Subtract an element of \(K\) to put it in \(C_K\). Pairing with \(\alpha t^m\), for \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_q\) and \(m\ge0\), makes every coefficient at infinity zero: since \(dt=-s^{-2}ds\), the residue selects its coefficient of \(s^{m+1}\). Varying \(\alpha\) uses the nondegenerate finite-field pairing. At a finite prime \(P\), now pair with rational functions having poles only at \(P\). Their local principal parts exhaust \(K_P/\mathcal O_P\), by the same Chinese remainder theorem. All other residues vanish. The Laurent-coefficient pairing therefore makes that component zero too. This proves \(K^\perp=K\).

For completeness, every continuous character of a local Laurent-series field is a Laurent-coefficient character of this form. Its open kernel bounds one end of the coefficient list; its values on the successive coefficient groups determine the other coefficients uniquely, using finite-field trace duality. This also identifies the topologies: annihilators of fractional ideals are fractional ideals. On a restricted product, continuity makes the character trivial on the integral groups outside finitely many places. Hence the local descriptions identify every character of \(\mathbb A_K\) with a unique parameter adèle. A character of \(C_K\) extends by one on \(K\) in (6.602), so its parameter lies in \(K^\perp=K\). This proves (6.601). Finite-group Fourier inversion applies to every finite quotient of \(C_K\). Averaging a continuous function over successively smaller open subgroups converges uniformly, proving Fourier uniqueness.

Proof for finite extensions in either characteristic. Every one-variable function field \(k\) over a finite field admits a separating element. Here is the algebraic point. For any transcendental \(t\) with \([k:\mathbb F_q(t)]=e\), Frobenius and the degree formula give \([k:k^p]=p\). Choose \(f\notin k^p\); then \(k=k^p(f)\), and \(k/\mathbb F_q(f)\) is finite separable. To check the last implication, a finite extension \(L/M\) is separable precisely when \(L=ML^p\). In the separable direction the minimal polynomial of a primitive element remains separable over \(M(\alpha^p)\), whereas \(\alpha\) is purely inseparable over that field, forcing equality. Conversely, iterate \(L=ML^p\). A sufficiently large common \(p\)-power of finitely many generators has separable minimal polynomial over \(M\), obtained by removing all its powers of \(X^p\). Thus the iterated equality puts all of \(L\) in its separable subextension. This proves the criterion and the separating-element assertion.

Take \(K=\mathbb Q\) for a number field and \(K=\mathbb F_q(f)\) for a function field. Choose trace-dual \(K\)-bases \(b_i,c_i\) of \(k\), and set \[ \psi_k(x)=\psi_K(\operatorname{Tr}_{k/K}x),\qquad \mathbb A_k\simeq\mathbb A_K^{[k:K]},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{k/K}(b_i c_j)=\delta_{ij}. \tag{6.603} \] The middle map is the additive basis map. To check its restricted-product topology, omit the finitely many places at which a basis vector or a trace-dual vector is nonintegral. There are only finitely many: each vector satisfies a monic polynomial whose coefficients have only finitely many denominators. At every remaining place an integral element has integral coordinates \(\operatorname{Tr}(x c_i)\), and integral coordinates give an integral element. At the exceptional places the finite-dimensional local basis maps are topological isomorphisms. Factoring a separable defining polynomial over a completion identifies the local tensor algebra with the product of the completions above that place, so this basis map is the asserted adelic map. It carries the diagonal \(k\) to \(K^{[k:K]}\). Trace duality gives compactness, discreteness, self-annihilation and the full character-group assertion from the corresponding rational case. Every local trace of a finite separable extension is a nonzero linear functional, hence surjective, proving local nontriviality of \(\psi_k\). The quotient is a finite product of rational additive quotients, so the Fourier uniqueness proved above transfers as well. \(\square\)

Normalize all rational unipotent quotients below to have volume one. Their compactness and the required disintegrations can be seen directly: order upper-triangular entries by their columns, choose a compact additive fundamental set for \(k\backslash\mathbb A\), and successively remove the rational part of each entry by left multiplication by a rational elementary matrix. Later entries change polynomially, but already treated entries do not change. This gives compact representatives. Multiplication and conjugation on the successive root coordinates are triangular with diagonal one; rational linear changes have adelic determinant of absolute value one by the product formula. Thus iterated integration over these additive quotients is invariant and has the stated normalization.

Lemma 6.275 — the successive nonzero Fourier coefficients. For \(1\le i\le n\), put \[ U^{(i)}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I_i&X\\0&u\end{pmatrix}:u\in U_{n-i}\right\}, \qquad \psi_i(u)=\psi\left(\sum_{j=i}^{n-1}u_{j,j+1}\right), \tag{6.604} \] where \(U_a\) denotes the upper unitriangular group of size \(a\), and \(U^{(n)}=1\). Let \(V_i\), for \(2\le i\le n\), consist of the entries in column \(i\) above the diagonal. Thus \(V_i\simeq\mathbb G_a^{i-1}\) and \(U^{(i-1)}=V_iU^{(i)}\), with \(U^{(i)}\) normal. Define \[ F_i(g)=\int_{[U^{(i)}]}\phi(ug)\overline{\psi_i(u)}\,du, \qquad C_{i,a}(g)=\int_{[V_i]}F_i(v(x)g)\overline{\psi(a x)}\,dx, \tag{6.605} \] where \([R]=R(k)\backslash R(\mathbb A)\) and \(a\in k^{i-1}\) is a row. Then \[ C_{i,0}=0,\qquad C_{i,e_{i-1}}=F_{i-1}. \tag{6.606} \] If \(F_i\ne0\), then \(F_{i-1}\ne0\).

Proof. The compact quotient integrals are absolute, including uniformly for \(g\) in a compact set. Conjugation by \(V_i\) preserves \(\psi_i\), since its additional root entries lie strictly above the simple root in column \(i+1\). Hence \(F_i(v(x)g)\) descends to \([V_i]\), and the disintegration above gives the second identity in (6.606).

For the constant coefficient, decompose \(U^{(i-1)}\) as the radical of the parabolic \((i-1,n-i+1)\), followed by the upper unitriangular group in its last block. The character in \(C_{i,0}\) is trivial on that radical. Integrate over it first. Cuspidality makes the integral zero, proving the first identity.

The rational group \(\mathrm{GL}_{i-1}(k)\) in the first block normalizes \(U^{(i)}\) and preserves \(\psi_i\). Consequently \(F_i(hg)=F_i(g)\) for such \(h\). Direct change of the column variable gives \[ C_{i,e_{i-1}}(h g)=C_{i,e_{i-1}h}(g). \tag{6.607} \] Every nonzero row is \(e_{i-1}h\): extend it to an invertible matrix by a basis completion. If \(F_i(g)\ne0\), its continuous function on \([V_i]\) is nonzero at zero. Fourier uniqueness and \(C_{i,0}=0\) give a nonzero coefficient with a nonzero row. Formula (6.607) and (6.606) make \(F_{i-1}\) nonzero. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.276 — global Whittaker injectivity in every degree. The map on smooth cuspidal functions \[ \phi\longmapsto W_\phi(g)= \int_{U_n(k)\backslash U_n(\mathbb A)} \phi(ug)\overline{\psi\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}u_{j,j+1}\right)}\,du \tag{6.608} \] is injective. It intertwines right translation and has left \((U_n(\mathbb A),\psi)\)-covariance. In particular every nonzero cuspidal automorphic representation of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb A)\) is globally generic.

Proof. For a nonzero \(\phi\), start with \(F_n=\phi\). Lemma 6.275 gives \(F_{n-1}\ne0\), then \(F_{n-2}\ne0\), and finally \(F_1=W_\phi\ne0\). This is a finite induction on compact quotient integrals; no rearrangement of an infinite Whittaker expansion is needed. Right equivariance is immediate. Left covariance follows by right translation of the variable in the unipotent quotient and the character identity. For \(n=1\) the map is the identity. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.277 — local genericity. Suppose an irreducible cuspidal representation is written in its algebraic restricted tensor-product realization \(\Pi=\bigotimes_v'\Pi_v\). Every finite local factor is generic for \(\psi_v\).

Proof. Theorem 6.276 makes \(\Lambda(\phi)=W_\phi(1)\) nonzero after a right translation. Pure tensors span, so choose one on which it is nonzero. Holding all factors but \(v\) fixed gives \[ \lambda_v(\xi)=\Lambda(\xi\otimes\xi^v),\qquad \lambda_v(\Pi_v(u)\xi)=\psi_v(u)\lambda_v(\xi),\qquad \lambda_v\ne0. \tag{6.609} \] This is the required Whittaker functional. No uniqueness or product formula for these functionals is used. The algebraic tensor realization is the one in Lesson 12: its finite tensor-algebra and one-dimensional-tail proof applies to a given admissible restricted product with these local groups. The assertion here concerns factors in that realization and does not supply a new spectral-existence theorem. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.278 — nonzero compact cuspidal Poincaré functions. Let \(\eta\) be a unitary character of \(k^\times\backslash\mathbb A^\times\). Prescribe finitely many local smooth compact-mod-centre functions \(f_v\), with central covariance \(\eta_v\), all satisfying \(f_v(1)\ne0\). Include all archimedean and all ramified-character places. Suppose one prescribed finite place \(v_*\) has the stronger vanishing property \[ \int_{R(k_{v_*})}f_{v_*}(a u b)\,du=0 \quad\text{for every proper parabolic radical }R \text{ and all }a,b\in H(k_{v_*}). \tag{6.610} \] After choosing the usual central-covariant maximal-compact indicators at the other places and shrinking one further finite component, the function \[ P_f(g)=\sum_{\gamma\in Z(k)\backslash H(k)}f(\gamma g) \tag{6.611} \] is smooth, nonzero, cuspidal, of central character \(\eta\), and compactly supported on \(H(k)Z(\mathbb A)\backslash H(\mathbb A)\). It is therefore square-integrable on that quotient.

Proof: local finiteness. Central covariance and \(\eta|_{k^\times}=1\) make (6.611) well defined. Conjugation on \(M_n\) embeds rational matrices modulo scalars into rational matrices of size \(n^2\). If two conjugation actions agree, their quotient commutes with every matrix unit, hence is scalar. Consequently for every compact \(C\subset H(\mathbb A)/Z(\mathbb A)\), \[ \#\{\gamma\bmod Z(k):\gamma\in C\}<\infty. \tag{6.612} \] Indeed its conjugation matrices lie in a compact adelic matrix set. Each rational entry has finitely many possibilities, since \(k\) is discrete and closed in \(\mathbb A\); compactness of its additive quotient was proved in Lemma 6.274, and the basis or number-field construction there also proves discreteness. Injectivity of conjugation gives (6.612). Apply it to the support of \(f\) times the inverse of any compact set of \(g\)'s. This proves uniform local finiteness of the sum and of its differentiated sums, hence smoothness.

Proof: nonvanishing. Start with a maximal-compact component at an extra finite place \(w\), outside the prescribed set. At \(g=1\), (6.612) leaves finitely many rational candidates. A noncentral rational matrix is noncentral at \(w\): its off-diagonal entries and differences of diagonal entries cannot become zero in a field completion unless they were already zero. In the Hausdorff local quotient \(H(k_w)/Z(k_w)\), shrink a principal subgroup \(J_w\) to exclude all these finitely many noncentral classes. Choose it inside the kernel of \(\eta_w\) on its central intersection. The central extension of \(1_{J_w}\) is well defined and has value one at the identity. Shrinking cannot introduce another rational candidate. Only the rational scalar class remains, so \[ P_f(1)=f(1)=\prod_v f_v(1)\ne0. \tag{6.613} \]

Proof: cuspidality and support. For a proper rational radical \(R\), integrate over its compact quotient. Uniform local finiteness justifies absolute unfolding. Right multiplication of \(R(k)\) on \(Z(k)\backslash H(k)\) is free, since a unipotent scalar is one. Thus \[ \int_{[R]}P_f(ug)\,du= \sum_{\gamma\in Z(k)\backslash H(k)/R(k)} \int_{R(\mathbb A)}f(\gamma u g)\,du=0. \tag{6.614} \] Each unfolded integral is absolute. Compact support modulo scalars, with the determinant fixed on \(\gamma Rg\), bounds the scalar absolute values and then all unipotent coordinates. This gives actual compact support for that integral; the same argument works uniformly on compact sets. Its local factor at \(v_*\) is zero by (6.610), proving the displayed zero. Compact representatives for \([R]\) also show directly that the absolute sum of these integrals is finite, before unfolding. Finally the support of \(P_f\) in the automorphic quotient is contained in the compact image of the support of \(f\) modulo the centre. A smooth function on this compact support is bounded, and quotient Haar measure is finite on compact sets. This proves square integrability. \(\square\)

Property (6.610) holds for a compact-mod-centre matrix coefficient of a smooth representation whose proper Jacquet modules vanish. To see the zero, choose a compact open subgroup of \(R\) fixing the coefficient vector. The radical is an increasing union of compact subgroups: in standard upper root coordinates use valuation lower bounds \(-M(j-i)\) on entry \((i,j)\). Multiplication and inversion preserve these bounds because root heights add. Zero coinvariants therefore say that a sufficiently large compact \(R\)-average of the vector is zero: write it as a finite sum of differences and enlarge the compact averaging group to contain their elements. Enlarge again to contain the compact support of its coefficient on \(R\). Its full coefficient integral is then zero. Left and right translations merely change the two vectors. This explains the stronger hypothesis in (6.610); unaveraged integrals on \(lR\) alone do not assert it for arbitrary \(aRb\).

Example 6.279 — a trace zero is not an operator zero. In the standard representation of \(S_3\) on the basis \(e_1-e_2,e_2-e_3\), the group-algebra element \(a=(12)-(23)\) acts as \[ \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix} -\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\ne0, \qquad\operatorname{Tr}(a)=0. \tag{6.615} \] Its traces on the trivial and sign representations are zero too. Thus vanishing traces on unwanted irreducibles do not make convolution by a test vanish on those representations. Theorem 6.278 constructs a nonzero smooth cuspidal function. Extracting an irreducible automorphic constituent with prescribed discrete-series components additionally requires a spectral-existence argument and a trace isolation or an actual local projection. Global genericity in Theorem 6.276 supplies one input to that problem; it does not by itself prove local generic pseudo-coefficient isolation or exact discrete-series globalization.

6.45 Regular mirabolic models and discrete-series genericity

In this subsection \(F\) is nonarchimedean, of either characteristic. Fix an additive character \(\psi\) trivial on \(\mathcal O\) and nontrivial on \(\varpi^{-1}\mathcal O\), with self-dual measure \(dx\), so \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O)=1\). Write \(q=|\mathcal O/\varpi\mathcal O|\). Put \(P_1=1\), and for \(n=m+1\) put \[ P_n=\left\{(h,x)=\begin{pmatrix}h&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}: h\in H_m=\mathrm{GL}_m(F),\ x\in F^m\right\},\qquad (h,x)(h',x')=(hh',x+hx'). \tag{6.616} \] Thus \(P_n\) fixes the last standard row. For the coordinate calculations use \[ dh=|\det h|^{-m}\prod_{i,j}dh_{ij},\qquad dp_n=|\det h|^{-1}dh\,dx,\qquad \Delta_{P_n}(h,x)=|\det h|^{-1}. \tag{6.617} \] Our modular convention is \(\int f(pp_0)\,dp=\Delta(p_0)^{-1}\int f(p)\,dp\). Direct left and right changes of variables in (6.616) prove (6.617). These densities need not give a maximal compact subgroup volume one. Multiplying a Haar measure by \(c>0\) gives an isometric regular model by multiplication of functions by \(c^{1/2}\); thus the coefficient embeddings of Theorem 6.35 apply with the corresponding formal degree.

Lemma 6.280 — row coordinates and their Haar density. Let \(Y_m=F^m\setminus\{0\}\), with row coordinates, and \(e=e_m\). Choose the first coordinate \(j\) at which \(|\xi_j|=\|\xi\|_\infty\). Let \(t_\xi\) have first \(m-1\) rows the standard rows other than \(e_j\), in increasing order, and last row \(\xi\). Then \[ e t_\xi=\xi,\qquad |\det t_\xi|=\|\xi\|_\infty, \qquad t_e=I_m, \qquad d\nu_m(\xi)=\frac{d\xi}{\|\xi\|_\infty}. \tag{6.618} \] The section is continuous on a finite clopen partition of \(Y_m\). For fixed \(\xi\ne0\), every \(h\in H_m\) has unique coordinates \[ \eta=\xi h,\qquad s=t_\xi h t_\eta^{-1}\in P_m, \qquad h=t_\xi^{-1}s t_\eta, \qquad dh=dp_m(s)\,d\nu_m(\eta). \tag{6.619} \] For \(m=1\), interpret \(dp_1\) as unit mass on the trivial group.

Proof. The pivot inequalities define clopen sets away from zero, and the determinant is \((-1)^{m-j}\xi_j\). At \(e\) the pivot is \(m\). Multiplying the middle expression in (6.619) by \(e\) proves that it lies in \(P_m\), and proves uniqueness.

It remains to compute the measure. First take \(\xi=e\), so \(h=s t_\eta\). Write \(s=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Its top \(m-1\) rows are obtained by right multiplication of the rows of \((A,b)\) by \(t_\eta\); the last row is \(\eta\). The additive Jacobian is \(|\det t_\eta|^{m-1}\). This remains true as \(\eta\) varies on a pivot chart, since the last-row variables make the full Jacobian block triangular. Moreover \(|\det h|=|\det A|\,|\det t_\eta|\). Hence \[ |\det h|^{-m}\,d h_{\mathrm{entries}} =\frac{dA\,db}{|\det A|^m} \frac{d\eta}{|\det t_\eta|}. \tag{6.620} \] The first factor is exactly \(dp_m\). For general fixed \(\xi\), left translation by \(t_\xi\) preserves \(dh\). This proves (6.619), including its normalization. \(\square\)

For a strongly continuous unitary representation \(\tau\) of \(P_m\), define a representation on \(L^2(Y_m,d\xi;\mathscr K_\tau)\) by \[ \begin{split} b(\xi,h)&=t_\xi h t_{\xi h}^{-1}\in P_m,\\ \bigl(\Sigma_n(\tau)(h,x)\Phi\bigr)(\xi) &=|\det h|^{1/2}\psi(\xi x)\tau(b(\xi,h))\Phi(\xi h). \end{split} \tag{6.621} \] The cocycle identity \(b(\xi,hh')=b(\xi,h)b(\xi h,h')\) proves the group law. The change \(\xi\mapsto\xi h\) has Jacobian \(|\det h|\), proving unitarity. Compact-open averages converge strongly to the identity in a strongly continuous unitary representation, so smooth fibre values are dense. Strong continuity follows first for compactly supported locally constant sections with such values. On their compact support the section and cocycle are continuous, and sufficiently small group elements fix the finitely many values and their partition. These sections are dense; unitary boundedness passes continuity to the completion.

Theorem 6.281 — the regular mirabolic decomposition. Let \(\lambda_{P_n}\) be left translation on \(L^2(P_n,dp_n)\). Then \[ \lambda_{P_n}\simeq 1_{L^2(Y_m,d\nu_m)}\otimes\Sigma_n(\lambda_{P_m}). \tag{6.622} \] Define \(\sigma_1=1\), \(\mathscr K_1=\mathbb C\), and recursively \[ \sigma_n=\Sigma_n(\sigma_{n-1}),\qquad \mathscr K_n=L^2(Y_{n-1},d\xi;\mathscr K_{n-1}). \tag{6.623} \] There is a separable Hilbert space \(\mathscr M_n\) such that \(\lambda_{P_n}\simeq1_{\mathscr M_n}\otimes\sigma_n\). No irreducibility assertion is needed for this decomposition.

Proof. Fourier transform the column variable using the positive kernel, and compensate for the density in (6.617): \[ \widehat f(h,\xi)=|\det h|^{-1/2} \int_{F^m}f(h,x)\psi(\xi x)\,dx. \tag{6.624} \] Additive Plancherel makes this a unitary map to \(L^2(H_m\times F^m,dh\,d\xi)\). That Plancherel identity follows by Fourier inversion on the compact additive quotients supporting locally constant tests, then density in \(L^2\). Left translation becomes \[ \widehat{\lambda(h_0,x_0)f}(h,\xi) =|\det h_0|^{1/2}\psi(\xi x_0) \widehat f(h_0^{-1}h,\xi h_0). \tag{6.625} \] The fibre \(\xi=0\) has additive measure zero: arbitrarily many distinct translates of a singleton lie in the compact group \(\mathcal O^m\), so a singleton cannot have positive measure. On its complement use (6.619), so the variables are \((\eta,\xi,s)\), with measure \(d\nu_m(\eta)d\xi\,dp_m(s)\). Formula (6.625) leaves \(\eta\) fixed and replaces \[ (\xi,s)\longmapsto (\xi h_0,b(\xi,h_0)^{-1}s). \tag{6.626} \] This is precisely (6.621) with the left regular fibre action. The change of variables is a measurable bijection on the displayed charts and preserves the computed measure. First applying it to compactly supported tests and then completing proves the unitary identity (6.622).

If the fibre representation is \(1_{\mathscr M}\otimes\tau\), (6.621) leaves the \(\mathscr M\)-coordinate fixed. Starting from \(P_1=1\), induction in (6.622) therefore gives (6.623), with \(\mathscr M_n=L^2(Y_{n-1},d\nu_{n-1})\otimes\mathscr M_{n-1}\). All the spaces are separable, since their local coordinate spaces are second countable. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.282 — smooth evaluation and a separating Whittaker functional. Write \(\psi_{U_n}(u)=\psi(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}u_{i,i+1})\). There is a linear functional \(\ell_n\) on the smooth vectors of \(\sigma_n\) satisfying \[ \ell_n(\sigma_n(u)v)=\psi_{U_n}(u)\ell_n(v). \tag{6.627} \] Its \(P_n\)-translates separate those smooth vectors. For \(J_n(a)=P_n\cap(1+\varpi^a M_n(\mathcal O))\), \(a\ge1\), it obeys \[ |\ell_n(v)|\le q^{a n(n-1)/4}\|v\| \qquad(v\in\mathscr K_n^{J_n(a)}). \tag{6.628} \]

Proof: evaluation is defined. In (6.623), first let \(\Phi\) be fixed by the embedded compact group \(L=1+\varpi^a M_m(\mathcal O)\subset H_m\). Its row orbit at \(e\) is \[ B=e+\varpi^a\mathcal O^m, \qquad\operatorname{vol}(B)=q^{-am},\qquad J=L\cap P_m=J_m(a). \tag{6.629} \] On \(B\) the pivot is \(m\) and \(t_\xi\in L\). Pull the section back to \(L\) by \(A(h)=\sigma_m(b(e,h))\Phi(eh)\). Probability Haar measure on \(L\) pushes forward to the normalized additive measure on \(B\): both are invariant under the transitive \(L\)-action, which has determinant of absolute value one. The pullback is therefore a well-defined \(L^2\) function. It has left \(J\)-covariance, and \(L\)-invariance of \(\Phi\) makes it right invariant on \(L\). Averaging right translations on this compact group makes \(A\) equal almost everywhere to one vector \(v\), with \(v\in\mathscr K_m^J\). The constant section \(v\) has precisely this pullback, because \(b(e,h)\in J\) for \(h\in L\). The pullback is an isometry after normalizing the measure of \(B\), hence injective. Consequently \(\Phi(\xi)=v\) almost everywhere on \(B\). Define \[ \operatorname{ev}_e\Phi=v\in\mathscr K_m^{J_m(a)},\qquad \|\operatorname{ev}_e\Phi\|\le q^{am/2}\|\Phi\|. \tag{6.630} \] Shrinking \(L\) leaves the same vector on an open intersection of positive measure, so the definition is independent of the chosen level. Every smooth vector is fixed by a sufficiently small such embedded \(L\). Translating this construction gives preferred point values at every nonzero row. They are locally constant sections and agree on overlaps, since almost-everywhere equality of locally constant sections implies equality everywhere. Thus (6.621) holds at these point values, rather than only on unspecified \(L^2\) representatives.

Proof: character, separation and bound. Set \(\ell_1=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C}\) and recursively \(\ell_n=\ell_m\operatorname{ev}_e\). For \(u=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u_m&x\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in U_n\), one has \(e u_m=e\), \(b(e,u_m)=u_m\), and \(|\det u_m|=1\). Hence \[ \operatorname{ev}_e(\sigma_n(u)\Phi) =\psi(x_m)\sigma_m(u_m)\operatorname{ev}_e\Phi. \tag{6.631} \] Induction gives (6.627). If \(\Phi\ne0\), a preferred value \(\Phi(\xi)\) is nonzero somewhere. Applying \(\sigma_n(t_\xi,0)\) brings this to a nonzero smooth value at \(e\), multiplied by \(|\det t_\xi|^{1/2}\). By induction, a \(P_m\)-translate of that value has nonzero \(\ell_m\). The same \(P_m\) embedded in \(H_m\) fixes \(e\); its action on the value has only the additional nonzero factor \(|\det p|^{1/2}\). This proves separation by translates.

For a \(J_n(a)\)-fixed vector the evaluation in (6.630) is \(J_m(a)\)-fixed. Multiply its bound by the inductive bound. Since \(am/2+a m(m-1)/4=a n(n-1)/4\), this proves (6.628). In particular the functional is continuous on each fixed-level Hilbert subspace. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.283 — restriction of the central regular representation. Let \(G_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), \(Z_n=F^\times I_n\), and let \(\omega\) be unitary. The restriction to \(P_n\) of left translation on \(L^2(Z_n\backslash G_n,\omega^{-1})\) is a Hilbert multiplicity of \(\lambda_{P_n}\), hence of \(\sigma_n\).

Proof. Use the first maximal pivot of a projective row, normalize that coordinate to one, and call the resulting representative \(y\). Before the pivot its coordinates are in \(\varpi\mathcal O\); after it they are in \(\mathcal O\). These finite clopen projective charts have additive coordinate measures \(dy\), and their total measure is \[ \nu(\mathbb P^{n-1}(F))= 1+q^{-1}+\cdots+q^{-(n-1)}. \tag{6.632} \] Use the same row section \(t_y\), now with \(|\det t_y|=1\). Every \(g\) has a unique decomposition on these charts \[ g=z p t_y,\qquad z\in F^\times,\ p\in P_n. \tag{6.633} \] The last row of \(g\) determines \(z\) and \(y\), and then determines \(p\). Write \(p=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The last row \(zy\) has additive Jacobian \(|z|^{n-1}\); the top \(n-1\) rows have Jacobian \(|z|^{n(n-1)}\). Since \(|\det g|=|z|^n|\det A|\), the matrix Haar density is exactly \[ dg=\frac{dz}{|z|}\, \frac{dA\,db}{|\det A|^n}\,dy =d^\times z\,dp_n\,dy. \tag{6.634} \] Here \(d^\times z=dz/|z|\). Thus the quotient norm is \[ \|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb P^{n-1}(F)}\int_{P_n} |f(p t_y)|^2\,dp_n\,dy. \tag{6.635} \] Central covariance has absolute value one. For \(p_0\in P_n\), left translation replaces \(p\) by \(p_0^{-1}p\) and leaves \(z,y\) unchanged. This proves the multiplicity assertion by an explicit isometry. No invariant measure on the projective space under all of \(G_n\) is asserted; only the displayed coordinate measure is used. Theorem 6.281 proves the last assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.284 — discrete-series genericity in every split degree. Every unitary discrete series \(\pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\) has a nonzero \(\psi_{U_n}\)-Whittaker functional on its smooth vectors. This holds in both field characteristics.

Proof. Fix a unit Hilbert vector \(v_0\). Schur orthogonality in Theorem 6.35 gives the closed isometric coefficient embedding \[ u\longmapsto d_\pi^{1/2}\langle u,\pi(g)v_0\rangle \quad\text{into }L^2(Z_n\backslash G_n,\omega^{-1}), \tag{6.636} \] intertwining \(\pi\) with left translation. Use the formal degree for the measures in (6.634), as permitted by (6.617). By Theorems 6.281 and 6.283 its restriction embeds into \(\mathscr M\otimes\mathscr K_n\), with \(P_n\) acting trivially on the multiplicity space \(\mathscr M\). Partial inner product against some vector of \(\mathscr M\) gives a nonzero bounded \(P_n\)-intertwiner \(T:\mathscr H_\pi\to\mathscr K_n\): otherwise all its coefficients on the dense elementary tensors would be zero.

Smooth \(G_n\)-vectors are dense. Boundedness and equivariance make \(T\) carry them to smooth \(P_n\)-vectors, and some such image is nonzero. The separating assertion of Theorem 6.282 then shows that \(\ell_nT\) is nonzero after translating that vector by an element of \(P_n\). Its \(U_n\)-equivariance is (6.627). The fixed-level bound there makes this a well-defined continuous functional on every fixed compact-open \(G_n\)-level. This is the required Whittaker functional.

If \(\psi_c(x)=\psi(cx)\), conjugation by \(\operatorname{diag}(c^{n-1},c^{n-2},\ldots,1)\) replaces \(\psi_{U_n}\) by \((\psi_c)_{U_n}\). Precomposing the functional with that diagonal action gives the assertion for every nontrivial additive character. For \(n=1\), \(U_1=1\) and the assertion is immediate. \(\square\)

Example 6.285 — sharp smooth evaluation and projective masses. For \(a\ge1\), set \(v_1=1\) and recursively \[ v_n(\xi)=1_{e+\varpi^a\mathcal O^{n-1}}(\xi)v_{n-1}. \quad \ell_n(v_n)=1,\qquad \|v_n\|^2=q^{-a n(n-1)/2}. \tag{6.637} \] These vectors are \(J_n(a)\)-fixed. Indeed the principal linear subgroup preserves the indicated row ball and its cocycle lies in \(J_{n-1}(a)\); its determinant has absolute value one. The column subgroup contributes \(\psi(\xi x)=1\), since \(\xi\) is integral and \(x\in\varpi^a\mathcal O^{n-1}\). The norm is the product of the row-ball volumes. Thus (6.628) is sharp. Evaluation is unbounded on the full Hilbert norm as \(a\to\infty\), although it is bounded at every fixed smooth level.

With the matrix Haar density, the compact part of \(P_n\) has volume \(\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-q^{-j})\). Formula (6.634) gives \[ (1-q^{-1})\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-q^{-j}) (1+q^{-1}+\cdots+q^{-(n-1)}) =\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1-q^{-j}), \tag{6.638} \] the matrix Haar volume of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O)\). The centre contributes the first factor. This checks both the projective density and the central normalization.

The conclusion of Theorem 6.284 is existence of a Whittaker functional. Its proof supplies neither its dimension nor uniqueness of a generic irreducible at a given cuspidal support. Generic pseudo-coefficient trace isolation, integral representation transfer and exact global spectral extraction remain additional assertions.

7. Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 7.1 — an unramified quadratic field. Let \(K/\mathbb Q_p\) be the unramified quadratic extension. Choose \(\xi\in\mathcal O_K^\times\) whose residue generates \(\mathbb F_{p^2}/\mathbb F_p\). Write explicitly the matching matrix and quaternion class, and their centralizers.

Exercise 7.14 — inseparable primary flags and compact germs. In Example 6.143 compute \(p(x_X)\) for \(X=E_{11}\) and \(X=I\). Determine the partitions, centralizer dimensions, orbit dimensions and the canonical kernel flags. For type \((2)\), check the dimension of the bundle in (6.320): its flag base, closed Levi orbit and radical. If a compact test has every proper translated constant term zero, which coefficient can remain in its germ expansion at \(P=p^2\)? Explain why this conclusion cannot be assigned to \(f_{\pi,m}\) merely from its known regular orbital values.

Exercise 7.15 — inseparable character values and a necessary quotient. Let \(F=\mathbb F_2((t))\), \(G=\mathrm{GL}_4(F)\), and let \(\gamma e_i=e_{i+1}\) for \(i<4\), \(\gamma e_4=te_1\). Prove that \(\gamma\) is \(F\)-irreducible and inseparable, find its stabilized chamber and the signs in (6.337), and compute its Steinberg character and the orbital integral of a unit Steinberg coefficient under both centralizer normalizations. For the repeated quadratic action \(s_0=s\oplus s\) of Example 6.143, show why \(\sigma(x)\) cannot replace \(\ell_{G_{s_0}}(x)\) in (6.329). Finally determine the type \((2)\) compact discrete-test coefficient in that example using the proved Schwartz argument.

Exercise 7.16 — quadratic lattice masses and the remaining character obstruction. For \(D=F\), \(q_F=2\), \(m=2\), and \(\boldsymbol n=(2,1)\), compute the additive stabilizer index, its invertible fraction, and the orbit cardinality in each quadratic ramification case. Calculate the two Cartan lists and the closed-primary Euler orbital. Explain how the exponential factors cancel in the Schwartz orbital sum. For the split degree-four character expansion (6.364), does its positive integral dimension sum alone imply that every coefficient is a nonnegative integer?

Exercise 7.17 — an inseparable fixed tree and a primary limit. In Example 6.168 compute the full fixed-vertex stabilizer volumes, the outward shell masses, the spherical factors and the exact convergence threshold. What is the closed germ on nearby elliptic regular classes? Next take \(p_j(T)=T^2+t^jT+t\), \(j\ge1\), over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\). With \(\alpha^2+t^j\alpha+t=0\) and \(\beta^2+\beta+1=0\), find the polynomial of \(\alpha+t^n\beta\) when \(n\ne j\), and prove that a sequence of such separable irreducible quartics tends to \((T^2-t)^2\). Finally compute \(h,\delta,m\) for a quadratic field in \(\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\), with \(D\) quaternion division. Distinguish the primary character-germ assertion from a closed-primary Schwartz bound in that rank.

Exercise 7.18 — paired lengths and a higher-rank singular orbital. In the characteristic-two model with \(Q=2\), determine the stabilizer residues and the orbit sizes for \(r=3,\boldsymbol n=(1)\) and \(r=4,\boldsymbol n=(1,1)\). Then compute \(B\), the Cartan list and the orbit size for \(r=4,\boldsymbol n=(2,1)\). Compute the closed Euler orbital, Steinberg degree and unit Iwahori Steinberg coefficient orbital in ranks three and four. Compare the rank-three normalization when \(d=4\) over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\). Explain why the unit \(u-\tau u\), rather than division by two, is the integral descent input.

Exercise 7.19 — valuation colors and exhaustive counting. In Example 6.184 compute every normalized orbit of index two and three in rank three, and the index-two orbits in rank four. Check each mass and compare their sums with the corresponding coefficients of (6.411). For a positive pair of length two, compute the four stabilizer depths in (6.402), its additive index, and its residual invertible fraction. Why do the linked residue blocks contribute one unit fraction rather than its square? Compute the rank-three and rank-four singular Steinberg orbitals, and explain which part of the proof turns the finite counts into an all-rank classification.

Exercise 7.20 — a quadratic action that is not an involution. Verify every relation in (6.428), prove that \(E/F\) is ramified and separable, and compute \(v_D(u-\tau u)\). In rank five, for \(\boldsymbol n=(2,1)\), calculate the exact mass, Cartan list, Euler orbital, Steinberg degree and unit Iwahori coefficient orbital. Check the criterion (6.427) in total degree ten. In mixed characteristic take \(E=\mathbb Q_2(\sqrt3)\) and \(\theta=1+\sqrt3\): find its Eisenstein polynomial and the recurrence coefficients \(a_\theta,b_\theta\). Explain why an involution identity is unnecessary for the stable intersection.

Exercise 7.21 — cubic submodules and weighted families. Over \(\mathbb F_8\), let \(z^3+z+1=0\). Exhibit a nonzero relation among the three vectors \((1,z),(1,z^2),(1,z^4)\), and explain why their lines do not give a direct sum. Count the normalized rank-three first-level lattices and their two centralizer orbits. For \(Q=2\), compute the masses of \(h_1,h_2,g_{1,0},g_{1,1},g_{2,0},g_{2,1}\). Calculate the Cartan list and both root heights in (6.438) at \(n=1\). Compare the index-two family mass with the total count, and state exactly what convergence (6.437) proves.

Exercise 7.22 — all cyclic quotients and cubic intermediate orbits. For \(r=3,Q=2,e=3\), count the normalized cyclic quotients of lengths one, two and three. Compute every mass \(w_{2,a}\) and \(w_{3,a}\), with the corresponding lengths of \(L_0/I\). Explain why the two equal masses at length two represent distinct orbits, and account for the entire index-two coefficient \(4248\). For the generator \(s=1+\theta\) in the cubic model, compute the exact Cartan list of every normalized length-\(n\) cyclic kernel. Determine the convergence threshold supplied by the primitive-row estimate, and explain its scope in ranks two and three.

Exercise 7.23 — dual masses and an intermediate intersection. At \(Q=2\), compute both cyclic orientations for \((u,v)=(3,1)\) and the dual family \((n,a)=(3,2)\): give quotient lengths, intersection lengths, Cartan lists and masses. For \(g_*\), use (6.458) to find \(L\cap E^3\), and use (6.459) to count additive and invertible stabilizer matrices. Check its Cartan list from the least valuations of \(A\) and \(A^{-1}\). Sum all index-four masses, including the cyclic quotients. Use (6.461) to count both noncyclic quotient types at index five. Explain why this proves a finite-index classification but does not establish the full cubic Schwartz integral, and why transposition requires the opposite algebra.

Exercise 7.24 — noncommutative cubic masses and a wild uniformizer. For \(d=6\), a totally ramified cubic field has quaternionic centralizer. At \(Q=4,r=3,n=2\), compute all cyclic-quotient orbit masses and their sum, and the equal-length quotient orbit \((2,2,0)\). Give the corresponding uniformizer Cartan lists. At \(Q=2,r=4,n=2\), compute every cyclic orbit and compare the sum with the primitive-row count. In Example 6.212 verify the trace, norm and Eisenstein identity, explain why the field is wild and \(\tau^3\ne1\), and compute its displayed mass. Finally, if a normalized rank-three cubic lattice has greatest quotient length \(u=5\), list the possible extreme Cartan deviations \((a,c)\) and the corresponding root heights.

Exercise 7.25 — the full height count and its trace consequence. Compute both columns of (6.489), their one-sided cumulative count at defect two, and their root-weighted sums. Derive the quadratic expression (6.484) by summing \(\min(v,u-v)\). Explain why the arbitrary-generator argument needs the compact stable-line/plane exclusion, rather than a bounded coordinate shift from a uniformizer. Compute all three quantities in (6.487) for \((Q,e,\delta)=(2,4,1)\) and \((4,3,2)\). State which primary partitions are covered and which general transfer assertions remain additional work.

Exercise 7.26 — coefficient colors and strict refinement bounds. In Example 6.228, prove that all three scalar colors are normalized, and compute the number of top cyclic over-lattices of types \((6,3,0)\) and \((3,1,1)\). Derive the counts \(576,64,56\) from the two rank-two primitive-row charts and the coefficient matrix. Compute the singular Euler, Steinberg-degree and unit-coefficient values for the unramified cubic and the mixed inseparable degree-six field. Explain why \(w\) is bounded, how the compact coefficient frame excludes an invariant plane, and why Corollary 6.226 covers all rank-three closed primary types without proving the general local representation correspondence.

Exercise 7.27 — rank four, real coefficients and trace excision. List the proper block sizes for all nonclosed primary partitions when \(hm=4\). Compute \(\eta_s\) and the closed compact germ for the inseparable quartic in Example 6.238. Verify the cycle and Cartan heights in (6.524). For \(P(x)=x^4\) over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\), compute the measure of \(\{x\in\mathcal O_F:v_F(P(x))\ge n\}\), and compare its exponent with Lemma 6.232. Derive the three-by-three table in Figure 20. Prove reality of the coefficients using inversion, compute the \(S_3\) example's identity value and norm, and state exactly which additional trace limit would prove elliptic orthogonality of a finite packet.

Exercise 7.28 — polynomial profiles and exact trace separation. Explain why the division average in (6.528) is unnormalized, why a locally constant profile on its compact polynomial image admits the central-covariant extension (6.530), and why changing the extension preserves the cocenter class when \(r\le4\). For a finite packet in Theorem 6.246, give an explicit sufficient inequality on \(n\) for invertibility of \(H_n\), and verify the exact trace values of (6.543). Compute \((B-A)A^{\mathsf t}\) for (6.546) and compare it with \(I-H\). Finally derive both constants in (6.545), retaining the centralizer degree and ramification index.

Exercise 7.29 — finite flag volumes and the central flat. For \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\), \(P\) upper triangular and \(J=1+\varpi_FM_2(\mathcal O_F)\), compute \(t,\operatorname{vol}(J),\operatorname{vol}(J_M),\operatorname{vol}(J_N)\) before central quotient and verify (6.548). Explain how the diagonal convolution calculation gives (6.555) modulo finite conjugation differences. For \(M=\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\times\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\), describe the flat, the product-cell stabilizer and the cancellation (6.560). Derive all factors in (6.570), including the separable and inseparable degrees. State precisely what (6.568) leaves to be proved for orthogonality.

Exercise 7.30 — finite flags, cyclic components and the trace normalization. Evaluate \(E_3\) on the three cycle types of \(S_3\), and compute the identity value and finite squared norm of its \(\mathrm{GL}_3(k)\) flag combination. For \(r=6,j=2\), describe the two vertex cycles, the signs of the two stable face types, and the dimensions of a compatible \(3+3\) flag in their graded pieces. For \(r=4,d=1,q_F=2,j=2\), compute \(u_2(\Omega^2)\). Verify the two halves in (6.600). Finally explain why (6.589) has no remaining formal-degree factor, and why (6.596)–(6.597) do not by themselves establish individual coefficient integrality or representation existence.

Exercise 7.31 — compact Fourier steps and rational support.

  1. In \(K=\mathbb F_2(t)\), with \(s=t^{-1}\), check the finite and infinite residues of \(t^{-1}dt\). In the representative group (6.602), detect an infinity component \(s^3+s^4\), and then a component \(t^2+t^3\) at the prime \(t\), by suitable rational parameters. Find trace-dual bases for \(\mathbb F_4(t)/\mathbb F_2(t)\), using \(\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0\).
  2. For \(n=4\), compute the dimensions of \(U^{(i)}\) and \(V_i\). At each stage identify the proper radical whose constant term makes \(C_{i,0}=0\). Explain why no assertion that \(F_i\) is itself a cusp form on \(\mathrm{GL}_i\) is needed.
  3. Put \(P=t^2+t+1\). Among matrices in \(\mathrm{GL}_2(K)\) with polynomial entries of degree less than three and determinant a unit at \(P\), prove that the inverse image of the scalar class modulo \(P^2\) contains only globally scalar matrices. Show that reduction modulo \(P\) alone does not suffice.
  4. Verify (6.615) and the traces of \((12)-(23)\) in all three irreducibles of \(S_3\). Explain precisely why a nonzero Poincaré function and local pseudo-coefficient trace zeros do not alone prove exact discrete-series globalization.

Exercise 7.32 — mirabolic densities and smooth evaluation.

  1. For \(m=2\), compute the \(\nu_2\)-measure of the shell \(\|\eta\|_\infty=q^{-b}\). Compute the Haar mass in (6.619) obtained by also requiring \(s\in P_2\cap\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathcal O)\). Give the values for \(q=2\), \(b=0,1,2\).
  2. Compute the three projective-chart masses for \(\mathbb P^2(F)\) when \(q=2\), and check the \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathcal O)\) volume in (6.638). Write the \(\sigma_2\) action explicitly. For \(n=3\), \(a=2\), compute the norm and evaluation of the vectors in (6.637), before and after normalization.
  3. In the finite group \(P_3(\mathbb F_2)\), compute the dimensions of the zero and nonzero last-column Fourier parts of the regular representation. Check the dimension of its nonzero part using the stabilizer \(P_2(\mathbb F_2)\). Explain why one must retain the zero part in this finite calculation.
  4. In Theorem 6.284, explain why a bounded nonzero component map \(T\) carries smooth vectors to the domain of \(\ell_n\), and why \(\ell_nT\) is nonzero. Identify exactly which multiplicity or uniqueness conclusions are not supplied by this argument.

Solution 7.1. Let \(\sigma\) be the nontrivial automorphism, \(t=\xi+\sigma\xi\), and \(n=\xi\sigma\xi\). The reduction of \(T^2-tT+n\) is irreducible and separable, so its lift is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_p\). In the cyclic model \[ D_p=K\oplus K\Pi,\qquad \Pi^2=p,\qquad \Pi a=\sigma(a)\Pi, \] the element \(\xi\) has that reduced polynomial. The matching matrix is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-n\\1&t\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the matrix of multiplication by \(\xi\) on \(K\) in the basis \(1,\xi\). Its centralizer is the multiplication copy of \(K^\times\); the quaternion centralizer is also \(K^\times\), by Theorem 1.1. Conjugation by \(\Pi\) exchanges \(\xi\) and \(\sigma\xi\), so either root defines the same class. This remains valid at \(p=2\), because unramified residue extensions are separable.

Exercise 7.2 — check the Steinberg character. Verify (2.3) for the trivial representation of \(D^\times\) and the Steinberg representation of \(G\), including an unramified unitary character twist.

Solution 7.2. An elliptic matrix has no invariant \(F\)-line. Proposition 2.2 consequently gives zero character for \(C^\infty(\mathbb P^1(F))\) on the elliptic regular set. Subtracting the character one of its constant subrepresentation gives \(\Theta_{\mathrm{St}}=-1\). The trivial quaternion character is one, proving the required minus sign. Under a twist, the left side becomes \(-\chi(\det g)\), while the quaternion side becomes \(\chi(\operatorname{nrd}b)\). The determinants and norms match by Theorem 1.1, so the negative relation persists. The central characters are both \(\chi(z^2)\). The same computation in fact works for any quasicharacter; unitarity only ensures that the twist belongs to the discrete-series set in (2.2).

Exercise 7.3 — three dimensions. Evaluate both sides of (4.3) for \(p=11,13,37\), showing the mass and elliptic corrections.

Solution 7.3. The complete substitutions are:

\(p\) \((s_4,s_3)\) mass \((p-1)/12\) class-number corrections \(h\) genus \((p+1)/12-e_2/4-e_3/3\)
11 \((-1,-1)\) \(5/6\) \(1/2+2/3\) 2 \(1-0-0=1\)
13 \((1,1)\) \(1\) \(0+0\) 1 \(7/6-1/2-2/3=0\)
37 \((1,1)\) \(3\) \(0+0\) 3 \(19/6-1/2-2/3=2\)

In each row the last column is \(h-1\), and equals \(\dim S_2\) by the differential dictionary. In particular the level-thirteen quaternion class space consists only of constants and has no cusp line.

Exercise 7.4 — what transfers at the identity? Explain how the local minus sign fits the identity contribution of the compact trace formula. Specify the analytic transfer input and why global multiplicities remain positive.

Solution 7.4. A scalar has a repeated characteristic-polynomial root and is not regular. Thus the identity conjugacy class is outside Theorem 1.1 and cannot be used as an extra regular matching class. What the transfer theorem provides is the identity-value relation (3.4): with its paired Haar measures, \(f'(1)=-f(1)\). Lemmas 2.11 and 2.20 prove this identity-value relation for every finite and real matching pair in the explicit paired measures. Theorem 2.22 and Corollary 2.31 prove the real and finite negative spectral identity (3.5), respectively; Lemmas 2.19 and 2.27 justify integration on tests meeting singular classes. Arthur, Lemma 25.2 and Theorem 25.1(b), treats the corresponding identity-value and spectral identities.

For a compact quotient, Lesson 18 gives the identity term \(\operatorname{vol}(X)f(1)\). The orbital integral itself is \(f(1)\), while the quotient volume is its geometric coefficient; they must not be conflated. Replacing the locally transferred identity value introduces the sign prescribed by (3.4). This accounts for that contribution once transfer has been established; the compact formula alone does not establish transfer or force a local sign. Proposition 2.2 independently checks the sign in the simplest representation. Lemma 3.2 proves that the two global quotient volumes in these paired measures both equal \(1/6\). At two ramified places, Lemma 3.3 gives zero averaged constant term. Theorem 3.4 then cancels the split semisimple weighted terms, the unipotent finite part, the continuous logarithmic derivative and its reflected endpoint. Determinant characters remain in the split discrete trace and correspond to norm characters in Section 3.6. Finally, the ramification set has even cardinality. The product of the local minus signs is one, by (3.6); Theorem 3.5 gives an equality of full discrete traces and Lemma 3.6 gives positive equal multiplicities.

Exercise 7.5 — an explicit Schwartz convolution constant. In Example 6.84 put \(Z_j=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-j}\), \(j=2,3,4\), and \(\beta=(q-1)/(q+1)\). Express \(C_4\) in these three convergent series. Give a numerical upper bound for the error after truncating its radial integral at \(\sigma\le R\), and state the resulting convolution estimate.

Solution 7.5. Set \(n=k+1\) in (6.192). Then \(1+\beta k=\beta n+(1-\beta)\), so direct expansion gives \[ C_4=1+\frac{q+1}{q}\left[ \beta^2(Z_2-1)+2\beta(1-\beta)(Z_3-1) +(1-\beta)^2(Z_4-1)\right]. \] Each series converges by comparison with \(\int_1^\infty x^{-j}dx\). Its omitted terms start at \(n>R+1\). For integer \(R\ge0\), monotonicity of \(x^{-j}\) bounds that series tail by \((R+1)^{1-j}/(j-1)\). Therefore, writing \(C_4(R)\) for the integral on \(\sigma\le R\), \[ 0\le C_4-C_4(R)\le\frac{q+1}{q}\left[ \frac{\beta^2}{R+1}+\frac{\beta(1-\beta)}{(R+1)^2} +\frac{(1-\beta)^2}{3(R+1)^3}\right]. \] Theorem 6.81 now reads \(p_N(f_1*f_2)\le C_4p_{N+4}(f_1)p_N(f_2)\) in this rank-two normalization. Any computed partial sum plus the displayed error is an explicit admissible upper bound for that constant; no evaluation of the \(Z_j\) in terms of other constants is needed.

Exercise 7.6 — a kernel flag and orbital homogeneity. Take \(r=6\) and nilpotent Jordan type \(\lambda=(3,2,1)\) over \(D\). Find the flag in Theorem 6.86, the centralizer and orbit dimensions over \(F\), and the dimension of its cotangent fibre. For \(a\in F^\times\), determine \(\mu_\lambda(\phi(a\,\cdot))\) and \(\widehat\mu_\lambda(\phi(a\,\cdot))\). Evaluate the corresponding unipotent orbital integral of a smooth discrete-series coefficient.

Solution 7.6. The columns are \((3,2,1)\), so the flag dimensions over \(D\) are \(3,5,6\). The flag is exactly \(\ker X\subset\ker X^2\subset\ker X^3=V\): if any flag of those dimensions is lowered by \(X\), its \(i\)-th space lies in \(\ker X^i\) and has the same dimension. The commuting algebra has \(F\)-dimension \((3^2+2^2+1^2)d^2=14d^2\), and its unit group is the centralizer. The orbit dimension is \((36-14)d^2=22d^2\). The flag and its cotangent fibre both have dimension \((3\cdot2+3\cdot1+2\cdot1)d^2=11d^2\).

Changing variables \(Y=aX\) in (6.194) gives \[ \mu_\lambda(\phi(a\,\cdot))=|a|_F^{-11d^2}\mu_\lambda(\phi). \] The parabolic Lie algebra in (6.200) has dimension \((36-11)d^2=25d^2\). Changing variables there gives \[ \widehat\mu_\lambda(\phi(a\,\cdot)) =|a|_F^{-25d^2}\widehat\mu_\lambda(\phi). \] These exponents come from additive \(F\)-dimensions; they require no exponential map or factorial. Finally the parabolic has three blocks and is proper. Equations (6.195), (6.197) and Theorem 6.77 show that the coefficient's orbital integral is absolutely convergent and zero, with any Haar normalization on this nontrivial orbit. \(\square\)

Exercise 7.7 — equal homogeneity degrees. In \(M_6(D)\), compare the nilpotent types \(\lambda=(3,3)\) and \(\nu=(4,1,1)\). Compute their column partitions, centralizer dimensions and scalar homogeneity degrees. Can scalar dilates of one compact test distinguish the two orbital functionals? Explain what tests the germ construction supplies instead.

Solution 7.7. The columns are \((2,2,2)\) and \((3,1,1,1)\). Both squared sums are \(12\), so both centralizers have \(F\)-dimension \(12d^2\), both orbits have dimension \((36-12)d^2=24d^2\), and both degrees in (6.206) are \(12d^2\). They are distinct orbits: their first kernel dimensions are \(2\) and \(3\), respectively.

For any one test \(\phi\), its scalar dilates have the two orbital coordinates \[ \bigl(\mu_\lambda(\phi(t\,\cdot)),\mu_\nu(\phi(t\,\cdot))\bigr) =|t|_F^{-12d^2} \bigl(\mu_\lambda(\phi),\mu_\nu(\phi)\bigr). \] Thus the coordinate vectors of all such dilates span a space of dimension at most one. Scalar sampling of that test cannot recover two independent orbital coordinates. If both coordinates vanish, it recovers neither. If they do not both vanish, the nonzero invariant functional \(\mu_\nu(\phi)\mu_\lambda-\mu_\lambda(\phi)\mu_\nu\) annihilates every scalar dilate, while Lemma 6.92 shows that this functional is not zero.

Theorem 6.93 instead supplies a finite collection of dual tests, including tests with coordinates \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) on these two measures and zero on every other nilpotent type. The compact-support expansion is uniform on their finite span. The coincidence of the two homogeneity degrees does not collapse these orbital coordinates and does not prove or disprove linear independence of the regular germ functions. \(\square\)

Exercise 7.8 — a separable degree-four elliptic class in characteristic two. Let \(F=\mathbb F_2((\varpi))\), and write the quaternion division algebra in its unramified cyclic model \(D=\mathbb F_4((\varpi))\oplus\mathbb F_4((\varpi))\Pi\), with \(\Pi^2=\varpi\) and \(\Pi a=a^2\Pi\) for \(a\in\mathbb F_4\). Choose \(a^2+a+1=0\), and put \(\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}0&\Pi\\1&\varpi a\end{pmatrix}\). Compute its reduced polynomial and prove that it is separable and irreducible. Show that \(\gamma\) inverts the edge joining \([\mathcal O_D^2]\) to \([e_1\Pi\mathcal O_D+e_2\mathcal O_D]\). For the Haar measures of Section 6.20, compute \(O_\gamma(W_{\log2})\) and \(O_\gamma(V_3)\), and give both values also when the maximal compact subgroup of the torus has volume one. One may use \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\), \(s>1\).

Solution 7.8. Over \(L=\mathbb F_4((\varpi))\), use the splitting matrices \(a\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(a,a^2)\) and \(\Pi\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&\varpi\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). They satisfy both cyclic relations. The reduced polynomial is the determinant of the resulting four-dimensional matrix polynomial. Eliminating its scalar upper-left block, first over \(L(X)\) and then as a polynomial identity, gives \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{rch}_\gamma(X) &=(X^2-\varpi aX)(X^2-\varpi a^2X)-\varpi\\ &=X^4+\varpi X^3+\varpi^2X^2+\varpi. \end{aligned} \tag{7.1} \] Here \(a+a^2=a^3=1\). The derivative is \(\varpi X^2\), relatively prime to the polynomial because its constant term is nonzero. For a root \(\theta\), the least valuation among its four terms must occur at least twice. If \(v_F(\theta)\le0\), the fourth-power term is the unique least term. If \(v_F(\theta)>0\), the cubic and quadratic terms have valuations greater than one, so \(4v_F(\theta)=1\). Thus the value group of \(F(\theta)\) contains \(1/4\); its ramification index, hence its degree, is at least four. The monic polynomial has degree four, so it is irreducible, and the extension is totally ramified. It follows that \(\gamma\) is elliptic regular, even in characteristic two.

Let \(\Lambda_0=e_1\mathcal O_D+e_2\mathcal O_D\) and \(\Lambda_1=e_1\Pi\mathcal O_D+e_2\mathcal O_D\). Its two columns show \(\gamma\Lambda_0=\Lambda_1\), since \(\varpi a\in\Pi\mathcal O_D\). The same calculation gives \(\gamma\Lambda_1=\Lambda_0\Pi\). Hence it swaps the two vertices, and its fixed set is their midpoint. Here \(d=2\), \(q=q_D=4\), \(\beta=3/5\), and \(e(F[\gamma]/F)=4\). Formula (6.233) gives \[ O_\gamma(W_{\log2})=\frac43,\qquad O_\gamma(V_3)=\frac{\zeta(3)+3\zeta(2)}{10}. \tag{7.2} \] For the second identity, substitute (6.228) in the inverted-edge sum (6.231), and set \(k=j+1\). The sum becomes \(2\sum_{k\ge1}(2/5+6k/5)(2k)^{-3}\), giving exactly (7.2). Its general exponent converges precisely for exponent greater than two, as in Corollary 6.104. Maximal-compact torus normalization divides both values by four: they are \(1/3\) and \((\zeta(3)+3\zeta(2))/40\). \(\square\)

Exercise 7.9 — why angular averaging is needed. Over \(F=\mathbb F_2((\varpi))\), let \[ \gamma=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\varpi\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad x_L=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi^{2L},\varpi^L,1),\quad L\ge1. \] Prove that \(\gamma\) is elliptic regular. Compute the two Cartan weights \(D_C(x_L)\) and \(D_C(x_L^{-1}\gamma x_L)^{1/2}\). Decide whether the integrand in (6.242), with \(k=1\), can be bounded by \(C\Xi(x_L)^2(1+\sigma(x_L))^m\) for fixed \(C,m\). Explain precisely how Theorem 6.110 nevertheless proves convergence at this class.

Solution 7.9. The reduced polynomial is \(X^3-\varpi\). Every root in an algebraic closure has valuation \(1/3\), so its field of definition has ramification index divisible by three and degree at least three. The cubic is therefore irreducible. Its derivative in characteristic two is \(X^2\), which is relatively prime to it, so it is separable. These are the elliptic regular hypotheses of Section 6.1.

The conjugate is monomial, with nonzero entries of valuations \(1-2L,L,L\). Multiplication by permutation matrices puts a monomial matrix in Cartan form, so its sorted Cartan valuations are \((L,L,1-2L)\), whereas those of \(x_L\) are \((2L,L,0)\). For \(\mathrm{GL}_3(F)\), \(D_C\) at \((a,b,c)\), \(a\ge b\ge c\), is \(q^{-((a-b)+(a-c)+(b-c))}=q^{-2(a-c)}\). Consequently \[ D_C(x_L)=q^{-4L},\qquad D_C(x_L^{-1}\gamma x_L)^{1/2}=q^{-3L+1},\qquad q=2. \tag{7.3} \] The two-sided bounds of Lemma 6.80 show that \[ \frac{\Xi(x_L^{-1}\gamma x_L)}{\Xi(x_L)^2} \ge c\frac{q^{L+1}}{(1+2L)^{2b}} \tag{7.4} \] for a fixed \(c>0\). Exponentials exceed every fixed power: for any \(a\ge0\), the ratio of consecutive terms of \(q^L/(1+2L)^a\) tends to \(q>1\), and is eventually larger than a fixed number greater than one. Thus the proposed bound fails for every fixed \(C,m\).

Corollary 6.108 bounds the integral over \(k\), rather than each integrand. Its proof accounts for the flag measure by the bounded kernel of Lemma 6.107. Lemma 6.109 transfers the decay factor in the orbital variable to \((1+\sigma(x))^{-s}\). The positive integral calculation (6.249) then bounds the orbital integral by a constant times \(\int_{G/Z}\Xi(x)^2(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}d\bar x\), which is finite for every integer \(s>2b+2\). The cutoff and elliptic coefficient identity follow from the same theorem. Neither step uses the pointwise estimate disproved in (7.4). \(\square\)

Exercise 7.10 — a lattice cut and a formal-degree quantum. For a rank-four vertex with normalized exponents \((8,5,1,0)\), compute \(p_3(x)\) and the two positive diagonals in (6.257). For \(N=2\), identify the input square norm supplied by (6.263). Separately, take \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\), \(D=F\), \(q=|\mathcal O_F/\varpi_F|\), and \(\operatorname{vol}(KZ/Z)=1\). Compute the quotient volumes of the full vertex and edge stabilizers, including edge inversions. Find a valid common quantum \(\alpha_G\) for (6.268) when \(q\) is odd and when it is even, and give the resulting fixed-level bound. Does that bound assert that any representation at the level exists?

Solution 7.10. The truncated exponents are \((3,3,1,0)\), and the remaining exponents are \((5,2,0,0)\). Each tuple is nonincreasing and nonnegative; their componentwise sum is \((8,5,1,0)\). They are the exponents of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). Thus \(\sigma(p_3x)=3\), and the path stops at \(k=8\). For \(N=2\), the kernel's squared weight is bounded by an input weight \(\ell^{11}\) in (6.263); the input square norm \(q_6\), whose squared weight is \(\ell^{12}\), suffices.

The vertex stabilizer is \(ZK\) and has quotient volume one, by Lemma 6.101 with \(d=1\). The subgroup fixing both ends of an edge is an Iwahori subgroup modulo \(Z\), of index \(q+1\) in the vertex stabilizer: reduction modulo \(\varpi_F\) identifies the neighbouring vertices with the \(q+1\) lines in a two-dimensional residue space. Its quotient volume is \(1/(q+1)\). The matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&\varpi_F\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) exchanges the ends of the standard edge in every characteristic. The full edge stabilizer has this pointwise stabilizer as a subgroup of index two, since its action on the two ends has kernel exactly the pointwise stabilizer. Its quotient volume is \(2/(q+1)\).

Formula (6.268) therefore places every formal degree in \[ \mathbb Z+\frac{q+1}{2}\mathbb Z. \tag{7.5} \] For odd \(q\), this group is \(\mathbb Z\), so \(\alpha_G=1\) is valid. For even \(q\), \(q+1\) is odd and the group is \(\tfrac12\mathbb Z\), so \(\alpha_G=1/2\) is valid. Positivity excludes zero and negative elements as formal degrees. Thus (6.269) bounds the number at a compatible level by \(\operatorname{vol}(JZ/Z)^{-1}\) for odd \(q\), and by \(2\operatorname{vol}(JZ/Z)^{-1}\) for even \(q\). These are upper bounds. They prove neither that the set is nonempty nor that any proposed member has the required representation or character identity. \(\square\)

Exercise 7.11 — fixed interiors and a matching pair's scalar values. A three-dimensional simplex has vertex permutation \((12)(34)\). Determine the dimension of its fixed interior and verify its contribution in (6.282). Then take \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\), where \(D\) has degree \(d\), and a division algebra \(\mathcal D\) of degree \(2d\). Give both maximal compact subgroups volume one and \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) central volume one. Compute the identity values of the matching Euler tests on \(G\) and \(\mathcal D^\times\), including the full edge stabilizer on the first group. Compare their regular orbital values and their identity values. What is the elliptic squared norm of their orbital class function?

Solution 7.11. There are two permutation cycles, so the fixed interior has dimension one. The permutation has sign \(+1\), and the alternating simplex factor is \((-1)^3=-1\). This equals \((-1)^1\), the contribution of its open fixed interval. Counting just a barycentre as a fixed vertex would give the wrong sign.

Put \(q=q_D=q_F^d\). By Lemma 6.101 the full vertex stabilizer has quotient volume \(d\). The actual-lattice subgroup fixing both ends of an edge is Iwahori, of index \(q+1\) in \(K\). The element \(\Pi I\) fixes both standard lattice classes and supplies the same \(d\) division-valuation cosets modulo central scalars. Hence the pointwise edge stabilizer has quotient volume \(d/(q+1)\). The matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&\Pi\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) exchanges the ends in either characteristic. The full edge stabilizer has twice that volume, namely \(2d/(q+1)\). There is one vertex orbit and one edge orbit. Formula (6.279) at the identity is consequently \[ \mathfrak e_G(1)=\frac1d-\frac{q+1}{2d} =-\frac{q-1}{2d}. \tag{7.6} \] The rank-one building for \(\mathcal D^\times\) is a point. Its central quotient consists of \(2d\) compact-unit valuation cosets, so has volume \(2d\). Its Euler test is the constant \(1/(2d)\) on the group modulo the centre. Thus \[ \mathfrak e_{\mathcal D^\times}(1)=\frac1{2d},\qquad \frac{\mathfrak e_G(1)}{\mathfrak e_{\mathcal D^\times}(1)}=-(q-1). \tag{7.7} \] Nevertheless both ordinary orbital integrals are one on every matching elliptic regular class, with quotient-volume-one torus measures. The nonelliptic regular classes of \(G\) have no match in the division group and give zero by Theorem 6.122. Thus this is precisely the matching pair in Corollary 6.123. Its orbital class function is the constant one on the elliptic class space, so its squared elliptic norm is one by (6.284). These are orbital values of test functions. The scalar identity is outside the regular-class comparison, and the displayed family alone does not assign irreducible representations. \(\square\)

Exercise 7.12 — a rank-three projection over a quaternion division algebra. Let \(q_F=2\), \(d=2\), \(r=3\), and give \(K\) and \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) volume one. Compute \(q_D,N,v_I,P_a(q_D^{-1}),C\) and the degree in (6.295). Compute the first four coefficients of \(P_a(t)\), the scalar Euler value, and its trace on every \(\pi_\eta\). If \(\eta\) is a primitive sixth root, distinguish \(\Phi_\eta(\tau)\) from the coefficient of its unit cyclic vector at \(\tau\). Compare the scalar Euler value with that on a division algebra of degree six. Do these calculations already identify their actual elliptic characters?

Solution 7.12. Here \(q_D=2^2=4\) and \(N=6\). Counting complete flags gives \([3]_4!=(1+4)(1+4+16)=105\), so \(v_I=1/105\). Formula (6.290) gives \[ P_a(1/4)=\frac{1-4^{-3}}{(1-4^{-1})^3}=\frac73, \qquad C=\frac6{105}\frac73=\frac2{15}, \qquad d_{\pi_\eta}=\frac{15}{2}. \tag{7.8} \] The independent product expression is \((4-1)(4^2-1)/6=15/2\). Also \(P_a(t)=(1+t+t^2)/(1-t)^2=1+3t+6t^2+9t^3+\cdots\). The full chamber stabilizer has quotient volume \(Nv_I=2/35\): its rotation group has six elements, although its permutation of three vertices has order three. Omitting the two rotations in the kernel would change the normalization.

Since \((-1)^{r-1}=1\), Corollary 6.129 gives \(\mathfrak e_G(1)=15/2\). Its trace on \(\pi_1\) is one and its trace on each of the other five \(\pi_\eta\) is zero. The function in (6.293) has \(\Phi_\eta(\tau)=\eta^{-1}\), whereas the unit-vector coefficient in (6.297) has value \(\eta\). The inverse phase is required by left translation and the convention that the inner product is linear in its first variable.

For a division algebra \(\mathcal D\) of degree six, its compact central quotient has six unit-valuation cosets, so \(\mathfrak e_{\mathcal D^\times}(1)=1/6\). The ratio of the two scalar Euler values is therefore \(45\). Their regular Euler orbital integrals still match by Corollary 6.123. The calculation constructs actual discrete series and determines their degrees and their traces of this test. It does not turn matching orbital values of Euler tests into an elliptic character identity, nor establish character orthogonality or the full representation transfer. \(\square\)

Exercise 7.13 — an apartment primitive and two torus measures. In the rank-two apartment let \(E_j=[j,j+1]\), oriented to the right. Its chain boundary has vertex coefficient \((\partial a)_j=a_{j-1}-a_j\). Give an infinite chain whose boundary is the single vertex \([0]\), and check the bounds (6.307). Explain why the constant fundamental chain is also allowed. Then let \(q_F=2\), \(d=2\), \(r=2\). Compute the zero germ for an unramified quartic elliptic field and a totally ramified quartic elliptic field, both with maximal-compact torus measure and with volume-one torus quotient. Among proposed discrete-series degrees \(9/4\) and \(5/4\), which does Corollary 6.136 exclude? For the other candidate, state the forced elliptic character value near one, without claiming its existence.

Solution 7.13. Take \(a_j=1\) for \(j<0\) and \(a_j=0\) for \(j\ge0\). Then \(a_{j-1}-a_j\) is one exactly at \(j=0\). The chamber distance from \(E_0\) is \(|j|\). Both this chain and the constant chain \(u_j=1\) satisfy every weighted bound, since \(q^{-|j|/2}(1+|j|)^M\) is bounded for every fixed \(M\). The first chain shows that the completed degree-zero class disappears; the second is a top cycle because its two coefficients cancel at every vertex. Its infinite support is essential. The ordinary compactly supported apartment complex instead has an augmentation in degree zero.

For the division group data, \(q_D=4\), \(N=4\), \(\epsilon=-1\), and \(d_{\mathrm{St}_G}=(4-1)/4=3/4\). Formula (6.312) gives \[ \Gamma_0^{\mathrm{MC}}(E_{\mathrm{unr}})=-\frac43, \qquad \Gamma_0^{\mathrm{MC}}(E_{\mathrm{tr}})=-\frac13, \qquad \Gamma_0^{\operatorname{vol}(T/Z)=1}=-\frac43. \tag{7.9} \] The ramification indices are one and four. Dividing by the torus quotient volume gives the maximal-compact normalization, rather than multiplying by it.

The proposed degrees give ratios \(3\) and \(5/3\) to \(d_{\mathrm{St}_G}\). The second ratio is not an integer, so degree \(5/4\) is impossible. If a discrete series of degree \(9/4\) exists, its actual elliptic character is \(-3\) sufficiently near one. Its compact test has maximal-compact orbital value \(-3\) in the unramified field and \(-3/4\) in the totally ramified field; multiplying by the respective quotient volumes gives \(-3\) in both cases. Integrality is a necessary condition, and this computation does not supply the representation of the remaining candidate degree. \(\square\)

Solution 7.14. For \(X=E_{11}\), \(u=0,v=1\), so \(p(x_X)\) has off-diagonal block \(s\), which is invertible. Its square is zero, its rank is two, and its kernel is the first standard \(F^2\). Thus the partition is \((2)\), with columns \(1,1\) and centralizer dimension \(2(1^2+1^2)=4\). Its orbit dimension is \(16-4=12\). For \(X=I\), \(u=v=0\), so the partition is \((1,1)\), its sole column is \(2\), its centralizer dimension is \(2\cdot2^2=8\), and its orbit dimension is \(8\). Its kernel flag is just \(0\subset V\); the chosen two-block flag is not its canonical kernel flag. \[ \begin{array}{c|ccc|c} \text{type }(2)&\dim(G/P)&\dim\mathcal O_s^M&\dim N&\dim Y\\ \hline &4&(4-2)+(4-2)&4&12 \end{array} \tag{7.10} \] The bundle dimension agrees with the orbit dimension. The full-measure condition is the complement of the two independent linear equations \(b+tc=0\), \(a+d=0\).

For a compact test under the exercise's constant-term hypothesis, Corollary 6.142 gives \(\nu_{(2)}(f)=0\). Only the closed-type coefficient \(\nu_{(1,1)}(f)\) can remain near \(p^2\). The compact discrete test \(f_{\pi,m}\) has prescribed regular and unipotent orbital values, but these are not the pointwise translated-constant-term hypothesis. Its type \((2)\) vanishing is proved by Theorem 6.149 and Corollary 6.150 through absolute Schwartz convergence and finite commutators. Equation (6.347) gives the resulting one-coefficient expression. Theorem 6.271 proves general elliptic character orthogonality. \(\square\)

Solution 7.15. We have \(\gamma^4=tI\). Every root of \(T^4-t\) has valuation \(1/4\), so a monic factor of degree \(j\) would have constant term of valuation \(j/4\). A nontrivial proper factor would contradict its integral valuation. Thus the polynomial is irreducible. Its derivative is zero in characteristic two. The field \(E=F[\gamma]\) is the purely inseparable degree-four extension with uniformizer \(\gamma\).

Put \(L_j=t\mathcal O_F^j\oplus\mathcal O_F^{4-j}\), \(0\le j<4\). Directly \(\gamma L_j=L_{j+1}\) for \(j<3\) and \(\gamma L_3=tL_0\). These are the vertices of a stabilized chamber. The type shift is one modulo four, so every stabilized simplex has all four types and is a chamber. By Theorem 6.148 applied to the trivial representation, their number is one: each contributes \((-1)^3(-1)=1\), and the character is one. Hence the displayed chamber is the unique one. Its permutation sign is \(-1\), and its Euler dimension sign is \(-1\). Equation (6.341), rather than a regular-semisimple assertion, gives the actual Steinberg character at this inseparable element.
