With \(K\)-volume one, \[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde\Theta_{\mathrm{St}}(\gamma)&=-1,& d_{\mathrm{St}}&=\frac{(2-1)(2^2-1)(2^3-1)}4=\frac{21}4,\\ O_\gamma(c_u)&=-\frac4{21} &&(\|u\|=1,\ \operatorname{vol}(E^\times/F^\times)=1),\\ O_\gamma^{\mathrm{mc}}(c_u)&=-\frac1{21} &&(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O_E^\times) =\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O_F^\times)=1). \end{aligned} \tag{7.11} \] The last line divides by \(e(E/F)=4\). This quotient-volume computation uses valuations and units and remains valid for this inseparable field.

For \(s_0=s\oplus s\), choose \(x_a=\operatorname{diag}(t^aI_2,I_2)\). It centralizes \(s_0\), so \(x_a^{-1}s_0x_a=s_0\), while \(\sigma(x_a)=|a|\) and \(\sigma(s_0)=1\). No bound of \(\sigma(x_a)\) by a fixed multiple of \(1+\sigma(x_a^{-1}s_0x_a)\) is possible. In contrast \(\ell_{G_{s_0}}(x_a)=0\), using \(x_a^{-1}\) itself in the centralizer.

The type \((2)\) element of Example 6.143 has the proper two-block flag with simple inseparable quadratic actions on its quotients. Theorem 6.147 proves convergence in those two blocks, Theorem 6.149 proves its full orbital Schwartz bound, and Corollary 6.150 gives \(\nu_{(2)}(f_{\pi,m})=0\). Formula (6.347) retains the closed type \((1,1)\) coefficient. Theorem 6.158 computes its closed germ: the elliptic character constant is the remaining coefficient divided by \(\eta_{s_0}=-1/4\). The value of the discrete-test coefficient depends on the representation; the general local transfer requires further arguments. \(\square\)

Solution 7.16. The tuple has \(m_1=m_2=1\), \(z=0\), and \(T=3\cdot2+1=7\). Both additive indices are \(2^7=128\). The stabilizer's invertible fraction is \(c_1(2)^2=1/4\). The full compact matrix algebra has invertible fraction \(c_2(2)=3/8\) in the ramified case and \(c_2(4)=45/64\) in the unramified case. Thus \[ \begin{aligned} w_{(2,1)}^{\mathrm{ram}} &=128\frac{3/8}{1/4}=192,& w_{(2,1)}^{\mathrm{unram}} &=128\frac{45/64}{1/4}=360,\\ \boldsymbol\nu^{\mathrm{ram}}&=(3,2,-1,-2),& \boldsymbol\nu^{\mathrm{unram}}&=(2,1,-1,-2),\\ \rho^{\mathrm{ram}}&=9,&\rho^{\mathrm{unram}}&=7,\\ \eta_s^{\mathrm{ram}}&=-\frac{2-1}{2\cdot2}=-\frac14,& \eta_s^{\mathrm{unram}}&=-\frac{4-1}{1\cdot2}=-\frac32. \end{aligned} \tag{7.12} \] The Cartan lists come directly from (6.355) with \(k=0\). For the two different values of \(e\), the centralizer is \(\mathrm{GL}_2(E)\) with its maximal compact subgroup of volume one; the Euler denominator retains \(e\). In particular the ramified field may be the inseparable \(F(\sqrt t)\) over \(F=\mathbb F_2((t))\).

For a general tuple the orbit mass is bounded by a fixed multiple of \(2^{T(\boldsymbol n)}\), while the spherical function is bounded by a fixed multiple of \(2^{-T(\boldsymbol n)}(1+n_1)^b\). At \(n_1=R\) there are only \(R+1\) tuples when \(m=2\). A Schwartz exponent greater than \(b+2\) therefore gives a convergent majorant \(C\sum_R(1+R)^{1+b-t}\). This is the positive convergence argument of Theorem 6.155; no cancellation between complex summands is used.

The final implication is false. On a compact group with two distinct one-dimensional characters, the coefficients \(1/2,1/2\) have positive integral dimension sum one without being integral. The coefficients \(2,-1\) have the same dimension sum without being nonnegative. These are counterexamples to an implication from the dimension sum alone, not claims that either pair occurs for a discrete series in (6.364). Theorem 6.271 proves orthogonality. Individual integrality, positivity and bijectivity require further arguments. \(\square\)

Solution 7.17. The full vertex volumes modulo \(F^\times\) are two for \(G\) and two for \(H\), giving ratio one. There is one fixed vertex in the chosen projection fiber at distance zero, and \(2\cdot4^{a-1}\) vertices at distance \(a\ge1\). Their displacement is \(2a\), and their spherical factor is \(4^{-a}(1+6a/5)\). Hence the positive shell summand is \(\tfrac12(1+6a/5)(1+2a)^{-t}\), comparable to \(a^{1-t}\). It is summable exactly for \(t>2\). The Euler coefficient is \(\eta_s=-1/4\), so the closed germ is \(-4/e(F[\gamma]/F)\) on nearby elliptic regular classes, and zero on nonelliptic regular classes, by Theorem 6.166. Its discrete character constant is \(-4O_s(f_{\pi,m_0})\), in the inverse-character convention. The orbital depends on the representation.

The polynomial \(p_j\) is Eisenstein and separable. Its field is ramified quadratic, while adjoining \(\beta\) is the unramified quadratic extension. The composite therefore has degree four, with independent automorphisms \(\alpha\mapsto\alpha+t^j\), \(\beta\mapsto\beta+1\). The four conjugates of \(\alpha+t^n\beta\) differ by \(0,t^j,t^n,t^j+t^n\), all distinct when \(j\ne n\). Thus the element has a separable irreducible polynomial of degree four. Put \[ A=T^2+t^nT+t^{2n}+t,\qquad B=t^j+t^n. \qquad Q_{j,n}=A^2+t^jBA+tB^2. \tag{7.13} \] The norm first over the unramified quadratic extension is \((T-\alpha)^2+t^n(T-\alpha)+t^{2n}=A+B\alpha\). Its norm over \(F\) is the displayed \(Q_{j,n}\). Its derivative is \(t^{j+n}(t^j+t^n)\ne0\). When \(n=j+1\), all coefficients of \(Q_{j,n}-(T^2-t)^2\) have valuation at least \(2j\), and its \(T^2\)-coefficient has valuation exactly \(2j\). This proves coefficient convergence to that inseparable primary polynomial. The norm computation is also an explicit instance of the two-stage limit in Lemma 6.164.

For the last question \(d=e=2\), so \(g=2\), \(h=e/g=1\), \(\delta=d/g=1\), and \(m=r/h=3\). The nonclosed partitions \((3)\) and \((2,1)\) have proper-flag blocks of dimensions at most two. Corollary 6.163 gives their absolute Schwartz orbitals and discrete-test zeros. The compact germ formula and nonzero closed Euler coefficient consequently give the character constant by Theorem 6.166, and Theorem 6.167 gives a finite complex elliptic character expansion. This germ argument needs only the compact closed orbital. For the purely inseparable quadratic field the separate paired-lattice argument in Theorem 6.173 proves the closed Schwartz bound, in every rank. Theorem 6.182 gives the unramified quadratic closed bounds in every even division degree; Theorem 6.188 supplies every ramified quadratic closed bound in either characteristic. Theorem 6.271 proves orthogonality. Individual integrality and positivity of the character coefficients require further arguments. \(\square\)

Solution 7.18. For \(r=3,\boldsymbol n=(1)\), the additive exponent is four. The positive pair has a \(1\)-by-\(1\) residue matrix over \(\mathbb F_4\), and the zero coordinate has its residue matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\). Their invertible fraction is \(c_1(4)c_1(2)=3/8\). Since \(c_3(2)=21/64\), the orbit size is \(2^4(21/64)/(3/8)=14\). Equivalently \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb F_2)\) has order \(168\), and the residue stabilizer has order \(12\).

For \(r=4,\boldsymbol n=(1,1)\), the exponent is eight. The equal pairs give a single \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_4)\) residue condition, with invertible fraction \(c_2(4)=45/64\). The full fraction is \(c_4(2)=315/1024\), giving orbit size \(256(315/1024)/(45/64)=112\). Its residue stabilizer has order \(180\), compared with \(\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb F_2)\) of order \(20160\).

For \((2,1)\), each positive length occurs once. The intersection lengths are \((2,2,1,1)\); the conjugate's Cartan list is \((3,2,0,-1)\), with \(\rho_G=7\), \(\sigma=4\), and \(B=14\). Thus \[ w_{(2,1)}=2^{14}\frac{315/1024}{(3/4)^2}=8960, \qquad \begin{aligned} r=3:&\quad \eta_s=\tfrac12,\quad d_{\mathrm{St}}=\tfrac{15}2,\quad O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}})=\tfrac1{15},\\ r=4:&\quad \eta_s=-\tfrac{21}8,\quad d_{\mathrm{St}}=\tfrac{2835}8,\quad O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}})=\tfrac1{135}. \end{aligned} \tag{7.14} \] The Euler formula uses centralizer \(\mathrm{GL}_r(E)\) with maximal compact volume one and \(e(E/F)=2\). The Steinberg degree uses \(q_D=4\), total degree \(2r\), and \(K\)-volume one. Their ratio, with the sign \((-1)^{r-1}\), is \(\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}(2^j+1)^{-1}\). These computations use an orbital trace and the finite Euler cocenter identity; they do not assign a character density at the singular element.

In division degree four over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\), the same rank-three calculation uses \(\delta=2,Q=4\): its mass is \(252\), its Euler value \(15/4\), its degree \(1275/4\), and its coefficient orbital \(1/85\). Both degree denominators retain the factor \(2r\delta=rd\).

Finally \(\tau u=u+1\), so \(u-\tau u=1\) in characteristic two. For a stable lattice, \(v-\tau v=b(u-\tau u)\) recovers its coefficient \(b\) by multiplication by a unit. The coefficient \(a=v-bu\) then lies in the lattice as well. This proves exact integral descent even though two is zero. In odd residue characteristic the corresponding difference is \(2u\), again a unit. Lemma 6.185 gives the unit condition for every ramified quadratic field by an Eisenstein generator and its quadratic recurrence. \(\square\)

Solution 7.19. Here \(q=4\), \(c_1=3/4\), \(c_2=45/64\), \(c_3=2835/4096\). In rank three the scalar-only orbit with \(z_1=2\) has mass \({3\brack2}_4=21\). The positive pair \(n=1\), with scalar color zero, has \(\rho=2\), \(B=4\), and mass \(4^4c_3/c_1^2=315\); both have index two. At index three the scalar-only orbit has \(z_1=3\) and mass one. The pair \(n=1\) with scalar color one still has mass \(315\), while \(n=2\) with color zero has \(\rho=4\), \(B=6\), and mass \(5040\). There are no two-pair possibilities in rank three.

In rank four and index two the scalar-only orbit has \(z_1=2\) and mass \({4\brack2}_4=357\). The other orbit has \(k=1,n=1,z_0=2,z_1=0\), so \(\rho=3\), \(B=6\), and mass \(4^6c_4/(c_2c_1)=5355\). A two-pair orbit has index at least four. Expanding (6.411) gives \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} r& a_0&a_1&a_2&a_3\\\hline 3&1&21&336&5356\\ 4&1&85&5712&369580 \end{array} \tag{7.15} \] Thus the orbit sums are exactly the coefficients requested.

For a length-two target and source, the congruence depths on \(c-\kappa(b)\pi,d-\kappa(a)\) are \(2,1\); the additional depths on \(a,b\) are both zero. Its additive index is \(4^3\). In rank two its residue matrix is \(\begin{psmallmatrix}\bar a&\bar b\\0&\bar\kappa(\bar a)\end{psmallmatrix}\). Exactly \(3/4\) of these matrices are invertible. The two diagonal entries are linked by an automorphism, so their two invertibility conditions are the same condition. The full rank-two mass is consequently \(4^3c_2/c_1=60\).

Finally \(\eta_s=(-1)^{r-1}\prod_{j<r}(4^j-1)/r\), and \(d_{\mathrm{St}}=\prod_{j<r}(4^j-1)/(2r)\). They are \(15,15/2\) in rank three, and \(-2835/4,2835/8\) in rank four. The Euler cocenter identity gives \(O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}})=\eta_s/[(-1)^{r-1}d_{\mathrm{St}}]=2\) in both. Finite numerical agreement alone does not prove exhaustiveness. Lemma 6.180 proves the formal identities in every rank, and Theorem 6.181 compares the cardinalities of a disjoint subset and the whole finite set at every index. That is the all-rank step. \(\square\)

Solution 7.20. In characteristic two, \(u^2=u+1\) and \(\Pi u+u\Pi=\Pi\). Therefore \[ \theta^2=t+t\Pi+t^2(u+1),\qquad t\theta=t\Pi+t^2u,\qquad u\theta=(\theta+t)u+\theta. \tag{7.16} \] These identities prove (6.428). The polynomial has constant term \(t(1+t)\) of valuation one and trace coefficient \(t\), so it is Eisenstein; its derivative is \(t\ne0\). Thus \(\theta\) generates a separable ramified quadratic field and \(v_D(\theta)=1\). Since \((\tau u-u)\theta=[\theta,u]=\Pi\), the difference has valuation zero. Also \([\theta^2,u]=t\Pi\ne0\), so \(\tau^2\ne1\).

Here \(Q=2\), \(z=1\), \(m_1=m_2=1\), and \(B=2(4\cdot2+2\cdot1)=20\). We have \(c_5(2)=9765/32768\), \(c_1(2)=1/2\), and \(c_1(4)=3/4\). Thus \(w=2^{20}(9765/32768)/[(1/2)(3/4)^2]=1111040\). The Cartan deviations are \((2,1,0,-1,-2)\), with baseline one, so the list is \((3,2,1,0,-1)\) and root height ten. The factors in (6.425) give \(\eta_s=(1\cdot3\cdot7\cdot15)/10=63/2\) and \(d_{\mathrm{St}}=(3\cdot15\cdot63\cdot255)/10=144585/2\). Their positive-sign ratio is \(1/2295\), also \([(2+1)(4+1)(8+1)(16+1)]^{-1}\). The spherical exponential \(4^{-10}\) cancels \(2^{20}\).

For \(N=10,d=2,r=5\), the proper degrees are \(2,5\). The first is quadratic and the second has \(m_5=5\gcd(2,5)/5=1\). Thus (6.427) holds. The resulting finite complex expansion and its integral dimension sum do not imply that each coefficient is a nonnegative integer.

Finally \(\theta=1+\sqrt3\) satisfies \(\theta^2=2\theta+2\); its polynomial \(T^2-2T-2\) is Eisenstein at two. Its recurrence coefficients are \(a_\theta=2\theta^{-1}\), \(b_\theta=2\theta^{-2}=1-a_\theta\). They are integral in \(E\), with \(a_\theta\) of \(E\)-valuation one and \(b_\theta\) a unit. If \(x=\tau y\in L\cap\tau L\), then \(\tau x=xa_\theta+yb_\theta\) lies in \(L\) and also in \(\tau L\). Equal volume turns inclusion into equality. This is the required stable-intersection argument, without assuming \(\tau^2=1\). \(\square\)

Solution 7.21. Put \(\alpha=z,\beta=z^2,\gamma=z^4\). Then \[ (\beta-\gamma)(1,\alpha)+(\gamma-\alpha)(1,\beta) +(\alpha-\beta)(1,\gamma)=(0,0). \tag{7.17} \] The first coordinate cancels by addition, and the second cancels by pairing the six products. All coefficients are nonzero, since the three conjugates are distinct. Any two vectors are independent by their different slopes. Thus their lines span dimension two and the three-dimensional sum domain has a one-dimensional kernel.

There are \((8^3-1)/(8-1)=73\) hyperplanes in \(\mathbb F_8^3\), of which \((2^3-1)/(2-1)=7\) are defined over \(\mathbb F_2\). The other \(66\) give the normalized index-one lattices. Proposition 6.194 splits them into coordinate ranks two and three, with masses \(7(8-2)=42\) and \((8-2)(8-4)=24\).

Here \(c_3(2)=21/64\), so the pair-family unit factor is \(c_3(2)/(1-1/2)^2=21/16\), and the cyclic-family unit factor is \(c_3(2)/(1-1/8)=3/8\). Consequently \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrr} \text{representative}&h_1&h_2&g_{1,0}&g_{1,1}&g_{2,0}&g_{2,1}\\\hline \text{mass}&42&1344&24&24&1536&192\\ \text{index}&1&2&1&2&2&3 \end{array} \tag{7.18} \] The cyclic \(g_{2,1}\)-conjugate has Cartan list \((2,2,-1)\), so its root height is \(3\). The original \(g_{2,1}\) has list \((2,1,0)\), giving \(2\rho=4\). Replacing \(1\) by arbitrary \(n\) makes the gap grow without bound, so a fixed error cannot repair the proposed inequality.

At index two the listed families contain exactly \(h_2,g_{2,0},g_{1,1}\), with total mass \(1344+1536+24=2904\). The total coefficient in (6.440) is \(4248\), leaving \(1344\) lattices outside these orbits. The first family in (6.437) has exponential cancellation and a two-parameter polynomial sum, while the second has a residual factor \(2^{-n}\). The stated convergence proves finiteness and cutoff tails for their contribution only. The full normalized-lattice bound is Theorem 6.218; it uses incidence counts in addition to the two family estimates. \(\square\)

Solution 7.22. Here \(q=8\), and the projective-hyperplane difference is \(73-7=66\). Formula (6.441) gives \[ B_{3,1}=66,\qquad B_{3,2}=66\cdot64=4224,\qquad B_{3,3}=66\cdot64^2=270336. \tag{7.19} \] Since \(c_3(2)=(1/2)(3/4)(7/8)=21/64\), (6.449) gives \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|r} n&a&\text{lengths of }L_0/I&w_{n,a}\\\hline 2&0&(2,2,2)&1536\\ 2&1&(2,2,1)&1344\\ 2&2&(2,2,0)&1344\\\hline 3&0&(3,3,3)&98304\\ 3&1&(3,3,2)&86016\\ 3&2&(3,3,1)&43008\\ 3&3&(3,3,0)&43008. \end{array} \tag{7.20} \] The length-three masses sum to \(270336\). The two length-two masses \(1344\) have different intersection lengths, hence are different orbits. The additional normalized quotient type \((1,1,0)\) has the orbit \(g_{1,1}\) of mass \(24\). The cyclic classification and total coefficient (6.440) give \(4224+24=4248\), leaving no further index-two lattice.

For \(s=1+\theta\), \(\alpha-s\alpha s^{-1}=(\alpha-\tau\alpha)\theta(1+\theta)^{-1}\). Every such difference has valuation at least one, and a coordinate whose residue is outside \(\mathbb F_2\) has valuation exactly one. Thus \(b=1\) in (6.445), \(k=0\), and \(M=n-1\) for \(n\ge1\). The exact Cartan list is \((n-1,0,1-n)\). In particular all length-one conjugates of this generator lie in \(K\); the unbounded length count is still offset by its Cartan growth after the fixed shift. The cyclic subseries converges for \(t>b_G+1\) by (6.447). In rank two every normalized nonstable quotient is cyclic, giving a full orbital bound. In rank three the quotient types with two positive lengths lie outside this subseries, so the estimate alone is not a full closed-primary orbital bound.

Solution 7.23. For \((u,v)=(3,1)\), \(R=3+\max(2,1)=5\) and \(c_3(2)/(1-2^{-3})=3/8\). The two masses are \((3/8)2^{15}=12288\), their quotients are \((3,1,0)\), and their intersections have lengths \((3,3,3)\). Their Cartan lists are \((3,2,-2)\) and \((4,0,-1)\), which distinguish the orbits. The dual family has \[ L_0/L:(3,1,0),\qquad L_0/I:(3,3,1),\qquad \boldsymbol\nu=(4,1,-2),\qquad w=2^{16}\frac{21/64}{1/2}=43008. \tag{7.21} \] For \(g_*\), the binary right coefficients in (6.458) force \(\alpha=\gamma=\beta=\varepsilon=0\), leaving only \(\delta\); hence \(L\cap E^3\) has lengths \((2,3,3)\). There are nine binary choices in \(B\) and the two scalar choices \(b,c\), with \(r(B)\) unique: \(2^{11}=2048\) additive stabilizers. Exactly the \(2^{10}=1024\) with \(c=1\) are invertible. The orbit has mass \(168\cdot2^{18}/1024=43008\). The entries of \(A,A^{-1}\) have least valuation \(-3\), so their opposite extreme Cartan exponents are \(3,-3\). Their determinant valuation zero gives middle exponent zero. The extra \(\theta\) shifts this to \((4,1,-2)\).

The five cyclic-quotient masses at length four, from (6.449), are \[ 6291456,\quad5505024,\quad2752512,\quad1376256,\quad1376256, \qquad\text{sum }17301504. \tag{7.22} \] The noncyclic total is \(1536+2\cdot12288+2\cdot43008=112128\). Together they give \(17413632\), the independent coefficient (6.464). Disjointness and equality of actual finite counts prove the index-four classification. A Schwartz integral also sums all higher indices, whose remaining quotient types and Cartan-weighted masses need bounds; this finite equality supplies no such infinite estimate. Finally \((AB)^t=B^tA^t\) is an identity over the opposite algebra when entries do not commute. Keeping that algebra explicit is necessary for the dual lattice construction and does not assume an algebra isomorphism to \(D\).

At index five, (6.461) gives \(b_{4,1}=24\cdot9\cdot8^5=7077888\) and \(b_{3,2}=24\cdot9\cdot8^3=110592\). The cyclic count is \(66\cdot64^4=1107296256\); their sum is \(1114484736\). This gives every quotient-type count at that index without specifying its individual centralizer orbits or their Cartan heights.

Solution 7.24. For \(Q=4\), \(c_3(4)=(3/4)(15/16)(63/64)\). Formula (6.471) gives \[ W_{3,2,0}=4^{12}\frac{45}{64}=11796480,\quad W_{3,2,1}=4^{11}\frac{945}{1024}=3870720,\quad W_{3,2,2}=1290240. \tag{7.23} \] Their sum is \(16957440\). Independently, (6.441) gives \((4161-21)64^2=16957440\). All three cyclic orbits have Cartan list \((4,2,0)\), since \(\delta=2,n=2\); their intersection lengths distinguish them. The equal-length quotient \((2,2,0)\) is one orbit with the same Cartan list and mass \(2880\cdot64^2=11796480\), by (6.473). The noncommutativity of the quaternionic \(\Delta\) does not change the residue fractions or the ordered right-module counts.

For \(Q=2,r=4\), the generating fractions are \(P_{4,3}=315/512\), \(P_{4,2}=105/128\). Hence \[ W_{4,2,0}=184320,\qquad W_{4,2,1}=80640,\qquad W_{4,2,2}=26880,\qquad\text{sum }291840. \tag{7.24} \] The independent primitive-row count is \((585-15)8^3=291840\). Their stable intersections have lengths \((2,2,2,0)\), \((2,2,1,0)\), \((2,2,0,0)\), respectively.

The polynomial of \(z\) in Example 6.212 has trace coefficient zero and pair coefficient two. Thus \(\operatorname{Tr}(z^2)=\operatorname{Tr}(z)^2-2\cdot2=2\) in \(\mathbb F_3\), while \(\operatorname{N}(z^2)=(-1)^2=1\). Expanding the ordered three factors in that example gives \(\theta^3=t+2t\theta+t^2\). The derivative of its Eisenstein polynomial is \(t\ne0\); its ramification degree is three in residue characteristic three, so it is separable and wild. Its cube is not central, so its conjugation does not have order three. The mass is \(3^{11}(8/9)(26/27)=729\cdot208=151632\).

For \(u=5\), (6.466)–(6.467) permit exactly \[ (a,c)=(5,3),(3,5),(5,4),(4,5),(5,5),\qquad \rho=8,8,9,9,10, \tag{7.25} \] as numerical possibilities under these constraints. The identities alone do not assert that every possibility occurs for every fixed quotient type or field. Counting lattices with each such height requires more than their total quotient-type count.

Solution 7.25. Here \(h=2\). For \(q=8,Q=2\), \(A=3/8\); for \(q=16,Q=2\), \(A=21/32\). Substitution in (6.483) gives \[ \begin{array}{c|r|r} k&q=8&q=16\\\hline 0&5505024&2642411520\\ 1&1376256&330301440\\ 2&196608&22020096. \end{array} \tag{7.26} \] At defect two the one-sided cumulative count is half the final row: \(98304\) and \(11010048\). The weighted sums are \[ \frac{21}{64}+\frac{21}{32}+\frac34=\frac{111}{64},\qquad \frac{315}{512}+\frac{315}{256}+\frac{21}{16}=\frac{1617}{512}. \tag{7.27} \] In general a strict middle length contributes \(A[2h(1-q^{-1})+1+q^{-1}]\). Pairing the terms at \(v,u-v\) gives \(\sum h=\lfloor u^2/4\rfloor\). Add the cyclic contribution \(C_3/q^2\) and the equal-length contribution \(A\) to obtain (6.484). Thus the root-weighted count grows quadratically in \(u\); the full majorant is summable for \(t>b_G+3\).

For an arbitrary generator, \(\max(a,c)\) is within a fixed constant of \(u\), while the smaller deviation can vary with the lattice. The compact-frame argument bounds this maximum by excluding invariant lines and planes; the incidence estimate separately controls how many lattices have each smaller deviation. A presumed bounded shift of every Cartan coordinate would replace these two proved facts by an unsupported assertion.

The Euler values, Steinberg degrees and unit coefficient orbitals are respectively \[ (1/4,\ 1275/4,\ 1/1275),\qquad (5/2,\ 28665/2,\ 1/5733). \tag{7.28} \] All three partitions \((1^3),(2,1),(3)\) of the stated primary fibre are covered, with the latter two giving zero discrete-test and Euler orbitals. This supplies ordinary Schwartz traces and the closed character germ for the totally ramified embedded-field family in division rank three. Theorem 6.271 proves elliptic orthogonality. This field/rank estimate does not prove the other noncompact orbital cases, individual transfer-coefficient integrality, or the general local and global representation correspondences.

Solution 7.26. In the basis \(1,\Pi,\Pi^2\), any scalar lattice \(L_0\Pi^w\), \(0\le w<3\), has a unit coefficient in position \(w\) in each coordinate. The coefficient matrix units carry these to all positions, so its saturation is \(L_0\). The surjections onto \(R_u\), normalized to first entry one, have \(q^{v+w}\) distinct kernels. Thus the two requested top counts are \[ 8^{3+0}=512,\qquad 8^{1+1}=64. \tag{7.29} \] The third positive least color is possible only because the coefficient order may enlarge a proper \(\mathcal O_D\)-ideal. It still preserves \(\mathfrak P^3\), so no normalized lattice has least length at least three.

A primitive row of a rank-two cyclic kernel of length three has either first entry one, or second entry one and first entry in \(\mathfrak P\). These charts contain \(q^3\) and \(q^2\) rows. Refining the fixed depth-one kernel forces the first chart \((1,y)\) with \(y\in\mathfrak P/\mathfrak P^3\), so the counts are \[ q^3+q^2=576,\qquad q^2=64, \qquad(q-1)q=56\quad(q=8). \tag{7.30} \] For the last count, use the three coefficient columns following (6.505). The first fixes the third coordinate; the other two span the first two coordinates precisely when \(a_1\ne0\). Then \(a_2\) is arbitrary. Normalization is therefore a genuine restriction on the 64 incidence refinements.

For the unramified cubic, (6.503) gives \((7\cdot63/3,7\cdot63/9,3)=(147,49,3)\). For \(E=\mathbb F_8((\Pi^3))\subset D\) of degree six, \(a_E=2,f_E=3,\delta=1,Q=8,q=64\), so \[ \eta_s=\frac{7\cdot63}{6}=\frac{147}{2},\quad d_{\mathrm{St}}=\frac{63\cdot4095}{18}=\frac{28665}{2},\quad O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}})=\frac1{195}. \tag{7.31} \] The relation \(s^2=z^2+t\) recovers \(z\) and \(\Pi^3\), proving that the specified \(s\) generates this inseparable field.

For a general residue degree \(f_E\), the proper stable lattice \(L_0\mathfrak P^{f_E}\) excludes \(w\ge f_E\). When \(v\ge f_E\), the deeper columns vanish in its coefficient quotient, so the remaining column must be coefficient-primitive. An invariant right \(D\)-plane descends to \(\Delta\); its integral lattice is \(\Sigma\)-stable and proper, so it cannot contain that column. This is the compact-frame contradiction. At closed primary rank three, \(hm=3\) forces either the embedded-field case \(h=1,m=3\), or the \(D\)-irreducible case \(h=3,m=1\). Together with the proper-flag cases, these prove Corollary 6.226. They do not determine individual elliptic expansion coefficients or supply local/global representation bijections.

Solution 7.27. If \(h=1,m=4\), the four nonclosed partitions have column lists \((1,1,1,1),(2,1,1),(2,2),(3,1)\), as in (6.523). If \(h=2,m=2\), the sole nonclosed partition \((2)\) has block sizes \((2,2)\). If \(h=4,m=1\), no nonclosed partition occurs. Every block has rank at most three, so Lemma 6.229 applies. For the quartic, \(Q=2,a_E=4,m=4,\delta=1\), hence \[ \eta_s=-\frac{(2-1)(4-1)(8-1)}{4\cdot4} =-\frac{21}{16},\qquad g_{P,(1^4)}(\gamma)=-\frac{16}{21e(F[\gamma]/F)} \quad(\gamma\text{ elliptic}). \tag{7.32} \] The compact Steinberg test has value \(21/16\) on this closed orbit because its nearby elliptic character is \(-1\). This conclusion concerns a compact test.

For the monomial matrix, the cycle sends \(1\to2\to4\to3\to1\). With \(\lambda=(3n,2n,n,0)\), the four source-minus-target valuations are \(n,2n,-2n,-n\), and sorting gives \((2n,n,-n,-2n)\). Its spread is \(4n\), and \[ \rho_G=\tfrac32(2n)+\tfrac12n-\tfrac12(-n)-\tfrac32(-2n)=7n. \tag{7.33} \] The independent residue coordinates of \(v\) prove normalization. Thus the greatest quotient length \(3n\) exceeds both extreme deviations \(2n\) by an unbounded amount.

Since \(v_F(x^4)=4v_F(x)\), the requested sublevel measure is \(2^{-\lceil n/4\rceil}\). At \(n=4j\) it equals \(2^{-j}\), so a uniform exponent larger than \(1/4\) is impossible for this polynomial. Its zero derivative causes no failure of the repeated-root proof of Lemma 6.232.

Formula (6.522) gives the table \[ \begin{array}{c|ccc} n\backslash m&1&2&3\\\hline 1&1&1&1\\ 2&1/2&1&1\\ 3&1/4&1/2&1. \end{array} \tag{7.34} \] For fixed \(m\) the entries continue to zero down the column; choosing \(m\ge n\) always gives one. This proves the nonuniformity for all indices, beyond the displayed table.

Conjugating the coefficient integral (6.510) and replacing \(b\) by \(b^{-1}\) gives the same integral, because \(F_\pi(b^{-1})=\overline{F_\pi(b)}\) and \(\chi_\rho(b^{-1})=\overline{\chi_\rho(b)}\). Thus every coefficient is real. In the finite \(S_3\) example, \[ F(1)=\frac{1-2+2\cdot2}{3}=1,\qquad \|F\|^2=\frac{1+4+4}{9}=1. \tag{7.35} \] Its fractional coefficients show that these numerical facts do not make it an irreducible character. For a packet in Theorem 6.234, the additional condition is \(\lim_n\operatorname{tr}\sigma((1-\zeta_n)f_\pi)=0\) for every ordered pair. The actual limit is \(\delta_{\sigma\pi}-H_{\sigma\pi}\), by (6.521). Uniform discriminant-tube integrability (6.518) is sufficient; neither pointwise stabilization nor the real finite expansion alone proves it. The general local and global representation correspondences require their further representation-theoretic conclusions.

Solution 7.28. The standard measure has \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal D^\times/Z)=N\). A conjugation-invariant test is therefore multiplied by \(N\) under \(A\); in particular \(A_{p_\rho}=\overline{\chi_\rho}\) for the trace-one test \(p_\rho=\overline{\chi_\rho}/N\). Dividing (6.528) by \(N\) would destroy this normalization of the transferred regular orbital.

The quotient-map argument of Lemma 6.240 gives a locally constant profile on the compact closed primary image \(X\). It has finitely many values. Separate the compact open value sets by disjoint compact open neighborhoods in the coefficient annulus, extend by those values, and take zero elsewhere. Average by (6.531), then extend across the scalar valuation annuli by (6.530). On \(X\) unit averaging preserves the profile because its unit covariance already holds. Thus the construction works even at inseparable primary polynomials. If two choices have the same profile, their transferred difference is zero on every primary orbit and has zero orbital on every other orbit by the proper-orbit Euler zeros for \(r\le4\). Lemma 6.239 makes it a finite commutator sum.

For \(N>1\), a sufficient inequality is \[ B_N\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^kM_i^2\Bigr) q_F^{-n/[N(N-1)]}<\frac1{2\|B\|_{\mathrm F}^2}. \tag{7.36} \] Indeed Theorem 6.234 bounds the entry error by the left-hand scalar coefficient times \(M_iM_j/(\sum M_i^2)\). For a unit vector \(c\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\sum_{ij}M_iM_j|c_i c_j|\le\sum_iM_i^2\). Thus (7.36) bounds the operator error by half the eigenvalue lower bound of (6.541). Every eigenvalue of \(H_n\) is positive. By definition \(\operatorname{Tr}\pi_\ell(\zeta_n f_{\pi_j})=(H_n)_{\ell j}\); multiplication by the \(i\)-th column of \(H_n^{-1}\) gives exactly \(\delta_{\ell i}\). For \(N=1\) use \(H_n=H\), with no exponent denominator.

For Example 6.250, \[ B-A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ -\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{3}{2}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad (B-A)A^{\mathsf t} =\begin{pmatrix}0&-\tfrac{1}{2}\\ -\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix} =I_2-H. \tag{7.37} \] Here \(\|B\|_{\mathrm F}^2=6\). The characteristic polynomial of \(H\) is \(\lambda^2-\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda+\tfrac{1}{4}\), giving eigenvalues \((3\pm\sqrt5)/4\). To verify the strict lower bound without a decimal approximation, \((3-\sqrt5)/4>1/6\) is equivalent to \(7>3\sqrt5\), and \(49>45\). The nonzero matrix in (7.37) exhibits exactly why a left inverse alone does not prove orthogonality.

At the quartic primary element of Example 6.249, Theorem 6.157 gives \[ \eta_s^G=\frac{(-1)^3(2-1)(2^2-1)(2^3-1)}{4\cdot4\cdot1} =-\frac{21}{16},\qquad \eta_b^{\mathcal D}=\frac1{4\cdot(16/4)}=\frac1{16}. \tag{7.38} \] The first denominator is \(a_E m\delta\), the second \(a_E\delta'\). Although these factors differ, \(A_{1/16}=1\) and both normalized orbitals in (6.534) equal one. \(\square\)

Solution 7.29. Put \(q=|\mathcal O_F/\varpi_F|\). Reduction identifies the flag quotient with \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q)\), so \(t=q+1\): its lines have representatives \((1,a)\) for \(a\in\mathbb F_q\), and \((0,1)\). Counting a nonzero first column and a second column outside its line gives \[ |\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_q)| =(q^2-1)(q^2-q)=q(q-1)^2(q+1). \] The chosen probability maximal-compact measures therefore give \[ \operatorname{vol}(J)=\frac1{q(q-1)^2(q+1)},\quad \operatorname{vol}(J_M)=\frac1{(q-1)^2},\quad \operatorname{vol}(J_N)=\frac1q. \tag{7.39} \] Their products give exactly (6.548). Quotienting the first two groups by their common central intersection divides both volumes by the same central measure and preserves the identity.

The function \(v_i=e_J(\,\cdot\,k_i^{-1})/t\) maps to \(e_{J_M}\) in its \(i\)-th Jacquet coordinate. Right convolution by \(a\) sends it to \(a(k_i^{-1}\,\cdot\,)/t\); applying \(q_i\) gives (6.554). The \(K\)-average is the sum of \(K_M\)-conjugacy averages of these diagonal entries by the equal-mass flag decomposition. Each compact conjugation average is finite at a common normal constancy level, and (6.526) makes its difference from the original entry a finite commutator sum.

For the indicated two-block Levi the flat has one coordinate, which may be written \[ \nu(m_1,m_2) =\frac{v_F\operatorname{Nrd}(m_1)}{2d} -\frac{v_F\operatorname{Nrd}(m_2)}{3d}. \tag{7.40} \] Its image lattice is \((6d)^{-1}\mathbb Z\), since \(\gcd(3,2)=1\). For every \(M^0\)-orbit of a product facet \(\sigma\), there is one flat vertex type and one flat edge type; both have stabilizer \(M^0\cap C_\sigma^M\) and coefficient \(W^{U_\sigma}\) with the same building orientation. Their modules occur in degrees \(p\) and \(p+1\) and cancel exactly. The cancellation is an equality of projective classes, not a limit of trace integrals.

For Example 6.259, \(U=\Pi^2\) satisfies \(U^3=t\). Its derivative is \(U^2\ne0\), and its valuation \(1/3\) proves irreducibility; this gives the separable degree three. Adjoining the unique square root \(\Pi\) has degree two by its valuation and is purely inseparable. Thus the full degree and ramification index are six. The centralizer in the degree-six division algebra is the maximal field \(E\), so the \(G\)-centralizer has \(m=6,\delta=1,q_\Delta=2\). The degree-36 division centralizer has degree \(36/6=6\) over \(E\). Hence \[ \eta_s=-\frac{1\cdot3\cdot7\cdot15\cdot31}{6\cdot6\cdot1} =-\frac{9765}{36}=-\frac{1085}{4}, \qquad \eta_b^{\mathcal D}=\frac1{6\cdot6}. \tag{7.41} \] Finally (6.568) proves a real left inverse and a strictly positive Gram matrix. Orthogonality is the additional assertion \[ (B-A)A^{\mathsf t}=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad AA^{\mathsf t}=I. \tag{7.42} \] Neither the positivity bound nor row independence proves this zero, as the exact matrices of Example 6.250 show. Theorem 6.271 proves it for the actual character matrices. Individual coefficient integrality and representation existence also require their own arguments. \(\square\)

Solution 7.30. The three circular face types give \[ E_3=1-\xi_{(1,2)}+\tfrac13\xi_{(1,1,1)}. \tag{7.43} \] The three-point permutation character has values \(3,1,0\) on identity, transposition and three-cycle; the regular character has values \(6,0,0\). Thus \(E_3\) has values \(0,0,1\). There are two three-cycles in \(S_3\), so its squared norm is \(2/6=1/3\). The finite Gram identity (6.574) gives the same norm for the flag combination on \(\mathrm{GL}_3(k)\). At identity, the number of lines is \(q^2+q+1\), and each line lies in \(q+1\) complete flags. Hence \[ U_3(1)=1-(q^2+q+1) +\frac{(q+1)(q^2+q+1)}3 =\frac{(q-1)(q^2-1)}3. \tag{7.44} \] Equality of these finite permutation Gram matrices does not identify their dimensions; the displayed dimension depends on \(q\).

For rank six, the two cycles are \(0\to2\to4\to0\) and \(1\to3\to5\to1\). Thus \(g=2,b=3\). A stable face containing zero is one of these triangles or the union of both cycles, modulo rotation. For the triangle, its dimension sign is positive and its three-cycle sign is positive. For all six vertices, its dimension sign is negative and the product of the two three-cycle signs is positive. The final signs are therefore \(+1,-1\), as \((-1)^{|T|-1}\) requires. The rotation stabilizer orders are \(3\) and \(6\). A compatible subspace of dimension three has dimension one in each of the three graded spaces of dimension two. Its proper finite radical average is zero by Lemma 6.261.

For rank four, \(g=b=2\). The \(F_g\)-parahoric has reductive quotient \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_2)^2\), with the two factors interchanged. Its index in \(K\) is the number of two-planes in \(\mathbb F_2^4\): \[ [K:P_{F_g}]=\frac{(2^4-1)(2^4-2)}{(2^2-1)(2^2-2)} =35. \] On the identity component product, the cyclic tensor flag trace is three, since its two flag indices must agree; it is not \(3^2\). Formula (6.578) consequently gives \[ u_2(\Omega^2)=\frac{35}{2} \left(1-\frac32\right)=-\frac{35}{4}. \tag{7.45} \] These are values of a rational test function, with its stated Haar normalization.

For \(\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\), the finite \(S_2\) function \(E_2\) is the indicator of its nonidentity element. Thus its squared norm, and that of (6.599), is \(1/2\). The positive-height kernels vanish by the separated finite radical average, giving \(\mathcal I_{e_0}(e_0)=1/2\). For the odd norm component put \(c=(q_F+1)/2\). The kernel value and its support volume are \[ c^2\operatorname{vol}(I)=\frac{q_F+1}{4},\qquad \operatorname{vol}(C_{\mathrm{edge}}/Z)=\frac2{q_F+1}. \] Their product is the other \(1/2\). Disjoint norm components give zero cross-terms, so the full pairing is one.

For the matrix unit, choose an orthonormal basis \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\) containing the finite-dimensional compression of \(\pi(f)\), and write its entries as \(A_{ij}\). Then \[ \mathcal I_f(E^\pi_{u,u}) =d_\pi\sum_{i,j}A_{ij} \int_Q\langle\pi(x)u,v_j\rangle \overline{\langle\pi(x)u,v_i\rangle}\,d\bar x =\sum_iA_{ii}. \tag{7.46} \] Each integral is absolute by Cauchy–Schwarz; Schur orthogonality supplies \(\delta_{ij}/d_\pi\), cancelling the prefactor. The trace is therefore the actual \(\operatorname{Tr}\pi(f)\). For a division transfer, the relation \(F_\pi=(-1)^{r-1}\Theta_\pi\) is exactly the sign in (6.597).

The resulting coefficient relations are \[ \sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}a_{\sigma\rho}=\delta_{\pi,\sigma}, \qquad B=A. \tag{7.47} \] They give real unit rows and their actual transfer traces. The rational \(S_3\) class function in Example 6.237 already has real unit norm and integral positive central dimension while having nonintegral character coefficients. Thus an integrality or representation-construction argument is still required for existence and bijectivity. \(\square\)

Solution 7.31.

  1. At \(t=0\), the residue of \(t^{-1}dt\) is one. At infinity it is the residue of \(-s^{-1}ds\), namely minus one, also one in characteristic two. Their sum is zero. There are no other residues. Pairing \(s^3+s^4\) with \(t^2\) gives residue \(-1=1\) at infinity, so the \(\mathbb F_2\)-character is \(-1\). Pairing \(t^2+t^3\) at the prime \(t\) with \(t^{-3}\) gives residue one. These are the two coefficient-detection steps of Lemma 6.274.

For the constant-field extension, \(\operatorname{Tr}(1)=0\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)=\alpha+\alpha^2=1\). Thus \[ (b_1,b_2)=(1,\alpha),\qquad(c_1,c_2)=(1+\alpha,1), \qquad\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}(b_i c_j)\bigr)_{i,j}=I_2. \tag{7.48} \] In particular zero trace of one does not make the trace map zero or make the trace pairing degenerate. For \(x=x_1+\alpha x_2\), the trace is \(x_2\); multiplication by \(1+\alpha\) extracts \(x_1\) instead.

  1. The upper-right rectangle and the last unipotent block give \[ \dim U^{(i)}=i(4-i)+\frac{(4-i)(3-i)}2,\qquad (\dim U^{(4)},\dim U^{(3)},\dim U^{(2)},\dim U^{(1)})=(0,3,5,6). \tag{7.49} \] The successive column dimensions are \(3,2,1\). At \(i=4,3,2\), the constant coefficient factors first through the radical of the parabolic \((3,1),(2,2),(1,3)\), respectively. Their dimensions are \(3,4,3\). The remaining last-block unipotent dimensions are \(0,1,3\), giving \(3,5,6\) as required. The retained character is trivial on the first radical, so the original cuspidality of \(\phi\) kills that inner integral. Only this constant coefficient must vanish. The induction applies Fourier uniqueness to a function on one compact additive quotient, followed by a rational basis change; it does not require a new cuspidality theorem for \(F_i\).

  2. A determinant unit puts the matrix in \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathcal O_P)\). If its projective class is the identity modulo \(P^2\), both off-diagonal entries and the difference of its diagonal entries are divisible by \(P^2\) in \(\mathcal O_P\). For a polynomial this is ordinary polynomial divisibility. Their degrees are less than three, whereas \(\deg P^2=4\), so all three polynomials are zero. The matrix is globally scalar. In contrast, \[ I_2+P E_{12}\equiv I_2\pmod P, \qquad I_2+P E_{12}\notin Z(K_P)J_{P^2}, \qquad\det(I_2+P E_{12})=1. \tag{7.50} \] This is a noncentral rational class retained by the first congruence and excluded by the second. It illustrates why the shrinking level depends on the actual finite candidate set.

  3. The two permutations send the basis vectors as follows: \((12)\) sends them to \(-v_1,v_1+v_2\), while \((23)\) sends them to \(v_1+v_2,-v_2\). These are exactly the two matrices in (6.615). Their difference has \[ \operatorname{Tr}(a)=0, \qquad\det(a)=-3,\qquad a\ne0. \tag{7.51} \] The trivial representation gives \(1-1=0\), and the sign representation gives \((-1)-(-1)=0\). Thus all irreducible traces vanish although the standard operator is nonzero. A pseudo-coefficient specifies traces. It need not annihilate every unwanted local representation as an operator, so a nonzero projection of a Poincaré function need not have the desired local component by that argument alone. One needs an actual spectral constituent and a justified trace isolation or local operator projection. Global genericity is proved in Theorem 6.276, but the local isolation of a discrete series among generic irreducibles and exact discrete-series globalization are additional assertions.

Solution 7.32.

  1. Additive measure gives the shell mass \(q^{-2b}(1-q^{-2})\). Its norm denominator in (6.618) is \(q^{-b}\), so \[ \nu_2\{\|\eta\|_\infty=q^{-b}\}=(1-q^{-2})q^{-b},\qquad \operatorname{vol}\{s\in P_2\cap K,\ \|\eta\|_\infty=q^{-b}\} =(1-q^{-1})(1-q^{-2})q^{-b}. \tag{7.52} \] Here the compact mirabolic mass is \(1-q^{-1}\): its scalar entry is a unit and its upper entry is integral. For \(q=2\), the row-shell masses are \(3/4,3/8,3/16\); the full masses are \(3/8,3/16,3/32\). The factor \(q^b\) from the row-norm denominator is essential.

  2. The first maximal unit coordinate of a normalized projective row has indices one, two or three. The chart coordinates before it lie in \(\varpi\mathcal O\), and those after it in \(\mathcal O\). Thus the masses are \(1,1/2,1/4\). The centre has compact mass \(1/2\) and \(P_3\cap K\) has mass \((1-1/2)(1-1/4)=3/8\). Consequently \[ \frac12\cdot\frac38\cdot\frac74 =\frac{21}{64} =(1-2^{-1})(1-2^{-2})(1-2^{-3}). \tag{7.53} \] Counting ordered independent residue columns gives the same matrix Haar volume. For \(P_2=F^\times\ltimes F\), the stabilizer in (6.621) is trivial and \(t_\xi=\xi\). Therefore \[ \bigl(\sigma_2(a,b)\Phi\bigr)(\xi) =|a|^{1/2}\psi(\xi b)\Phi(\xi a), \qquad\Phi\in L^2(F^\times,d\xi). \tag{7.54} \] This action is unitary for additive \(d\xi\); replacing the half-power by one would not be unitary for that measure. For \(n=3,a=2,q=2\), (6.637) gives \[ \|v_3\|^2=2^{-6},\qquad\|v_3\|=\frac18, \qquad\ell_3(v_3)=1,\qquad \ell_3(8v_3)=8. \tag{7.55} \] The last vector has norm one. This attains the fixed-level bound, without defining evaluation on the entire Hilbert completion.

  3. There are six elements of \(H_2=\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_2)\) and four column characters. Exactly one character is zero. Thus the two Fourier parts have dimensions six and eighteen. The stabilizer of the last nonzero row has two elements, the group \(P_2(\mathbb F_2)\), and the orbit has size three. The induced regular-stabilizer fibre has dimension \(3\cdot2=6\); its multiplicity is three. Hence \[ |P_3(\mathbb F_2)|=24=6+18, \qquad18=3\cdot(3\cdot2). \tag{7.56} \] The finite zero row has mass \(1/4\), not zero. Moreover the smaller finite stabilizer also has its own zero Fourier part. Dropping either positive-mass part would invalidate the finite regular decomposition. Theorem 6.281 removes zero rows only for the infinite local field with nonatomic additive Haar measure.

  4. A smooth \(G_n\)-vector is fixed by a compact open \(J\). Equivariance makes its image under \(T\) fixed by \(J\cap P_n\), and hence by some \(J_n(a)\). Theorem 6.282 defines evaluation on that space and bounds it by \(q^{a n(n-1)/4}\). Boundedness of \(T\), together with density of smooth vectors, gives a nonzero smooth image. Some \(P_n\)-translate of that image has nonzero \(\ell_n\), by separation; equivariance makes the same statement for \(\ell_nT\) on a translated input. The Whittaker character identity follows from (6.627).

The Hilbert multiplicity space can have many components, and the argument chooses one nonzero component map. It does not calculate the number of independent Whittaker functionals, prove mirabolic irreducibility, classify generic irreducibles, or establish uniqueness at a given cuspidal support. None of those assertions is needed for this existence proof. Local generic trace isolation, integral Jacquet–Langlands transfer and global spectral extraction remain separate proof obligations.

8. Proofs and prerequisites

The class matching is fully proved in Theorem 1.1, the trivial/Steinberg character calculation in Proposition 2.2, the complete real local correspondence in Lemmas 2.3–2.4 and Theorem 2.5, and the all-prime dimension equality in Theorem 4.2. Lemma 2.6, Theorem 2.7 and Proposition 2.8 prove the finite-place regular character theorem, including compact split elements, in all characteristics. They include the exact tree complex, uniform fixed-tube trace stabilization, principal/special character formulas and finite elliptic compact-type sum. Section 2.4 proves finite-place smooth transfer, including the inseparable support needed in characteristic two, by the signed Euler test and the exact orbital-coordinate lift. Lemma 2.11 proves the full two-term scalar orbital germ and the negative scalar-value identity for every matching pair. Proposition 2.12 proves the paired formal degree for special representations. Lemma 2.13, Theorem 2.14 and Corollary 2.15 prove the whole depth-zero local bijection, its negative character identity on every regular elliptic class, paired formal degrees, and every determinant/norm twist of that family. The finite-tree character argument includes deep scalar-residue classes and all residue characteristics. Theorem 2.16 proves the full Schur constant for every irreducible admissible compact induction, Corollary 2.17 computes the division degree and reduces equality to an explicit dimension-volume identity, and Proposition 2.18 calculates the unramified and ramified inducing volumes in every characteristic. Theorem 2.30 proves the all-level bijection, character identity and paired type dimensions by the quaternion construction and elliptic orthogonality. Lemmas 2.19–2.21 and Theorem 2.22 prove real character integration across the singular set, the scalar-value identity for every matching pair, and real smooth/spectral transfer with common-support polynomially bounded wave tests. The Gaussian orbital example computes the scalar sign directly. Sections 2.8–2.10 supply the full finite representation construction, arbitrary-test character integration, Fourier comparison, elliptic orthogonality, all-level bijection, full factor and formal-degree equality, and every-pair spectral transfer. Sections 3.3–3.6 prove the full global quaternion correspondence over \(\mathbb Q\): equal paired volumes, absolute discrete traces, the truncated-kernel comparison, cancellation of the split/unipotent/continuous terms, the residual characters, and positive outside trace separation. The real proof includes the principal/complementary square-integrability exclusions, a trace-class regularization of the disk character and explicit paired formal degrees (2.23)–(2.24). Both level examples, the order calculation, the Brandt matrices and all thirty exercise solutions include their computations. Sections 6.16–6.18 give the Schwartz trace calculus, explicit nilpotent and unipotent orbital measures, unipotent orbital continuity, compact-support germ expansions and scalar homogeneity. Exercises 7.6–7.7 compute division-matrix kernel flags and explain coincident homogeneity degrees. Section 6.19 gives the uniform Schwartz constant terms and polynomially weighted orbital reduction. Section 6.20 proves the exact elliptic radial sums, sharp Schwartz convergence and actual elliptic coefficient–character formula in division rank two. Exercise 7.8 computes a separable degree-four example in characteristic two with both torus normalizations. Section 6.21 proves the compact flag-kernel estimate, angular spherical bound, quantitative elliptic conjugator bound, every-rank elliptic convergence and coefficient formula, and polynomially weighted regular convergence. Exercise 7.9 distinguishes the angular estimate from a false pointwise bound. Section 6.22 proves a completed Schwartz resolution, higher-extension vanishing for tempered pairs with a discrete-series member, compact pseudo-coefficients, the cellular formal-degree formula and fixed-level finiteness of discrete series. Exercise 7.10 computes a lattice cut and a rank-two formal-degree quantum. Section 6.23 proves the finite-commutator identity for compact discrete tests, all their ordinary regular orbital values, a division-norm fixed-set contraction, explicit matching Euler tests in every degree, and the probability normalization of elliptic class measure. Exercise 7.11 computes fixed-interior signs and distinguishes regular orbital matching from scalar test values. Section 6.24 constructs the Iwahori sign discrete series by an explicit Schwartz projection, proves its irreducibility, admissibility and formal degree, computes the Euler test on this family and gives an absolute elliptic character moment bound. Exercise 7.12 computes a rank-three division example and its cyclic phases. Section 6.25 proves a bounded apartment contraction, the signed Euler cocenter identity and actual norm-character-family transfer in every degree; it computes the general zero-orbit germ, near-identity elliptic discrete characters and integral formal-degree ratios. Figure 5 shows the rank-two apartment averages and their Hecke coefficients. Exercise 7.13 checks an infinite primitive, both torus measures and the degree integrality obstruction. Section 6.26 classifies every primary fibre, constructs locally finite orbital measures and compact-test germs including inseparable elements, proves compact parabolic descent and gives finite germ expressions for elliptic discrete characters. Figure 6 and Exercise 7.14 compute the two inseparable primary types in dimension four. Section 6.27 proves a quotient conjugator bound for every closed orbit, identifies the exact nilpotent obstruction to the flag submersion, constructs actual character densities on the whole D-irreducible open set including inseparable elements, and extends Schwartz convergence and discrete-test vanishing to one-chain primary orbits. Its double-primary germ formula has one remaining coefficient. Figure 7 and Exercise 7.15 compute the inseparable quartic chamber, both coefficient-orbital measures and the necessity of the centralizer quotient. Section 6.28 counts all saturated quadratic lattices in odd division degree, proves the resulting absolute Schwartz orbitals for every linear or quadratic primary partition, computes the Euler orbital at every closed primary element, and gives the quadratic closed germ and finite elliptic character expansions for split \(\mathrm{GL}_4\). The dimension sum does not establish individual coefficient integrality or positivity; elliptic orthogonality is Theorem 6.271. Figure 8 and Exercise 7.16 give exact lattice counts, ramification factors and the convergent shell estimate. Section 6.29 proves all ordinary orbital Schwartz bounds in division rank two by an exact tree displacement and weighted shell count, and proper-flag bounds and discrete-test vanishing in rank three. It constructs compact conjugacy representatives for bounded reduced polynomials, proves the finite-extension index and embedding rules including inseparable fields, and evaluates primary germs at multiplicity at most two and throughout rank three. Its elliptic character extension criterion gives finite complex character expansions and finite elliptic \(L^2\) norms in every division rank at most three, every inner form of degrees four and six, and the further split degrees specified there. Figure 9 and Exercise 7.17 compute an inseparable quaternion fixed tree, its sharp positive convergence threshold and an explicit primary polynomial limit. These statements leave individual character coefficients and general representation transfer as additional conclusions; elliptic orthogonality is Theorem 6.271. Section 6.30 constructs an integral involution model for ramified quadratic fields in even division degree under its specified odd-residue or inseparable characteristic-two hypotheses. It proves exact fixed-lattice descent, paired lattice normal forms and stabilizer masses over the noncommutative fixed division algebra, every-rank absolute Schwartz convergence, primary-partition vanishing and closed germs, and a singular Steinberg coefficient orbital. Figure 10 and Exercise 7.18 compute paired lengths and exact masses, with formal-degree and Haar factors in division degrees two and four. Section 6.31 proves the unramified quadratic lattice normal forms and exact orbit masses in every even division degree and both characteristics. Its partition and finite-series identities establish exhaustiveness in all ranks and indices. The resulting Schwartz bounds extend primary-partition traces and closed germs to these fields and give the singular unit Iwahori Steinberg orbital two. Figure 11 and Exercise 7.19 compute the two valuation colors and exact normalized-lattice counts. Section 6.32 proves the ramified quadratic recurrence, stable sums and intersections, exact coefficient descent and stabilizer masses without an involution hypothesis. It gives every linear or quadratic primary Schwartz trace and closed germ in every rank, division degree and field characteristic, including wild separable fields. Its elliptic extension criterion covers every inner form of degree eight and of twice a prime degree, with finite complex character expansions and their stated limits. Figure 12 and Exercise 7.20 compute a separable characteristic-two wild field, its rank-five masses and the mixed-characteristic Eisenstein recurrence. Section 6.33 proves the higher-degree Eisenstein recurrence, integral Moore-matrix descent, exact stable lattice sums and intersections, and the total normalized-lattice series for totally ramified fields whose degree divides the division degree. Its cubic examples give the two first-level orbit masses, a three-submodule obstruction to direct-sum classification, and two infinite families with exact stabilizers and Cartan heights. Their convergent contributions and the explicit index-two count distinguish these families from a full cubic orbital bound. Figure 13 and Exercise 7.21 compute the finite-field quotient, masses and root-height counterexample. Section 6.34 counts every normalized cyclic quotient in all totally ramified degrees dividing the division degree, proves their exact Cartan heights and restricted Schwartz bounds for every field generator, and classifies every cubic cyclic-quotient orbit with its exact mass. Its integral dual-module argument includes inseparable cubic fields. Figure 14 and Exercise 7.22 compute the intermediate cubic orbits and the complete index-two count. Quotients with several positive lengths remain outside that restricted convergence estimate. Section 6.35 proves normalized opposite-algebra lattice duality with exact orbit masses and conjugate Cartan lists, and the complete dual-cyclic Schwartz subseries in every totally ramified degree dividing the division degree. It gives the cubic dual families, both cyclic orientations and the count of every cubic elementary quotient type in either characteristic. Over the specified characteristic-two cubic field it proves an intermediate-intersection stabilizer explicitly and classifies every normalized lattice through index four by an independent exact total count. Figure 15 and Exercise 7.23 compute the dual masses and finite cubic configurations. The complete rank-three estimate is Section 6.37. Section 6.36 proves exact normalized power heights in every totally ramified degree dividing the division degree and an exact extreme-Cartan identity for every totally ramified cubic field. Its integral right-module dual gives complete cubic cyclic-quotient orbit classifications and masses in every division rank, including noncommutative centralizers. It describes the dual families, counts every rank-three elementary quotient type, and proves that each equal-positive-length type is one orbit with its full subseries bound. Figure 16 and Exercise 7.24 compute quaternionic-centralizer masses and a wild separable characteristic-three uniformizer whose conjugation is not periodic. The unequal-length estimates in division rank three are Section 6.37. Section 6.37 proves the full ordinary Schwartz orbital bound in division rank three for every generator of every totally ramified field embedded in the division algebra. Its incidence count gives the exact uniformizer height distribution in all such degrees and the exponential saving for arbitrary generators. It proves the primary-partition traces and zeros, closed character germ and singular Steinberg coefficient orbital for this family, including wild and inseparable extensions. Figure 17 and Exercise 7.25 compute interior height counts in degrees three and four. Section 6.38 treats fields with nontrivial residue extension. Section 6.38 constructs an integral coefficient order for every field embedded in the division algebra. Finite least-length colors, compact coefficient-primitive frames and an actual top-cyclic incidence bound prove ordinary Schwartz convergence, polynomial tails and traces for every such closed orbit in division rank three. The primary-module dichotomy and the proper-flag bounds then cover every ordinary orbital in division ranks at most three, in both characteristics. It gives the residue-degree factor in the closed Euler and singular Steinberg values, the closed character germ, and a mixed inseparable example. Figure 18 and Exercise 7.26 distinguish ambient refinement counts from coefficient-normalized counts. General higher-rank noncompact closed orbitals, arbitrary-test character integration, individual transfer coefficients and the full local and global representation correspondences remain separate obligations. Section 6.39 proves Schwartz traces and zeros for every proper-flag orbit in division rank four, and gives every rank-four primary closed compact germ without assuming closed-orbit Schwartz convergence there. It proves finite real elliptic character expansions for every division rank at most four, and reality in the earlier finite-expansion ranges. Polynomial sublevel estimates give quantitative elliptic discriminant tails and compact finite-level trace approximants to their Gram matrices. Its exact complementary trace limit and uniform fixed-space integrability criterion distinguish those results from full elliptic orthogonality. Figures 19–20 and Exercise 7.27 give an inseparable quartic, a rank-four Cartan limit and explicit concentration and character-coefficient examples. Corollary 6.272 proves vanishing of the stated trace limits. Higher-rank noncompact closed orbitals, individual coefficient integrality and the full local and global representation transfers require further arguments. Section 6.40 proves smooth transfer of every division-group test to every inner form of the same degree, using central-covariant polynomial profiles and the Euler function. In division ranks at most four it gives the inverse profile and a canonical linear cocenter isomorphism, elliptic discrete-character independence and uniqueness of any such discrete-series transfer candidate. Its exact finite trace duality proves positive-definite elliptic Gram matrices and exact separation of finite packets by regular-support tests. Figures 21–22 and Exercise 7.28 display the normalization, matrix identities and complementary trace limits. Orthogonality and the transfer-test trace identity are Theorem 6.271 and Corollary 6.272. Coefficient integrality, representation-transfer existence and the general global correspondences require additional arguments. Section 6.41 gives a finite principal Jacquet model with exact Haar factors and proves compatibility of normalized constant terms with algebraic projective traces. A cubical resolution along the proper Levi central flat cancels identical projective modules, proving every proper ordinary orbital of compact Euler–Poincaré tests zero in every division rank and both characteristics. It gives all closed primary compact germs, finite real elliptic character expansions, the inverse linear cocenter map, elliptic independence and finite regular-support trace separation in every rank. Figures 23–24 and Exercise 7.29 display the finite flag normalization, central-flat cancellation and an inseparable rank-six example. General closed Schwartz convergence, individual coefficient integrality and full local and global representation transfer require additional arguments. The complementary-trace limit is Corollary 6.272. Sections 6.42–6.43 construct very cuspidal Euler representatives by rational finite flag characters, including Frobenius and cyclic graded pieces. Their conjugation kernels define continuous Schwartz traces. A uniform discriminant estimate on conjugation overlaps proves the cutoff limit and the elliptic pairing, giving the cuspidal trace identity, elliptic discrete-series orthogonality and actual vanishing of complementary transfer traces in every rank and both characteristics. Figures 25–26 and Exercise 7.30 display the finite cycles, kernel comparison and exact normalizations. Individual coefficient integrality, representation existence and completeness, general noncompact closed Schwartz estimates, arbitrary-test character integration and the full global correspondences require further arguments. Section 6.44 proves global Whittaker injectivity for smooth cuspidal functions on GLn over number fields and function fields, with a function-field additive-duality proof and compact successive Fourier integrals. It extracts local Whittaker functionals from a given tensor realization and constructs nonzero compact cuspidal Poincaré functions using one translated-unipotent-zero component and one shrinking auxiliary place. Figures 27–28 and Exercise 7.31 give the Fourier steps, rational-support isolation, trace-dual constants and the distinction between trace and operator zeros. Section 6.45 gives explicit row-section Haar densities, the regular mirabolic Hilbert decomposition, preferred smooth evaluation and its sharp principal-level norm bound. The central regular representation restricts to a mirabolic regular multiplicity by a projective-row calculation. A discrete-series coefficient embedding therefore gives a nonzero Whittaker functional for every split degree in both field characteristics. Figures 29–30 and Exercise 7.32 display the exact measures, functional maps, projective masses and the positive zero Fourier fibre in finite models. Whittaker multiplicity one and local generic trace isolation are separate assertions. A discrete-series globalization still needs spectral extraction and local generic trace isolation. Corollary 4.1 is deduced from the proved global theorem and earlier course results; the independent dimension calculation is not substituted for the theorem.

The following references specify the prerequisites and related treatments:

  • Local quadratic embedding: Voight, Corollary 13.4.5; Skolem–Noether and double centralizer: NOE-HYP-04, Theorems 2.1 and 3.1. The real quadratic embedding is explicit in \(\mathbb H\).
  • Local Jacquet–Langlands: Jacquet–Langlands, Theorem 15.1 and Proposition 15.5; Deligne, §3.2.8; positive characteristic: Badulescu, Theorem 1.1. The finite-place regular character theorem, recalled in Badulescu–Roche, §2.5 before Theorem 2.5, is proved here in Theorem 2.7. The real/tempered transfer formulation is Arthur, §25, Theorem 25.1. Theorem 2.14 and Corollary 2.15 prove the finite local bijection and paired formal degrees for the entire depth-zero family and all its determinant/norm twists; Proposition 2.12 proves the special case. Theorem 2.16 and Proposition 2.18 prove every compact-induction formal degree and both positive-level inducing volumes. Sections 2.8–2.10 prove all positive-level cases, their general correspondence, full elliptic character identity and the dimension identity (2.64), including primitive residue-characteristic-two types. Lemma 2.27 proves the full finite character distribution, not only its regular restriction. The real local bijection and formal degrees are proved in Section 2.2.
  • Finite-place smooth test transfer and scalar identity values are proved in Theorem 2.10 and Lemma 2.11 in every characteristic. Real smooth/scalar/spectral transfer and real arbitrary-test character integration are proved in Lemmas 2.19–2.21 and Theorem 2.22. Arthur, Theorem 25.1(a)–(b) and Lemma 25.2, gives a related treatment; Corollary 2.31 supplies the finite general spectral assertion using the full own character proof. The invariant comparison reference is Theorems 25.5–25.6 and equation (25.28). Our Theorem 3.4 proves the needed noncompact comparison through the piecewise truncated kernel and the exact Maass–Selberg identity; Theorem 3.5 combines it with the compact formula.
  • The full global discrete-spectrum theorem, with real ramification: Badulescu–Renard, §18.1, Theorem 18.1, with introductory Theorem 1.4, in the author preprint. Its residual-spectrum discussion is Proposition 18.2. Historical quaternion references are Jacquet–Langlands, Theorems 14.4 and 16.1, with the qualifications described in Section 3. The rational-field quaternion theorem used here is proved in Lemmas 3.2–3.3, Theorems 3.4–3.5 and Lemma 3.6. The higher-degree statement is given in Section 6; its general transfer proof is not established here.
  • Genus-zero \(X(1)\), branching and Riemann–Hurwitz: Modular curves and their genus, Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.2 and Section 3; holomorphic differentials and their dimension: Dimension formulas for congruence subgroups, Theorems 2.1 and 4.1. General Riemann–Hurwitz and Riemann–Roch are background theorems stated there.
  • Quaternion reciprocity, orders, ideal classes and the norm-count/Hecke rules: Lesson 17, Sections 2–5. The mass formula is proved in Lesson 17, Theorem 4.3; the full-norm Eichler expression and class-number evaluation were proved in Lesson 18, Theorem 5.3 and equation (6.3).
  • Classical/adelic and local fixed-line inputs: Lesson 2, Theorem 4.1; Lesson 8, Theorems 2.1, 3.2, 4.3 and 5.1; Lesson 11, Theorem 7.1; Lesson 13, Theorems 3.2 and 4.1. The discrete spectrum, global genericity and multiplicity inputs are Lessons 12, 14 and 15. The exceptional induction sequence used in (2.9) is Lesson 7, Theorem 4.2.
  • Higher-degree local transfer: Arthur, Theorem 25.1; Badulescu 2002, Theorem 1.1. Function-field global transfer and multiplicity one: Badulescu–Roche, Theorems 2.5, 3.2–3.3, with the central quotient explained in §§3.2–3.3. Hodge/cohomological realizations are discussed, rather than proved or used, in Ichino–Prasanna's introduction.

References

Free full text. The division-matrix primary modules, orbital densities and compact germs used here are proved in Section 6.26.

  • Guy Henniart and Marie-France Vignéras, Representations of GL_n(D) near the identity, arXiv:2305.06581v3 (10 October 2024), Remark 12.3(3), for a related rank-two near-identity character formula. Free author preprint. The apartment, cocenter, zero-germ and degree-ratio arguments used here are proved in Section 6.25.

  • Thomas J. Haines, Robert E. Kottwitz and Amritanshu Prasad, Iwahori-Hecke algebras, arXiv:math/0309168v3 (16 April 2009), Sections 1.1–1.3. Free author preprint. Section 6.24 gives the division-chain double cosets, convolution recurrences and projection construction used here.

  • Ralf Meyer, Homological algebra for Schwartz algebras of reductive p-adic groups, arXiv:math/0501548v2 (2 June 2005), Sections 4.2–6.1, Proposition 36, Theorems 39–41, Definitions 33–34 and Sections 7.2–7.4. Kottwitz, “Harmonic Analysis on Reductive p-adic Groups and Lie Algebras,” in Harmonic Analysis, the Trace Formula, and Shimura Varieties, Clay Mathematics Proceedings 4 (2005), 393–522, §§6.1–6.4 and Lemma 27.1. Pejhan, “Holomorphic Discrete Series of SU(1,1): Orthogonality Relations, Character Formulas, and Multiplicities in Tensor Product Decompositions,” 2025, Section II, equations (8)–(9), and Section IV, equation (22). Author preprint. The disk model and opposite rotation convention are discussed there; the trace-class argument is in Section 2.2.

  • R. Meyer and M. Solleveld, “Resolutions for representations of reductive p-adic groups via their buildings,” 2009 author preprint, Definition 2.1, Lemma 2.6, Theorems 2.4 and 2.12, and Proposition 4.1. Author PDF; arXiv record. Section 6.11 proves the all-rank division-lattice enclosure, face identities, finite support projections, cofinal convex exhaustions and uniform elliptic fixed-simplex finiteness; its finite alternating trace is distinguished from the character-density assertion.

  • W. Casselman, Introduction to admissible representations of p-adic groups, Chapter II, “Smooth representations,” revision of 16 June 2019, §§9–10, especially Proposition II.10.2 and Lemma II.10.4. Author notes. Section 6.5 proves its coefficient, formal-degree and finite trace-test assertions directly.

  • W. Casselman, Introduction to admissible representations of p-adic groups, Chapter III, “Induced representations and the Jacquet module,” revision of 29 April 2019, §§3–5, especially Lemmas III.5.2–III.5.4. Casselman, Introduction to the Theory of Admissible Representations of p-adic Reductive Groups, draft of 1 May 1995, §§4.1–4.4, especially Proposition 4.2.3, Theorem 4.2.4, Corollary 4.2.5, Theorems 4.3.3 and 4.4.6, and §§5.2–5.3.
